abstract: Error propagation nets have been shown to be able to learn a variety of tasks in which a static input pattern is mapped outo a static output pattern. This paper presents a generalisation of these nets to deal with time varying, or dynamic patterns, and three possible architectures are explored. As an example, dynamic nets are applied to tbe problem of speech coding, in which a time sequence of speech data are coded by one net and decoded by another. The use of dynamic nets gives a better signal to noise ratio than that achieved using static nets.

paragraphs: The paper extends error-propagation networks from fixed patterns to patterns that vary over time. In the static setting, a network learns a mapping between an input pattern and an output pattern. The dynamic setting makes a time-varying pattern itself the subject of the learned mapping, which is especially relevant to speech.

The authors explore three possible architectures for this extension. They apply dynamic networks to speech coding using a pair of networks: one encodes a sequence of speech data, and another decodes it. This creates a concrete task in which the learned transformation must support reconstruction of a signal unfolding over time.

The reported result is a better signal-to-noise ratio with dynamic networks than with static networks. That means the reconstructed speech signal has a stronger signal relative to noise under the reported comparison. The contribution is both an architectural generalization of error propagation and an application showing that treating speech as a dynamic pattern can improve coding quality.
summary.tldr: Dynamic error-propagation networks encode and decode speech sequences with a better signal-to-noise ratio than static networks.

title: Static and Dynamic Error Propagation Networks with Application to Speech Coding

abstract: Recent experimental work on the stimulus velocity dependent time resolving power of the neural units, situated in the highest order optic ganglion of the blowfly, revealed the at first sight amazing phenomenon that at this high level of the fly visual system, the time constants of these units which are involved in the processing of neural activity evoked by moving objects, are -roughly spoken(cid:173) inverse proportional to the velocity of those objects over an extremely wide range. In this paper we will discuss the implementation of a two dimensional heterodyne adaptive filter construction into a computer simulation model. The features of this simulation model include the ability to account for the experimentally observed stimulus-tuned adaptive temporal behaviour of time constants in the fly visual system. The simulation results obtained, clearly show that the application of such an adaptive processing procedure delivers an improved imaging technique of moving patterns in the high velocity range. A FEW REMARKS ON THE FLY VISUAL SYSTEM

paragraphs: The paper starts from an observation about motion processing in the blowfly visual system. Neural units in a high-level optic ganglion change their temporal response according to object speed: over a wide range, their time constants are approximately inversely proportional to velocity. Faster motion therefore corresponds to shorter response times.

The authors implement a two-dimensional adaptive heterodyne filter in a computer simulation. The model is designed to account for this stimulus-dependent adjustment of temporal behavior. Its key connection to the biological observation is that the processing timescale adapts to the moving input, allowing the modeled response to vary with the speed being processed.

The simulations show improved imaging of moving patterns at high velocities when this adaptive procedure is applied. The result links a measured property of the fly's visual system to a useful image-processing method. The paper's contribution is both an account of adaptive neural timing and a demonstration that incorporating such timing into a filter can improve the handling of rapidly moving patterns.
summary.tldr: A simulated adaptive heterodyne filter models speed-dependent fly visual responses and improves imaging of rapidly moving patterns.

title: An Adaptive and Heterodyne Filtering Procedure for the Imaging of Moving Objects

abstract: A novel learning control architecture is used for navigation. A sophisti(cid:173) cated test-bed is used to simulate a cylindrical robot with a sonar belt in a planar environment. The task is short-range homing in the pres(cid:173) ence of obstacles. The robot receives no global information and assumes no comprehensive world model. Instead the robot receives only sensory information which is inherently limited. A connectionist architecture is presented which incorporates a large amount of a priori knowledge in the form of hard-wired networks, architectural constraints, and initial weights. Instead of hard-wiring static potential fields from object models, myarchi(cid:173) tecture learns sensor-based potential fields, automatically adjusting them to avoid local minima and to produce efficient homing trajectories. It does this without object models using only sensory information. This research demonstrates the use of a large modular architecture on a difficult task.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a robot can find its way toward a nearby goal while avoiding obstacles using limited sensory information. The test environment simulates a cylindrical robot equipped with a belt of sonar sensors moving in a plane. The robot has neither global information nor a comprehensive model of its surroundings, so navigation must depend on what its sensors reveal.

The proposed controller combines learning with substantial knowledge built into its design. That knowledge appears in fixed networks, architectural restrictions, and initial connection weights. Its central mechanism is a learned, sensor-based potential field: sensory readings help shape the guidance that directs movement toward the goal and around obstacles.

Learning adjusts these fields to avoid local minima, situations where the guidance can trap the robot instead of advancing it toward its destination. The abstract reports efficient homing trajectories without requiring object models. The contribution is a demonstration that a large, modular neural architecture can combine prior structure with adaptation to address a navigation task under restricted perception.
summary.tldr: A modular neural controller learns sensor-based guidance for obstacle-avoiding navigation without a comprehensive world model.

title: A Connectionist Learning Control Architecture for Navigation

abstract: HARMONET, a system employing connectionist networks for music pro(cid:173) cessing, is presented. After being trained on some dozen Bach chorales using error backpropagation, the system is capable of producing four-part chorales in the style of J .s.Bach, given a one-part melody. Our system solves a musical real-world problem on a performance level appropriate for musical practice. HARMONET's power is based on (a) a new coding scheme capturing musically relevant information and (b) the integration of backpropagation and symbolic algorithms in a hierarchical system, com(cid:173) bining the advantages of both.

paragraphs: HARMONET is a system that expands a single melody into a four-part chorale in the style of J. S. Bach. The authors train its neural networks using error backpropagation on roughly a dozen Bach chorales. The task is musical production: the system must generate a harmonized piece from the supplied melodic line.

The authors attribute its capabilities to two design choices. First, a new representation captures musically relevant information. Second, a hierarchical architecture combines backpropagation-trained networks with symbolic algorithms. The representation determines what musical information is available to the learning system, while the hierarchy brings learned processing and explicit symbolic procedures into one solution.

The paper reports performance suitable for musical practice. This is a claim about completing the harmonization task in a useful musical form, rather than merely recognizing patterns in existing compositions. The broader contribution is an example of how a neural system’s practical abilities can depend on its input coding and its integration with other algorithms, alongside learning from examples.
summary.tldr: HARMONET combines neural learning, musical representations, and symbolic algorithms to turn a melody into a Bach-style four-part chorale.

title: HARMONET: A Neural Net for Harmonizing Chorales in the Style of J. S. Bach

abstract: A model of the hippocampus as a central element in rat naviga(cid:173) tion is presented. Simulations show both the behaviour of single cells and the resultant navigation of the rat. These are compared with single unit recordings and behavioural data. The firing of CAl place cells is simulated as the (artificial) rat moves in an en(cid:173) vironment. This is the input for a neuronal network whose output, at each theta (0) cycle, is the next direction of travel for the rat. Cells are characterised by the number of spikes fired and the time of firing with respect to hippocampal 0 rhythm. 'Learning' occurs in 'on-off' synapses that are switched on by simultaneous pre- and post-synaptic activity. The simulated rat navigates successfully to goals encountered one or more times during exploration in open fields. One minute of random exploration of a 1m2 environment allows navigation to a newly-presented goal from novel starting po(cid:173) sitions. A limited number of obstacles can be successfully avoided.

paragraphs: This paper models how hippocampal place-cell activity could support rat navigation. Simulated CA1 cells provide input to a neural network that chooses the next travel direction on each theta cycle. Each cell is described by both its spike count and its firing time relative to the hippocampal theta rhythm, so timing contributes to the representation.

Learning uses on-off synapses that become active when presynaptic and postsynaptic activity occur together. The simulations track both individual-cell behavior and the resulting movement of the artificial rat. The authors compare these with single-unit recordings and behavioral data, connecting the proposed cellular mechanism to navigation at the level of the whole animal.

The simulated rat reaches goals encountered during open-field exploration. One minute of random exploration in a one-square-meter environment supports navigation to a newly presented goal from unfamiliar starting positions. The model also avoids a limited number of obstacles. These findings demonstrate navigation using the specified spike-timing representation and simple synaptic learning rule within the tested environments.
summary.tldr: A place-cell navigation model uses spike timing and simple synaptic learning to reach goals from unfamiliar starting positions.

title: Using hippocampal 'place cells' for navigation, exploiting phase coding

abstract: In this paper we consider speech coding as a problem of speech modelling. In particular, prediction of parameterised speech over short time segments is performed using the Hierarchical Mixture of Experts (HME) (Jordan & Jacobs 1994). The HME gives two ad(cid:173) vantages over traditional non-linear function approximators such as the Multi-Layer Percept ron (MLP); a statistical understand(cid:173) ing of the operation of the predictor and provision of information about the performance of the predictor in the form of likelihood information and local error bars. These two issues are examined on both toy and real world problems of regression and time series prediction. In the speech coding context, we extend the principle of combining local predictions via the HME to a Vector Quantiza(cid:173) tion scheme in which fixed local codebooks are combined on-line for each observation.

paragraphs: The paper approaches speech coding through the problem of modeling speech. It uses a hierarchical mixture of experts to predict parameterized speech over short time intervals. The model combines local predictions, making the predictor’s organization part of its statistical description rather than treating prediction solely as an input-output calculation.

The authors emphasize two advantages over traditional nonlinear approximators such as multilayer perceptrons: a statistical account of how the predictor operates and information about its performance through likelihoods and local error bars. These outputs describe more than a predicted value. They provide a way to examine how well the model accounts for observations and how uncertainty varies locally.

The paper studies these properties on synthetic and real regression and time-series problems. It also extends the local-combination principle to vector quantization for speech coding. In that scheme, fixed local codebooks are combined online for each observation. This carries the mixture approach from predicting acoustic vectors into adapting the representation used to encode them.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical mixtures of experts provide speech predictions with local uncertainty information and motivate observation-dependent combinations of quantization codebooks.

title: Non-linear Prediction of Acoustic Vectors Using Hierarchical Mixtures of Experts

abstract: The mathematical framework for factorizing equivalence classes of multivariate functions is formulated in this paper. Independent component analysis is shown to be a special case of this decompo(cid:173) sition. Using only the local geometric structure of a class repre(cid:173) sentative, we derive an analytic solution for the factorization. We demonstrate the factorization solution with numerical experiments and present a preliminary tie to decorrelation.

Independent component analysis is shown to be a special case of this decompo(cid:173) sition. Using only the local geometric structure of a class repre(cid:173) sentative, we derive an analytic solution for the factorization. We demonstrate the factorization solution with numerical experiments and present a preliminary tie to decorrelation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical framework for decomposing equivalence classes of functions with several variables. The object being factorized is therefore a class of related functions, with an individual representative providing information about that class. The central question is how to uncover a component structure from the mathematical properties of such a representative.

The authors derive an analytic factorization solution using only local geometric structure. This makes the relationship between local information and the larger decomposition the core of the method. They also show that independent component analysis fits inside their framework as a special case, connecting a familiar decomposition problem to a more general mathematical treatment.

Numerical experiments demonstrate the factorization solution, and the paper offers a preliminary connection to decorrelation. That connection is presented as an initial link rather than a completed equivalence. The contribution combines a general formulation with an analytic solution, showing how an established component-analysis problem can be understood within a broader class of factorizations.
summary.tldr: A general factorization framework derives an analytic solution from local geometry and includes independent component analysis as a special case.

title: Factorizing Multivariate Function Classes

abstract: Cortical amplification has been proposed as a mechanism for enhancing the selectivity of neurons in the primary visual cortex. Less appreciated is the fact that the same form of amplification can also be used to de-tune or broaden selectivity. Using a network model with recurrent cortical circuitry, we propose that the spatial phase invariance of complex cell responses arises through recurrent amplification of feedforward input. Neurons in the network respond like simple cells at low gain and com(cid:173) plex ceUs at high gain. Similar recurrent mechanisms may playa role in generating invariant representations of feedforward input elsewhere in the visual processing pathway.

Less appreciated is the fact that the same form of amplification can also be used to de-tune or broaden selectivity. Using a network model with recurrent cortical circuitry, we propose that the spatial phase invariance of complex cell responses arises through recurrent amplification of feedforward input. Neurons in the network respond like simple cells at low gain and com(cid:173) plex ceUs at high gain. Similar recurrent mechanisms may playa role in generating invariant representations of feedforward input elsewhere in the visual processing pathway.

paragraphs: This paper examines how recurrent circuitry could produce the spatial-phase invariance associated with complex cells in visual cortex. Spatial-phase invariance means a response is less sensitive to the precise spatial alignment of the input pattern. The authors propose that recurrent amplification of feedforward input can generate this property within a network model.

The key observation is that amplification can broaden selectivity as well as sharpen it. In the proposed network, neurons show simple-cell-like responses at low gain and complex-cell-like responses at high gain. Changing the strength of amplification therefore changes the response pattern expressed by the modeled neurons, connecting the two behaviors through the same recurrent mechanism.

The finding gives recurrent amplification a possible role in generating invariance, alongside its proposed role in enhancing selectivity. The authors also suggest that similar mechanisms may contribute to invariant representations elsewhere in visual processing. That broader application remains a possibility; the concrete result described here is the gain-dependent transition between simple- and complex-cell-like responses in the network model.
summary.tldr: A recurrent visual-cortex model shifts from simple-cell-like to complex-cell-like responses as amplification gain increases.

title: Recurrent Cortical Amplification Produces Complex Cell Responses

abstract: Two developments of nonlinear latent variable models based on radial basis functions are discussed: in the first, the use of priors or constraints on allowable models is considered as a means of preserving data structure in low-dimensional representations for visualisation purposes. Also, a resampling approach is introduced which makes more effective use of the latent samples in evaluating the likelihood.
originalAbstract: Two developments of nonlinear latent variable models based on radial basis functions are discussed: in the first, the use of priors or constraints on allowable models is considered as a means of preserving data structure in low-dimensional representations for visualisation purposes. Also, a resampling approach is introduced which makes more effective use of the latent samples in evaluating the likelihood.

paragraphs: The paper develops two aspects of nonlinear latent variable models built with radial basis functions. These models provide a setting for representing data through latent variables, including low-dimensional representations intended for visualization. The work addresses both what kinds of representations the model should permit and how its likelihood can be evaluated using latent samples.

The first development considers priors or constraints on the allowable models as a way to preserve data structure in a low-dimensional view. A visualization is useful when its arrangement retains meaningful structure from the data. Restricting or favoring particular models provides a way to bring that objective into the construction of the representation.

The second development introduces a resampling approach that makes more effective use of latent samples during likelihood evaluation. It concerns the computation used to assess the model, complementing the first development's concern with representational structure. Together, the two contributions address the quality of the visual representation and the use of samples in evaluating the nonlinear latent variable model.
summary.tldr: The paper develops structure-preserving model constraints and more effective likelihood resampling for radial basis function latent variable models.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis Using Radial Basis Function Latent Variable Models

abstract: When applying unsupervised learning techniques like ICA or tem(cid:173) poral decorrelation, a key question is whether the discovered pro(cid:173) jections are reliable. In other words: can we give error bars or can we assess the quality of our separation? We use resampling meth(cid:173) ods to tackle these questions and show experimentally that our proposed variance estimations are strongly correlated to the sepa(cid:173) ration error. We demonstrate that this reliability estimation can be used to choose the appropriate ICA-model, to enhance signifi(cid:173) cantly the separation performance, and, most important, to mark the components that have a actual physical meaning. Application to 49-channel-data from an magneto encephalography (MEG) ex(cid:173) periment underlines the usefulness of our approach.

paragraphs: Unsupervised methods such as independent component analysis can discover projections that separate observed data into components. A further question is whether those projections are reliable. This paper addresses that question by estimating uncertainty, aiming to provide information analogous to error bars and to assess the quality of the resulting separation.

The authors use resampling methods to estimate variance in the discovered projections. Experimentally, their variance estimates are strongly correlated with separation error. That relationship is useful because it connects an uncertainty measure to the quality of the separation, giving the reliability estimate a practical interpretation beyond simply describing variation across resampled data.

The paper demonstrates uses of reliability estimation for choosing an ICA model, substantially improving separation performance, and identifying components with physical meaning. An application to 49-channel magnetoencephalography data illustrates its usefulness on a neural recording problem. The contribution is thus both an uncertainty estimate and a demonstration that the estimate can guide model selection and interpretation of extracted components.
summary.tldr: Resampling-based reliability estimates correlate with ICA separation error and help select models and identify meaningful components.

title: Estimating the Reliability of ICA Projections

abstract: Pairwise data in empirical sciences typically violate metricity, ei(cid:173) ther due to noise or due to fallible estimates, and therefore are hard to analyze by conventional machine learning technology. In this paper we therefore study ways to work around this problem. First, we present an alternative embedding to multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) that allows us to apply a variety of classical ma(cid:173) chine learning and signal processing algorithms. The class of pair(cid:173) wise grouping algorithms which share the shift-invariance property is statistically invariant under this embedding procedure, leading to identical assignments of objects to clusters. Based on this new vectorial representation, denoising methods are applied in a sec(cid:173) ond step. Both steps provide a theoretically well controlled setup to translate from pairwise data to the respective denoised met(cid:173) ric representation. We demonstrate the practical usefulness of our theoretical reasoning by discovering structure in protein sequence data bases, visibly improving performance upon existing automatic methods.

paragraphs: Scientific datasets often describe relationships between pairs of objects rather than giving each object a conventional feature vector. Noise or unreliable estimates can make those relationships violate metric properties, complicating their use with standard learning methods. This paper develops a two-stage route from such pairwise measurements to a denoised metric representation.

First, the authors propose a vector embedding as an alternative to multidimensional scaling. This representation makes classical machine-learning and signal-processing tools available. It also preserves cluster assignments for a particular class of pairwise grouping algorithms: those with the stated shift-invariance property. That qualification matters because the preservation result is tied to this algorithmic property.

Second, denoising methods operate on the new vector representation. The authors provide theoretical control over both stages, connecting the original pairwise data to the cleaned metric form. They demonstrate the approach by finding structure in protein sequence databases and report visibly improved performance over existing automatic methods. The work thus links a representation argument to a practical denoising application.
summary.tldr: A vector embedding followed by denoising converts problematic pairwise data into a metric representation with useful preservation properties.

title: Going Metric: Denoising Pairwise Data

abstract: The problem of super-resolution involves generating feasible higher resolution images, which are pleasing to the eye and realistic, from a given low resolution image. This might be attempted by us- ing simple (cid:12)lters for smoothing out the high resolution blocks or through applications where substantial prior information is used to imply the textures and shapes which will occur in the images. In this paper we describe an approach which lies between the two extremes. It is a generic unsupervised method which is usable in all domains, but goes beyond simple smoothing methods in what it achieves. We use a dynamic tree-like architecture to model the high resolution data. Approximate conditioning on the low resolution image is achieved through a mean (cid:12)eld approach.

This might be attempted by us- ing simple (cid:12)lters for smoothing out the high resolution blocks or through applications where substantial prior information is used to imply the textures and shapes which will occur in the images. In this paper we describe an approach which lies between the two extremes. paragraphs: Super-resolution aims to produce a plausible, visually realistic higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution one. The paper places its approach between two alternatives: smoothing enlarged image blocks and using substantial prior knowledge about the textures and shapes expected in a particular application. It seeks more structure than simple smoothing while retaining broad applicability.

The proposed method is unsupervised and models high-resolution image data with a dynamic tree-like architecture. This architecture supplies the model of image structure used to generate a feasible detailed image. The abstract presents the approach as generic and usable across domains, rather than dependent on extensive application-specific information.

To connect the high-resolution model to the observed low-resolution image, the method uses mean-field approximation for conditioning. This is the step that brings the available image evidence into the generation process. The contribution is a middle route for super-resolution: a structured statistical model intended to go beyond smoothing without requiring rich knowledge of a particular image category. Its conditioning procedure is explicitly approximate.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised dynamic tree model uses approximate conditioning to generate plausible higher-resolution images beyond simple smoothing.

title: Dynamic Structure Super-Resolution

abstract: We develop and test new machine learning methods for the predic- tion of topological representations of protein structures in the form of coarse- or (cid:12)ne-grained contact or distance maps that are transla- tion and rotation invariant. The methods are based on generalized input-output hidden Markov models (GIOHMMs) and generalized recursive neural networks (GRNNs). The methods are used to pre- dict topology directly in the (cid:12)ne-grained case and, in the coarse- grained case, indirectly by (cid:12)rst learning how to score candidate graphs and then using the scoring function to search the space of possible con(cid:12)gurations. Computer simulations show that the pre- dictors achieve state-of-the-art performance. 1 Introduction: Protein Topology Prediction Predicting the 3D structure of protein chains from the linear sequence of amino acids is a fundamental open problem in computational molecular biology [1]. Any approach to the problem must deal with the basic fact that protein structures are translation and rotation invariant. To address this invariance, we have proposed a machine learning approach to protein structure prediction [4] based on the predic- tion of topological representations of proteins, in the form of contact or distance maps. The contact or distance map is a 2D representation of neighborhood rela- tionships consisting of an adjacency matrix at some distance cuto(cid:11) (typically in the range of 6 to 12 (cid:23)A), or a matrix of pairwise Euclidean distances. Fine-grained maps are derived at the amino acid or even atomic level. Coarse maps are obtained by looking at secondary structure elements, such as helices, and the distance between their centers of gravity or, as in the simulations below, the minimal distances be- tween their C(cid:11) atoms. Reasonable methods for reconstructing 3D coordinates from contact/distance maps have been developed in the NMR literature and elsewhere

paragraphs: The paper predicts protein structure through contact or distance maps, which describe relationships between parts of a protein. These representations stay the same when the protein is translated or rotated. A contact map records neighborhood relationships, while a distance map records pairwise distances, allowing the prediction target to express structure without depending on spatial orientation.

The methods use generalized input-output hidden Markov models and generalized recursive neural networks. For fine-grained representations, topology is predicted directly at the amino-acid or atomic scale. For coarse representations built from secondary-structure elements, the method first learns to score candidate graphs, then uses that scoring function to search possible configurations.

Computer simulations report state-of-the-art predictive performance. The two prediction routes adapt the learning strategy to the chosen structural resolution: direct map prediction for fine detail and learned scoring with search for coarser arrangements. The contribution concerns predicting topological representations that capture structural relationships. Its use of invariant targets addresses the fact that a protein's structure should not depend on where it is placed or how it is turned.
summary.tldr: Generalized hidden Markov models and recursive neural networks predict invariant protein contact or distance maps, with reported state-of-the-art simulation results.

title: Prediction of Protein Topologies Using Generalized IOHMMs and RNNs

abstract: Decoding is a strategy that allows us to assess the amount of information neurons can provide about certain aspects of the visual scene. In this study, we develop a method based on Bayesian sequential updating and the particle ﬁltering algorithm to decode the activity of V1 neurons in awake monkeys. A distinction in our method is the use of Volterra ker- nels to ﬁlter the particles, which live in a high dimensional space. This parametric Bayesian decoding scheme is compared to the optimal linear decoder and is shown to work consistently better than the linear optimal decoder. Interestingly, our results suggest that for decoding in real time, spike trains of as few as 10 independent but similar neurons would be sufﬁcient for decoding a critical scene variable in a particular class of visual stimuli. The reconstructed variable can predict the neural activity about as well as the actual signal with respect to the Volterra kernels.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much information about a visual scene can be recovered from the activity of V1 neurons in awake monkeys. Decoding turns recorded neural responses into an estimate of a scene variable, making it possible to assess what those responses reveal about the visual input.

The authors develop a parametric Bayesian decoder that updates its estimates sequentially using particle filtering. Its distinguishing feature is the use of Volterra kernels to filter particles in a high-dimensional space. The method therefore combines sequential probabilistic estimation with the specified relationship between the visual signal and neural activity. In the reported comparisons, it consistently performs better than the optimal linear decoder.

The results suggest that real-time decoding of a critical variable could require as few as ten independent, similar neurons for a particular class of stimuli. This is a conditional finding about that setting. The reconstructed variable also predicts neural activity about as well as the actual signal when assessed through the Volterra kernels, supporting the reconstruction's relevance to the modeled neural responses.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian particle-filter decoder outperforms an optimal linear decoder and suggests that a small population of similar, independent V1 neurons could support real-time decoding.

title: Decoding V1 Neuronal Activity using Particle Filtering with Volterra Kernels

abstract: Stimulus selectivity of sensory neurons is often characterized by estimating their receptive field properties such as orientation selectivity. Receptive fields are usually derived from the mean (or covariance) of the spike-triggered stimulus ensemble. This approach treats each spike as an independent message but does not take into account that information might be conveyed through patterns of neural activity that are distributed across space or time. Can we find a concise description for the processing of a whole population of neurons analogous to the receptive field for single neurons? Here, we present a generalization of the linear receptive field which is not bound to be triggered on individual spikes but can be meaningfully linked to distributed response patterns. More precisely, we seek to identify those stimulus features and the corresponding patterns of neural activity that are most reliably coupled. We use an extension of reverse-correlation methods based on canonical correlation analysis. The resulting population receptive fields span the subspace of stimuli that is most informative about the population response. We evaluate our approach using both neuronal models and multi-electrode recordings from rabbit retinal ganglion cells. We show how the model can be extended to capture nonlinear stimulus-response relationships using kernel canonical correlation analysis, which makes it possible to test different coding mechanisms. Our technique can also be used to calculate receptive fields from multi-dimensional neural measurements such as those obtained from dynamic imaging methods.

This paper broadens that view to activity patterns distributed across neurons or time, asking for a concise description of stimulus processing by an entire population.

The method extends reverse correlation using canonical correlation analysis. It identifies stimulus features and neural response patterns that are most reliably coupled. The contribution is a shared framework for linking stimulus structure to distributed neural activity.
summary.tldr: Population receptive fields link stimulus features to distributed neural activity through canonical correlation analysis, with a kernel extension for nonlinear relationships.

title: Receptive Fields without Spike-Triggering

abstract: We propose a randomized algorithm for large scale SVM learning which solves the problem by iterating over random subsets of the data. Crucial to the algorithm for scalability is the size of the subsets chosen. In the context of text classification we show that, by using ideas from random projections, a sample size of O(log n) can be used to obtain a solution which is close to the optimal with a high probability. Experiments done on synthetic and real life data sets demonstrate that the algorithm scales up SVM learners, without loss in accuracy.

In the context of text classification we show that, by using ideas from random projections, a sample size of O(log n) can be used to obtain a solution which is close to the optimal with a high probability. paragraphs: Training a support vector machine on a large dataset can make the amount of data processed at each step a central computational concern. This paper proposes a randomized learning algorithm that repeatedly works with randomly selected subsets of the data. Its scalability depends especially on how large those subsets need to be.

The theoretical contribution addresses that question in the context of text classification. Using ideas from random projections, the authors show that a sample size growing as O(log n) can produce a solution close to the optimum with high probability. This connects the computational shortcut to a probabilistic approximation guarantee, rather than relying only on the intuition that a small sample might be representative.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate improved scalability without loss of accuracy in the reported evaluations. Together, the theory and experiments support using small randomized subsets to make SVM learning more manageable. The near-optimality guarantee is stated for the text-classification setting, while the experimental results provide evidence about the algorithm’s practical behavior.
summary.tldr: Randomized training on small data subsets scales SVM learning, with a high-probability near-optimality result for text classification.

title: A Randomized Algorithm for Large Scale Support Vector Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of multiple kernel learning (MKL), which can be formulated as a convex-concave problem. In the past, two efficient methods, i.e., Semi-Infinite Linear Programming (SILP) and Subgradient Descent (SD), have been proposed for large-scale multiple kernel learning. Despite their success, both methods have their own shortcomings: (a) the SD method utilizes the gradient of only the current solution, and (b) the SILP method does not regularize the approximate solution obtained from the cutting plane model. In this work, we extend the level method, which was originally designed for optimizing non-smooth objective functions, to convex-concave optimization, and apply it to multiple kernel learning. The extended level method overcomes the drawbacks of SILP and SD by exploiting all the gradients computed in past iterations and by regularizing the solution via a projection to a level set. Empirical study with eight UCI datasets shows that the extended level method can significantly improve efficiency by saving on average 91.9% of computational time over the SILP method and 70.3% over the SD method.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning involves an optimization problem with a convex-concave structure. The paper targets the computational cost of solving it, focusing on two existing approaches: subgradient descent and semi-infinite linear programming. Both are useful for large problems, but the authors identify different weaknesses in how they construct and update candidate solutions.

Subgradient descent uses the gradient at the current solution without exploiting the full collection of earlier gradients. Semi-infinite linear programming builds a cutting-plane approximation but does not regularize the approximate solution it produces. The proposed method extends a level method for nonsmooth optimization to address both issues within the convex-concave setting.

The algorithm retains information from previously computed gradients and regularizes its solution through projection onto a level set. On eight UCI datasets, it saves an average of 91.9% of computational time relative to semi-infinite linear programming and 70.3% relative to subgradient descent. These are empirical efficiency gains on the evaluated datasets, supporting the value of combining accumulated gradient information with controlled solution updates.
summary.tldr: An extended level method accelerates multiple kernel learning by reusing past gradients and regularizing updates through level-set projection.

title: An Extended Level Method for Efficient Multiple Kernel Learning

abstract: The concave-convex procedure (CCCP) is a majorization-minimization algorithm that solves d.c. (difference of convex functions) programs as a sequence of convex programs. In machine learning, CCCP is extensively used in many learning algorithms like sparse support vector machines (SVMs), transductive SVMs, sparse principal component analysis, etc. Though widely used in many applications, the convergence behavior of CCCP has not gotten a lot of specific attention. Yuille and Rangarajan analyzed its convergence in their original paper, however, we believe the analysis is not complete. Although the convergence of CCCP can be derived from the convergence of the d.c. algorithm (DCA), their proof is more specialized and technical than actually required for the specific case of CCCP. In this paper, we follow a different reasoning and show how Zangwills global convergence theory of iterative algorithms provides a natural framework to prove the convergence of CCCP, allowing a more elegant and simple proof. This underlines Zangwills theory as a powerful and general framework to deal with the convergence issues of iterative algorithms, after also being used to prove the convergence of algorithms like expectation-maximization, generalized alternating minimization, etc. In this paper, we provide a rigorous analysis of the convergence of CCCP by addressing these questions: (i) When does CCCP find a local minimum or a stationary point of the d.c. program under consideration? (ii) When does the sequence generated by CCCP converge? We also present an open problem on the issue of local convergence of CCCP.

paragraphs: The concave-convex procedure solves problems whose objectives are differences of convex functions by repeatedly solving convex subproblems. It is used in methods including sparse and transductive support vector machines and sparse principal component analysis. The paper examines what can rigorously be concluded about the behavior of this iterative process.

The authors argue that the original convergence analysis is incomplete and that deriving the result from the broader difference-of-convex algorithm uses more specialized machinery than CCCP requires. They instead apply Zangwill's general convergence theory for iterative algorithms, obtaining a simpler framework for the proof.

The analysis addresses when CCCP reaches a local minimum or stationary point and when the generated sequence itself converges. These are distinct questions: characterizing possible limiting solutions and establishing convergence of the sequence require separate attention. The paper also identifies an open question about local convergence. Its contribution clarifies convergence reasoning for a widely used procedure without claiming that CCCP universally finds a global optimum.
summary.tldr: The paper uses Zangwill's convergence theory to rigorously analyze when CCCP approaches stationary solutions and when its iterates converge.

title: On the Convergence of the Concave-Convex Procedure

abstract: Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) model sequential decision-making problems under uncertainty and partial observability. Unfortunately, some problems cannot be modeled with state-dependent reward functions, e.g., problems whose objective explicitly implies reducing the uncertainty on the state. To that end, we introduce rho-POMDPs, an extension of POMDPs where the reward function rho depends on the belief state. We show that, under the common assumption that rho is convex, the value function is also convex, what makes it possible to (1) approximate rho arbitrarily well with a piecewise linear and convex (PWLC) function, and (2) use state-of-the-art exact or approximate solving algorithms with limited changes.
originalAbstract: Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) model sequential decision-making problems under uncertainty and partial observability. Unfortunately, some problems cannot be modeled with state-dependent reward functions, e.g., problems whose objective explicitly implies reducing the uncertainty on the state. To that end, we introduce rho-POMDPs, an extension of POMDPs where the reward function rho depends on the belief state. We show that, under the common assumption that rho is convex, the value function is also convex, what makes it possible to (1) approximate rho arbitrarily well with a piecewise linear and convex (PWLC) function, and (2) use state-of-the-art exact or approximate solving algorithms with limited changes.

paragraphs: A decision maker may care both about what happens and about how much uncertainty remains. Standard partially observable Markov decision processes describe decisions when the underlying state cannot be observed directly. However, rewards tied to that underlying state cannot express some objectives that explicitly reward reducing uncertainty.

The paper introduces rho-POMDPs, in which rewards depend on the belief state: the decision maker’s current distribution of possibilities about the hidden state. This makes the current state of knowledge part of what an action can improve. An information-seeking objective can therefore be represented directly within the reward function.

The main result assumes that the belief-dependent reward is convex and establishes that the value function is convex too. Under this assumption, the reward can be approximated arbitrarily closely by a piecewise linear, convex function. This structure allows existing exact and approximate POMDP solvers to be adapted with limited changes, connecting the richer objective to established computational methods.
summary.tldr: Belief-dependent rewards extend POMDPs to uncertainty-reduction objectives while retaining useful convex structure under a convexity assumption.

title: A POMDP Extension with Belief-dependent Rewards

abstract: We propose a simple and novel framework for MCMC inference in continuous-time discrete-state systems with pure jump trajectories. We construct an exact MCMC sampler for such systems by alternately sampling a random discretization of time given a trajectory of the system, and then a new trajectory given the discretization. The first step can be performed efficiently using properties of the Poisson process, while the second step can avail of discrete-time MCMC techniques based on the forward-backward algorithm. We compare our approach to particle MCMC and a uniformization-based sampler, and show its advantages.
originalAbstract: We propose a simple and novel framework for MCMC inference in continuous-time discrete-state systems with pure jump trajectories. We construct an exact MCMC sampler for such systems by alternately sampling a random discretization of time given a trajectory of the system, and then a new trajectory given the discretization. The first step can be performed efficiently using properties of the Poisson process, while the second step can avail of discrete-time MCMC techniques based on the forward-backward algorithm. We compare our approach to particle MCMC and a uniformization-based sampler, and show its advantages.

paragraphs: Some systems occupy discrete states but change state at times that can occur anywhere along a continuous timeline. This paper studies inference for such systems when their trajectories consist of jumps between states. It proposes an exact Markov chain Monte Carlo framework that connects continuous-time trajectories with computations performed on a sampled discretization of time.

The sampler alternates between two conditional steps. First, it samples a random time discretization given the current trajectory, using properties of the Poisson process to do so efficiently. Second, it samples a new trajectory given that discretization. This second step can use discrete-time MCMC techniques based on the forward-backward algorithm.

The discretization is therefore part of the sampling procedure and changes with the trajectory. That construction allows the authors to retain an exact MCMC formulation while using discrete-time computational tools. They compare their approach with particle MCMC and a uniformization-based sampler and report advantages. The main contribution is a simple alternating framework that makes established discrete-time inference techniques useful for continuous-time jump systems.
summary.tldr: An exact MCMC sampler alternates random time discretizations and trajectories to infer continuous-time systems with discrete states.

title: MCMC for continuous-time discrete-state systems

abstract: We study the problem of adaptive control of a high dimensional linear quadratic (LQ) system. Previous work established the asymptotic convergence to an optimal controller for various adaptive control schemes. More recently, an asymptotic regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ was shown for $T \gg p$ where $p$ is the dimension of the state space. In this work we consider the case where the matrices describing the dynamic of the LQ system are sparse and their dimensions are large. We present an adaptive control scheme that for $p \gg 1$ and $T \gg \polylog(p)$ achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(p \sqrt{T})$. In particular, our algorithm has an average cost of $(1+\eps)$ times the optimum cost after $T = \polylog(p) O(1/\eps^2)$. This is in comparison to previous work on the dense dynamics where the algorithm needs $\Omega(p)$ samples before it can estimate the unknown dynamic with any significant accuracy. We believe our result has prominent applications in the emerging area of computational advertising, in particular targeted online advertising and advertising in social networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies adaptive control for high-dimensional linear quadratic systems whose dynamics are initially unknown. Its key structural assumption is that the matrices describing those dynamics are sparse. The question is how this structure changes the amount of experience needed to approach the cost of an optimal controller.

The authors present a control scheme with regret bounded by a quantity scaling as p times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where p is the state dimension and T is the time horizon. This result applies in the stated regime of large p and T much larger than a polylogarithmic function of p.

They also state that average cost reaches a factor of 1 plus epsilon of the optimum after a horizon scaling polylogarithmically in p and proportionally to inverse epsilon squared. The comparison is with prior work on dense dynamics requiring at least order-p samples for meaningful estimation. The result identifies sparsity as a route to favorable learning requirements; advertising applications are presented as prospective uses.
summary.tldr: Exploiting sparse dynamics yields adaptive-control guarantees with favorable sample requirements for high-dimensional linear quadratic systems.

title: Efficient Reinforcement Learning for High Dimensional Linear Quadratic Systems

abstract: Language users are remarkably good at making inferences about speakers' intentions in context, and children learning their native language also display substantial skill in acquiring the meanings of unknown words. These two cases are deeply related: Language users invent new terms in conversation, and language learners learn the literal meanings of words based on their pragmatic inferences about how those words are used. While pragmatic inference and word learning have both been independently characterized in probabilistic terms, no current work unifies these two. We describe a model in which language learners assume that they jointly approximate a shared, external lexicon and reason recursively about the goals of others in using this lexicon. This model captures phenomena in word learning and pragmatic inference; it additionally leads to insights about the emergence of communicative systems in conversation and the mechanisms by which pragmatic inferences become incorporated into word meanings.

paragraphs: Understanding an utterance involves reasoning about what a speaker intends, while learning a word involves discovering what it means. This paper treats those activities as closely connected. A learner can use an inference about a speaker's intention to interpret an unfamiliar word, and conversation can introduce expressions whose meanings are still being established.

The proposed model assumes that language learners jointly approximate a shared external lexicon. They also reason recursively about other agents' goals in using that lexicon: interpreting language involves considering how someone else approaches communication. This combines probabilistic accounts of pragmatic inference and word learning within a single model, allowing uncertainty about meanings and reasoning about intentions to interact.

The authors report that the model captures phenomena from both word learning and pragmatic interpretation. It also offers insights into how communicative systems emerge during conversation and how interpretations initially supplied by context can become incorporated into word meanings. The significance is a unified account of learning and use, grounded in the stated shared-lexicon assumption.
summary.tldr: A shared-lexicon model unifies word learning and pragmatic interpretation through recursive reasoning about other speakers' communicative goals.

title: Learning and using language via recursive pragmatic reasoning about other agents

abstract: Category models for objects or activities typically rely on supervised learning requiring sufficiently large training sets. Transferring knowledge from known categories to novel classes with no or only a few labels however is far less researched even though it is a common scenario. In this work, we extend transfer learning with semi-supervised learning to exploit unlabeled instances of (novel) categories with no or only a few labeled instances. Our proposed approach Propagated Semantic Transfer combines three main ingredients. First, we transfer information from known to novel categories by incorporating external knowledge, such as linguistic or expert-specified information, e.g., by a mid-level layer of semantic attributes. Second, we exploit the manifold structure of novel classes. More specifically we adapt a graph-based learning algorithm - so far only used for semi-supervised learning - to zero-shot and few-shot learning. Third, we improve the local neighborhood in such graph structures by replacing the raw feature-based representation with a mid-level object- or attribute-based representation. We evaluate our approach on three challenging datasets in two different applications, namely on Animals with Attributes and ImageNet for image classification and on MPII Composites for activity recognition. Our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transfer and semi-supervised approaches on all datasets.

This paper combines transfer learning with semi-supervised learning so that unlabeled examples of those categories also contribute. Its Propagated Semantic Transfer method links knowledge about established categories with the organization of the new data.

The approach has three ingredients. External semantic knowledge, including linguistic or expert information, connects known and novel categories. A graph-based learning algorithm then exploits the manifold structure of novel classes in zero-shot and few-shot settings. Finally, object- or attribute-based intermediate representations improve local graph neighborhoods compared with using raw features.

The authors evaluate the approach on Animals with Attributes and ImageNet for image classification, and MPII Composites for activity recognition. It consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art transfer and semi-supervised methods across these datasets. The findings support using semantic relationships and unlabeled-data structure together: semantic information enables transfer, while the graph lets the available novel examples shape how that information is propagated.
summary.tldr: Propagated Semantic Transfer combines semantic knowledge and graphs of unlabeled examples to improve zero-shot and few-shot recognition on three datasets.

title: Transfer Learning in a Transductive Setting

abstract: We investigate architectures of discriminatively trained deep Convolutional Networks (ConvNets) for action recognition in video. The challenge is to capture the complementary information on appearance from still frames and motion between frames. We also aim to generalise the best performing hand-crafted features within a data-driven learning framework. Our contribution is three-fold. First, we propose a two-stream ConvNet architecture which incorporates spatial and temporal networks. Second, we demonstrate that a ConvNet trained on multi-frame dense optical flow is able to achieve very good performance in spite of limited training data. Finally, we show that multi-task learning, applied to two different action classification datasets, can be used to increase the amount of training data and improve the performance on both. Our architecture is trained and evaluated on the standard video actions benchmarks of UCF-101 and HMDB-51, where it is competitive with the state of the art. It also exceeds by a large margin previous attempts to use deep nets for video classification.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in video requires information about both appearance and movement. A still frame provides spatial information, while changes between frames provide temporal information. This paper develops a two-stream convolutional network architecture with separate spatial and temporal networks to capture these complementary sources within a learned approach to action recognition.

The temporal network is trained on dense optical flow across multiple frames. The authors show that this motion input supports very good performance despite limited training data. They also apply multi-task learning across two action classification datasets, increasing the amount of training data available and improving performance on both datasets.

The architecture is trained and evaluated on UCF-101 and HMDB-51, where it is competitive with the state of the art and substantially exceeds earlier deep-network approaches to video classification. The findings support an architecture that explicitly represents appearance and motion, while showing that motion-focused learning and training across datasets can help address the limited-data setting considered.
summary.tldr: Separate appearance and motion ConvNets achieve competitive video action recognition, with multi-task training improving results on both evaluated datasets.

title: Two-Stream Convolutional Networks for Action Recognition in Videos

abstract: Recent object detection systems rely on two critical steps: (1) a set of object proposals is predicted as efficiently as possible, and (2) this set of candidate proposals is then passed to an object classifier. Such approaches have been shown they can be fast, while achieving the state of the art in detection performance. In this paper, we propose a new way to generate object proposals, introducing an approach based on a discriminative convolutional network. Our model is trained jointly with two objectives: given an image patch, the first part of the system outputs a class-agnostic segmentation mask, while the second part of the system outputs the likelihood of the patch being centered on a full object. At test time, the model is efficiently applied on the whole test image and generates a set of segmentation masks, each of them being assigned with a corresponding object likelihood score. We show that our model yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art object proposal algorithms. In particular, compared to previous approaches, our model obtains substantially higher object recall using fewer proposals. We also show that our model is able to generalize to unseen categories it has not seen during training. Unlike all previous approaches for generating object masks, we do not rely on edges, superpixels, or any other form of low-level segmentation.

Such approaches have been shown they can be fast, while achieving the state of the art in detection performance. In this paper, we propose a new way to generate object proposals, introducing an approach based on a discriminative convolutional network. Our model is trained jointly with two objectives: given an image patch, the first part of the system outputs a class-agnostic segmentation mask, while the second part of the system outputs the likelihood of the patch being centered on a full object. At test time, the model is efficiently applied on the whole test image and generates a set of segmentation masks, each of them being assigned with a corresponding object likelihood score. We show that our model yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art object proposal algorithms. In particular, compared to previous approaches, our model obtains substantially higher object recall using fewer proposals. We also show that our model is able to generalize to unseen categories it has not seen during training. Unlike all previous approaches for generating object masks, we do not rely on edges, superpixels, or any other form of low-level segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper improves the proposal stage of object detection, where a system identifies candidate objects before classification. Its approach uses a discriminative convolutional network to propose segmented objects. The aim is to produce useful candidates efficiently, so the later classifier receives a smaller collection that still covers many objects in the image.

title: Learning to Segment Object Candidates

abstract: We propose a pool-based non-parametric active learning algorithm for general metric spaces, called MArgin Regularized Metric Active Nearest Neighbor (MARMANN), which outputs a nearest-neighbor classifier. We give prediction error guarantees that depend on the noisy-margin properties of the input sample, and are competitive with those obtained by previously proposed passive learners. We prove that the label complexity of MARMANN is significantly lower than that of any passive learner with similar error guarantees. Our algorithm is based on a generalized sample compression scheme and a new label-efficient active model-selection procedure.

We prove that the label complexity of MARMANN is significantly lower than that of any passive learner with similar error guarantees. Our algorithm is based on a generalized sample compression scheme and a new label-efficient active model-selection procedure.

paragraphs: MARMANN is an active learning algorithm that builds a nearest-neighbor classifier from a pool of examples. Instead of receiving labels without choosing which examples matter, it selectively requests labels. It works in general metric spaces, so its formulation relies on distances between examples rather than requiring a particular coordinate representation.

The method combines a generalized sample compression scheme with a procedure for choosing a model while using few labels. These components connect the task of retaining a useful representation of the sample with the task of deciding where additional labeling is worthwhile. The resulting classifier remains a nearest-neighbor rule.

The paper provides prediction-error guarantees that depend on the sample's noisy-margin properties, making the guarantee sensitive to separation and noise in the input. Those guarantees are competitive with earlier passive learners. At comparable guaranteed error, the authors prove significantly lower label complexity than any passive learner, establishing a theoretical benefit from choosing which labels to request.
summary.tldr: MARMANN selectively requests labels to obtain nearest-neighbor prediction guarantees with significantly lower label complexity than comparable passive learners.

title: Active Nearest-Neighbor Learning in Metric Spaces

abstract: In a regression task, a predictor is given a set of instances, along with a real value for each point. Subsequently, she has to identify the value of a new instance as accurately as possible. In this work, we initiate the study of strategic predictions in machine learning. We consider a regression task tackled by two players, where the payoff of each player is the proportion of the points she predicts more accurately than the other player. We first revise the probably approximately correct learning framework to deal with the case of a duel between two predictors. We then devise an algorithm which finds a linear regression predictor that is a best response to any (not necessarily linear) regression algorithm. We show that it has linearithmic sample complexity, and polynomial time complexity when the dimension of the instances domain is fixed. We also test our approach in a high-dimensional setting, and show it significantly defeats classical regression algorithms in the prediction duel. Together, our work introduces a novel machine learning task that lends itself well to current competitive online settings, provides its theoretical foundations, and illustrates its applicability.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression as a competition between two predictors. Each player earns credit for the proportion of examples on which its prediction is closer to the correct value than its opponent’s prediction. This changes the learning objective: success depends on winning individual comparisons against another predictor, rather than simply pursuing accuracy without reference to a competitor.

The authors adapt the probably approximately correct learning framework to this prediction duel. They then develop an algorithm that finds a linear predictor serving as a best response to an opponent whose predictor need not be linear. The algorithm has linearithmic sample complexity, and its running time is polynomial when the input dimension is fixed.

Experiments also examine a high-dimensional setting, where the approach significantly beats classical regression algorithms under the duel’s scoring rule. These results support the usefulness of explicitly modeling competition in prediction tasks. The theoretical efficiency statement retains its fixed-dimension condition, while the experimental finding concerns competitive wins under the proposed payoff.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a theoretically grounded regression algorithm that competes by predicting more accurately than a given opponent on as many examples as possible.

title: Best Response Regression

abstract: Finding the maximum a-posteriori (MAP) assignment is a central task in graphical models. Since modern applications give rise to very large problem instances, there is increasing need for efficient solvers. In this work we propose to improve the efficiency of coordinate-minimization-based dual-decomposition solvers by running their updates asynchronously in parallel. In this case message-passing inference is performed by multiple processing units simultaneously without coordination, all reading and writing to shared memory. We analyze the convergence properties of the resulting algorithms and identify settings where speedup gains can be expected. Our numerical evaluations show that this approach indeed achieves significant speedups in common computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: Maximum a-posteriori inference asks for the most probable joint assignment in a graphical model. Large instances make efficient optimization increasingly important. This paper focuses on solvers that use dual decomposition and coordinate minimization, and asks whether their updates can run faster when several processors work at the same time.

The proposed approach performs message-passing updates asynchronously. Multiple processing units read and write shared memory without coordinating their updates with one another. This changes the execution of the solver: individual updates can proceed while other processors are also updating the shared state. The central technical question is how this concurrent execution affects convergence and when it provides a speed advantage.

The authors analyze convergence properties and identify settings in which speedups can be expected. Numerical evaluations on common computer vision tasks show significant improvements in speed. The result supports asynchronous parallel execution as a way to accelerate this class of inference solvers, with the analysis tying that benefit to particular settings.
summary.tldr: Asynchronous shared-memory updates accelerate coordinate-minimization MAP solvers, with convergence analysis and significant speedups on computer vision tasks.

title: Asynchronous Parallel Coordinate Minimization for MAP Inference

abstract: Many applications of machine learning, for example in health care, would benefit from methods that can guarantee privacy of data subjects. Differential privacy (DP) has become established as a standard for protecting learning results. The standard DP algorithms require a single trusted party to have access to the entire data, which is a clear weakness, or add prohibitive amounts of noise. We consider DP Bayesian learning in a distributed setting, where each party only holds a single sample or a few samples of the data. We propose a learning strategy based on a secure multi-party sum function for aggregating summaries from data holders and the Gaussian mechanism for DP. Our method builds on an asymptotically optimal and practically efficient DP Bayesian inference with rapidly diminishing extra cost.

paragraphs: Learning from sensitive data creates a tension between useful statistical results and protecting the people represented in the data. The paper studies Bayesian learning with differential privacy when information is distributed across parties, each holding only one or a few samples. This setting makes reliance on a single holder of the complete dataset especially undesirable.

The proposed strategy combines two components with distinct roles. A secure multiparty sum aggregates summaries supplied by data holders, while the Gaussian mechanism provides differential privacy. The aggregation mechanism supports learning from distributed contributions, and the privacy mechanism protects the learning results. Together, they address the centralized trust requirement and excessive noise described for standard approaches.

The strategy builds on Bayesian inference that is asymptotically optimal under differential privacy and practically efficient, with additional cost that diminishes rapidly. The asymptotic qualification matters: it describes behavior in a limiting regime rather than identical performance at every sample size. The contribution brings this inference approach into a setting where the original data remain distributed among many small holders.
summary.tldr: Secure aggregation and Gaussian privacy noise enable efficient differentially private Bayesian learning from many small distributed datasets.

title: Differentially private Bayesian learning on distributed data

abstract: Adversarial training has proved to be competitive against supervised learning methods on computer vision tasks. However, studies have mainly been confined to generative tasks such as image synthesis. In this paper, we apply adversarial training techniques to the discriminative task of learning a steganographic algorithm. Steganography is a collection of techniques for concealing the existence of information by embedding it within a non-secret medium, such as cover texts or images. We show that adversarial training can produce robust steganographic techniques: our unsupervised training scheme produces a steganographic algorithm that competes with state-of-the-art steganographic techniques. We also show that supervised training of our adversarial model produces a robust steganalyzer, which performs the discriminative task of deciding if an image contains secret information. We define a game between three parties, Alice, Bob and Eve, in order to simultaneously train both a steganographic algorithm and a steganalyzer. Alice and Bob attempt to communicate a secret message contained within an image, while Eve eavesdrops on their conversation and attempts to determine if secret information is embedded within the image. We represent Alice, Bob and Eve by neural networks, and validate our scheme on two independent image datasets, showing our novel method of studying steganographic problems is surprisingly competitive against established steganographic techniques.

paragraphs: Steganography hides the existence of a message by embedding it in an apparently ordinary medium, such as an image. The challenge is therefore to convey information while avoiding evidence that secret communication is taking place. This paper applies adversarial training to learn both an image-based hiding algorithm and a detector of hidden information.

The training setup is a game among three neural networks. Alice embeds a secret message in an image, Bob attempts to recover the message, and Eve attempts to determine whether the image contains secret information. Their competing objectives connect successful communication with resistance to detection. This extends adversarial training beyond the image-generation tasks that motivated much of the earlier work.

The authors report that their unsupervised training scheme produces a hiding algorithm competitive with established steganographic techniques on two independent image datasets. They also show that supervised training of the adversarial model produces a robust steganalyzer. The findings demonstrate that the same competitive framework can support both concealment and detection, with its effectiveness established through the reported image evaluations.
summary.tldr: Three competing neural networks learn to hide, recover, and detect secret messages in images, producing competitive steganography and detection methods.

title: Generating steganographic images via adversarial training

abstract: The design of flow control systems remains a challenge due to the nonlinear nature of the equations that govern fluid flow. However, recent advances in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) have enabled the simulation of complex fluid flows with high accuracy, opening the possibility of using learning-based approaches to facilitate controller design. We present a method for learning the forced and unforced dynamics of airflow over a cylinder directly from CFD data. The proposed approach, grounded in Koopman theory, is shown to produce stable dynamical models that can predict the time evolution of the cylinder system over extended time horizons. Finally, by performing model predictive control with the learned dynamical models, we are able to find a straightforward, interpretable control law for suppressing vortex shedding in the wake of the cylinder.

paragraphs: Designing controls for fluid flow is challenging because the governing dynamics are nonlinear. Accurate computational fluid simulations offer a way to learn models that could support controller design. This paper studies that possibility for airflow around a cylinder, using simulation data as the basis for learning how the system changes over time.

The proposed method is grounded in Koopman theory and learns both forced and unforced dynamics. Covering both cases means addressing the flow's evolution with and without external forcing. The authors show that their learned dynamical models are stable and can predict the cylinder system over extended time horizons, making them useful for considering the future consequences of control actions.

They then use the learned models within model predictive control. For the studied cylinder system, this produces a straightforward and interpretable control law that suppresses vortex shedding in the wake. The contribution therefore links learned dynamics to a concrete control outcome, showing how simulation-based modeling can inform an understandable intervention in a nonlinear flow.
summary.tldr: Models learned from fluid simulations support long-horizon prediction and an interpretable control law for suppressing vortex shedding behind a cylinder.

title: Deep Dynamical Modeling and Control of Unsteady Fluid Flows

abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.
