paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends on how training examples are transformed and which distinctions those transformations preserve. This paper studies that dependence for graphs. It focuses on three properties emphasized in self-supervised learning: ignoring task-irrelevant changes, separating classes in a representation space, and retaining enough information in augmented examples to recover labels.

Graphs have a discrete, non-Euclidean structure, making these properties difficult to assume. The authors analyze generalization when contrastive learning uses generic graph augmentations. Their theory identifies limitations of these transformations and the need for task-relevant augmentations. Empirically, generic augmentations on common benchmarks fail to induce the desired task-relevant invariances and yield only marginal improvements over simple, untrained baselines.

The theory also motivates a synthetic benchmark where task-relevant information can be controlled and optimal augmentations are specified in advance. This makes it possible to examine augmentation quality against a known target. Experiments expose additional limitations in advanced approaches, including automated augmentation. The findings connect graph representation quality to the information that an augmentation preserves, rather than treating augmentation as an interchangeable training component.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments show that graph contrastive learning depends strongly on augmentations preserving information relevant to the task.

title: Analyzing Data-Centric Properties for Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: The use of black-box models (e.g., deep neural networks) in high-stakes decision-making systems, whose internal logic is complex, raises the need for providing explanations about their decisions. Model explanation techniques mitigate this problem by generating an interpretable and high-fidelity surrogate model (e.g., a logistic regressor or decision tree) to explain the logic of black-box models. In this work, we investigate the issue of fairwashing, in which model explanation techniques are manipulated to rationalize decisions taken by an unfair black-box model using deceptive surrogate models. More precisely, we theoretically characterize and analyze fairwashing, proving that this phenomenon is difficult to avoid due to an irreducible factor---the unfairness of the black-box model. Based on the theory developed, we propose a novel technique, called FRAUD-Detect (FaiRness AUDit Detection), to detect fairwashed models by measuring a divergence over subpopulation-wise fidelity measures of the interpretable model. We empirically demonstrate that this divergence is significantly larger in purposefully fairwashed interpretable models than in honest ones. Furthermore, we show that our detector is robust to an informed adversary trying to bypass our detector. The code implementing FRAUD-Detect is available at https://github.com/cleverhans-lab/FRAUD-Detect.

paragraphs: An interpretable surrogate model can explain a complex model by approximating its decisions. Fairwashing manipulates that explanation so an unfair underlying model appears more acceptable. This paper analyzes why such deception is difficult to avoid, identifying the unfairness of the original black-box model as an irreducible factor in the phenomenon.

The authors develop FRAUD-Detect from their theoretical analysis. It measures a divergence across subpopulation-specific fidelity measures, where fidelity concerns how closely the explanation follows the original model. Examining agreement separately for subpopulations gives the detector a signal about how the surrogate represents the underlying decisions across different groups.

Experiments find that this divergence is significantly larger for deliberately fairwashed explanations than for honest ones. The authors also report robustness against an informed adversary attempting to evade the detector. These are empirical detection results alongside a theoretical characterization of the underlying problem. Together, they show why auditing an explanation's relationship to the black-box model across subpopulations can help expose deceptive presentations of model fairness.
summary.tldr: FRAUD-Detect identifies fairwashed explanations by measuring differences in how faithfully they represent a black-box model across subpopulations.

title: Washing The Unwashable : On The (Im)possibility of Fairwashing Detection

abstract: We consider privacy in the context of streaming algorithms for cardinality estimation. We show that a large class of algorithms all satisfy $\epsilon$-differential privacy, so long as (a) the algorithm is combined with a simple down-sampling procedure, and (b) the input stream cardinality is $\Omega(k/\epsilon)$. Here, $k$ is a certain parameter of the sketch that is always at most the sketch size in bits, but is typically much smaller. We also show that, even with no modification, algorithms in our class satisfy $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy, where $\delta$ falls exponentially with the stream cardinality. Our analysis applies to essentially all popular cardinality estimation algorithms, and substantially generalizes and tightens privacy bounds from earlier works. Our approach is faster and exhibits a better utility-space tradeoff than prior art.

paragraphs: Cardinality estimation uses a compact summary of a data stream to estimate how many distinct items it contains. This paper investigates the privacy of a broad class of such streaming algorithms. Its results show that privacy guarantees can follow from the estimators’ existing behavior, with different guarantees depending on whether a down-sampling step is added.

With simple down-sampling, the algorithms satisfy epsilon-differential privacy provided the stream’s distinct-item count is sufficiently large, scaling as k divided by epsilon. Here, k is a sketch parameter bounded by the sketch’s size in bits and typically much smaller. Both the down-sampling procedure and the cardinality condition are part of this guarantee.

Without modifying the algorithms, the authors also establish approximate differential privacy, with the delta parameter decreasing exponentially as cardinality grows. The analysis covers essentially all popular cardinality estimators and strengthens earlier privacy bounds. The proposed approach is also reported to be faster and to improve the tradeoff between estimation utility and storage space compared with prior work.
summary.tldr: A broad class of cardinality estimators has privacy guarantees, including pure differential privacy with down-sampling and sufficiently large stream cardinality.

title: Order-Invariant Cardinality Estimators Are Differentially Private

abstract: The success of reinforcement learning in a variety of challenging sequential decision-making problems has been much discussed, but often ignored in this discussion is the consideration of how the choice of reward function affects the behavior of these algorithms. Most practical RL algorithms require copious amounts of reward engineering in order to successfully solve challenging tasks. The idea of this type of ``reward-shaping'' has been often discussed in the literature and is used in practical instantiations, but there is relatively little formal characterization of how the choice of reward shaping can yield benefits in sample complexity for RL problems. In this work, we build on the framework of novelty-based exploration to provide a simple scheme for incorporating shaped rewards into RL along with an analysis tool to show that particular choices of reward shaping provably improve sample efficiency. We characterize the class of problems where these gains are expected to be significant and show how this can be connected to practical algorithms in the literature. We show that these results hold in practice in experimental evaluations as well, providing an insight into the mechanisms through which reward shaping can significantly improve the complexity of reinforcement learning while retaining asymptotic performance.

paragraphs: Reward shaping changes the learning signals supplied to a reinforcement learning agent. Although practical systems often depend heavily on reward engineering, its effect on the amount of experience needed to learn has received less formal treatment. This paper examines why particular shaping choices can reduce that sample requirement.

The authors build on novelty-based exploration to introduce a simple way to incorporate shaped rewards. They also develop an analysis tool that proves sample-efficiency improvements for particular choices of shaping. The guarantees are selective: the paper characterizes a class of problems where substantial gains are expected, rather than claiming that any modified reward will help.

The analysis connects these ideas to practical algorithms, and experiments support the predicted benefits. The reported improvement concerns learning more efficiently while retaining asymptotic performance, so the role of shaping is to improve the learning process without sacrificing its eventual performance in the studied setting. The work provides a formal account of mechanisms behind a technique widely used in practice.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how particular reward-shaping choices can provably reduce reinforcement learning sample needs while retaining asymptotic performance.

title: Unpacking Reward Shaping: Understanding the Benefits of Reward Engineering on Sample Complexity

abstract: Recent work has leveraged the popular distributionally robust optimization paradigm to combat overfitting in classical logistic regression. While the resulting classification scheme displays a promising performance in numerical experiments, it is inherently limited to numerical features. In this paper, we show that distributionally robust logistic regression with mixed (\emph{i.e.}, numerical and categorical) features, despite amounting to an optimization problem of exponential size, admits a polynomial-time solution scheme. We subsequently develop a practically efficient cutting plane approach that solves the problem as a sequence of polynomial-time solvable exponential conic programs. Our method retains many of the desirable theoretical features of previous works, but---in contrast to the literature---it does not admit an equivalent representation as a regularized logistic regression, that is, it represents a genuinely novel variant of the logistic regression problem. We show that our method outperforms both the unregularized and the regularized logistic regression on categorical as well as mixed-feature benchmark instances.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust logistic regression seeks to combat overfitting by accounting for uncertainty in the data distribution. Previous formulations discussed in this paper are limited to numerical features. The authors extend the approach to datasets containing categorical features as well as mixtures of categorical and numerical inputs.

Although the resulting optimization problem has exponential size, they show that it admits a polynomial-time solution scheme. They then develop a practical cutting-plane method that solves a sequence of exponential conic programs, each solvable in polynomial time. This distinction matters: a formulation can be enormous when written out explicitly while still permitting a more efficient route to its solution.

The new model retains many theoretical properties of earlier approaches, but it cannot be represented as an equivalent regularized logistic regression problem. It therefore introduces a distinct form of logistic regression rather than merely another regularization choice. Experiments on categorical and mixed-feature benchmarks report improvements over both ordinary and regularized logistic regression, supporting the practical relevance of the extension.
summary.tldr: The paper makes distributionally robust logistic regression tractable for mixed numerical and categorical features and reports improved benchmark performance.

title: Wasserstein Logistic Regression with Mixed Features

abstract: This paper studies the fundamental problem of learning energy-based model (EBM) in the latent space of the generator model. Learning such prior model typically requires running costly Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Instead, we propose to use noise contrastive estimation (NCE) to discriminatively learn the EBM through density ratio estimation between the latent prior density and latent posterior density. However, the NCE typically fails to accurately estimate such density ratio given large gap between two densities. To effectively tackle this issue and further learn more expressive prior model, we develop the adaptive multi-stage density ratio estimation which breaks the estimation into multiple stages and learn different stages of density ratio sequentially and adaptively. The latent prior model can be gradually learned using ratio estimated in previous stage so that the final latent space EBM prior can be naturally formed by product of ratios in different stages. The proposed method enables informative and much sharper prior than existing baselines, and can be trained efficiently. Our experiments demonstrate strong performances in terms of image generation and reconstruction as well as anomaly detection.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn an energy-based prior in a generator’s latent space. Such a prior determines which hidden representations the generator favors. Learning it typically involves costly Markov chain Monte Carlo computations. The authors instead investigate noise contrastive estimation, which learns through a discriminative density-ratio estimation problem.

The central obstacle is that estimating the ratio between the latent prior and posterior becomes unreliable when those distributions are far apart. The proposed method divides that task into several adaptive stages. Each stage estimates a ratio and uses the previous stage’s estimate to progressively update the prior. The final energy-based prior is formed through the product of the ratios learned across stages.

This staged construction makes a large distributional gap manageable through successive estimation problems. The authors report efficient training and priors that are more informative and substantially sharper than existing baselines. Experiments show strong performance in image generation, image reconstruction, and anomaly detection, connecting the improved latent prior to several uses of the generator.
summary.tldr: Adaptive density-ratio estimation learns a latent energy-based prior through successive updates that bridge a difficult prior–posterior gap.

title: Adaptive Multi-stage Density Ratio Estimation for Learning Latent Space Energy-based Model

abstract: Universal Domain Adaptation (UniDA) aims to transfer knowledge from a source domain to a target domain without any constraints on label sets. Since both domains may hold private classes, identifying target common samples for domain alignment is an essential issue in UniDA. Most existing methods require manually specified or hand-tuned threshold values to detect common samples thus they are hard to extend to more realistic UniDA because of the diverse ratios of common classes. Moreover, they cannot recognize different categories among target-private samples as these private samples are treated as a whole. In this paper, we propose to use Optimal Transport (OT) to handle these issues under a unified framework, namely UniOT. First, an OT-based partial alignment with adaptive filling is designed to detect common classes without any predefined threshold values for realistic UniDA. It can automatically discover the intrinsic difference between common and private classes based on the statistical information of the assignment matrix obtained from OT. Second, we propose an OT-based target representation learning that encourages both global discrimination and local consistency of samples to avoid the over-reliance on the source. Notably, UniOT is the first method with the capability to automatically discover and recognize private categories in the target domain for UniDA. Accordingly, we introduce a new metric H^3-score to evaluate the performance in terms of both accuracy of common samples and clustering performance of private ones. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the advantages of UniOT over a wide range of state-of-the-art methods in UniDA.

A model needs to identify target examples belonging to shared categories while handling categories unique to the target. Existing methods often use manually chosen thresholds and group all target-private examples together, obscuring their internal category structure.

They introduce the H³-score to evaluate both accuracy on common examples and clustering of private examples. Extensive experiments report advantages over a wide range of state-of-the-art methods. The contribution expands adaptation beyond deciding whether an example is known, toward organizing the new categories present in the target.
summary.tldr: UniOT uses optimal transport to align shared classes without preset thresholds and discover distinct target-private categories.

title: Unified Optimal Transport Framework for Universal Domain Adaptation

abstract: We propose the first unified theoretical analysis of mixed sample data augmentation (MSDA), such as Mixup and CutMix. Our theoretical results show that regardless of the choice of the mixing strategy, MSDA behaves as a pixel-level regularization of the underlying training loss and a regularization of the first layer parameters. Similarly, our theoretical results support that the MSDA training strategy can improve adversarial robustness and generalization compared to the vanilla training strategy. Using the theoretical results, we provide a high-level understanding of how different design choices of MSDA work differently. For example, we show that the most popular MSDA methods, Mixup and CutMix, behave differently, e.g., CutMix regularizes the input gradients by pixel distances, while Mixup regularizes the input gradients regardless of pixel distances. Our theoretical results also show that the optimal MSDA strategy depends on tasks, datasets, or model parameters. From these observations, we propose generalized MSDAs, a Hybrid version of Mixup and CutMix (HMix) and Gaussian Mixup (GMix), simple extensions of Mixup and CutMix. Our implementation can leverage the advantages of Mixup and CutMix, while our implementation is very efficient, and the computation cost is almost neglectable as Mixup and CutMix. Our empirical study shows that our HMix and GMix outperform the previous state-of-the-art MSDA methods in CIFAR-100 and ImageNet classification tasks.

paragraphs: Mixed sample data augmentation trains models using combinations of examples, with Mixup and CutMix among the prominent methods. This paper develops a unified theoretical account of these strategies by examining their effect on the training loss. It shows that the analyzed mixing strategies act as regularization at the pixel level and on the network’s first-layer parameters.

The analysis also explains why different ways of mixing examples need not have the same effect. CutMix regularizes input gradients according to distances between pixels, whereas Mixup does so without that dependence. The theoretical results support possible improvements in generalization and adversarial robustness, while indicating that the best mixing strategy depends on the task, dataset, or model parameters.

Using these insights, the authors introduce HMix, a hybrid of Mixup and CutMix, and GMix, or Gaussian Mixup. Both are simple extensions with similarly small computational overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet classification show that these methods outperform the previous leading mixed-sample augmentation methods, supporting the practical usefulness of the loss-based analysis.
summary.tldr: A unified loss-based analysis explains mixed-sample augmentation and motivates two extensions that improve classification in the reported experiments.

title: A Unified Analysis of Mixed Sample Data Augmentation: A Loss Function Perspective

abstract: Recursion is the fundamental paradigm to finitely describe potentially infinite objects. As state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms cannot directly reason about recursion, they must rely on the practitioner's ingenuity in designing a suitable "flat" representation of the environment. The resulting manual feature constructions and approximations are cumbersome and error-prone; their lack of transparency hampers scalability. To overcome these challenges, we develop RL algorithms capable of computing optimal policies in environments described as a collection of Markov decision processes (MDPs) that can recursively invoke one another. Each constituent MDP is characterized by several entry and exit points that correspond to input and output values of these invocations. These recursive MDPs (or RMDPs) are expressively equivalent to probabilistic pushdown systems (with call-stack playing the role of the pushdown stack), and can model probabilistic programs with recursive procedural calls. We introduce Recursive Q-learning---a model-free RL algorithm for RMDPs---and prove that it converges for finite, single-exit and deterministic multi-exit RMDPs under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Recursion describes a process that can invoke another instance of itself or another procedure. Standard reinforcement-learning algorithms cannot directly reason about this structure, leaving practitioners to construct flattened representations and approximations. This paper develops learning methods for environments whose recursive organization is represented explicitly, avoiding that dependence on manually designed flattening.

The environment consists of Markov decision processes that can call one another. Each component has entry and exit points corresponding to the inputs and outputs of an invocation. These recursive MDPs have the expressive power of probabilistic pushdown systems, with a call stack recording nested invocations. They can therefore describe probabilistic programs containing recursive procedure calls.

The authors introduce Recursive Q-learning, a model-free algorithm for this setting. They prove convergence under mild assumptions for the stated finite, single-exit, and deterministic multi-exit RMDP cases. The guarantee is tied to these specified cases. The broader contribution is to make recursion part of the learning framework itself, enabling policies to be learned for structured environments without first hiding their recursive organization.
summary.tldr: Recursive Q-learning directly handles environments with nested procedure calls and has convergence guarantees for specified recursive-MDP cases.

title: Recursive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent studies have shown that episodic reinforcement learning (RL) is not more difficult than bandits, even with a long planning horizon and unknown state transitions. However, these results are limited to either tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) or computationally inefficient algorithms for linear mixture MDPs. In this paper, we propose the first computationally efficient horizon-free algorithm for linear mixture MDPs, which achieves the optimal $\tilde O(d\sqrt{K} +d^2)$ regret up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm adapts a weighted least square estimator for the unknown transitional dynamic, where the weight is both \emph{variance-aware} and \emph{uncertainty-aware}. When applying our weighted least square estimator to heterogeneous linear bandits, we can obtain an $\tilde O(d\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^K \sigma_k^2} +d)$ regret in the first $K$ rounds, where $d$ is the dimension of the context and $\sigma_k^2$ is the variance of the reward in the $k$-th round. This also improves upon the best known algorithms in this setting when $\sigma_k^2$'s are known.

paragraphs: A long planning horizon need not create a large statistical penalty in episodic reinforcement learning, but earlier horizon-free results had important restrictions. They applied either to tabular models or to computationally inefficient algorithms for linear mixture Markov decision processes. This paper provides a computationally efficient horizon-free algorithm for the latter setting.

The method estimates unknown transition dynamics using weighted least squares. Its weights account for both variance and uncertainty, bringing both considerations into the estimation procedure. The resulting regret scales as d times the square root of K, plus d squared, up to logarithmic factors. The authors establish that this rate is optimal up to those factors.

The same estimator also applies to heterogeneous linear bandits. There, the regret bound depends on the square root of the sum of reward variances, multiplied by the context dimension, plus an additional dimension term, again up to logarithmic factors. This improves on the best known algorithms in the stated setting when the reward variances are known.
summary.tldr: Variance- and uncertainty-aware estimation enables computationally efficient horizon-free learning with near-optimal regret for linear mixture MDPs.

title: Computationally Efficient Horizon-Free Reinforcement Learning for Linear Mixture MDPs

abstract: The quest for human imitative AI has been an enduring topic in AI research since inception. The technical evolution and emerging capabilities of the latest cohort of large language models (LLMs) have reinvigorated the subject beyond academia to cultural zeitgeist. While recent NLP evaluation benchmark tasks test some aspects of human-imitative behaviour (e.g., BIG-bench's `human-like behavior' tasks), few, if not none, examine *creative problem solving* abilities. Creative problem solving in humans is a well-studied topic in cognitive neuroscience with standardized tests that predominantly use ability to associate (heterogeneous) connections among clue words as a metric for creativity. Exposure to misleading stimuli --- distractors dubbed *red herrings* --- impede human performance in such tasks via the *fixation effect* and Einstellung paradigm. In cognitive neuroscience studies, such fixations are experimentally induced by pre-exposing participants to orthographically similar incorrect words to subsequent word-fragments or clues. The popular British quiz show Only Connect's *Connecting Wall* segment essentially mimics Mednick's Remote Associates Test (RAT) formulation with built-in, deliberate red herrings, that makes it an ideal proxy dataset to explore and study fixation effect and Einstellung paradigm from cognitive neuroscience in LLMs. In addition to presenting the novel Only Connect Wall (OCW) dataset, we also report results from our evaluation of selected pre-trained language models and LLMs (including OpenAI's GPT series) on creative problem solving tasks like grouping clue words by heterogeneous connections, and identifying correct open knowledge domain connections in respective groups. We synthetically generate two additional datasets: OCW-Randomized, OCW-WordNet to further analyze our red-herrings hypothesis in language models.The code and link to the dataset is available at [url](https://github.com/TaatiTeam/OCW).

paragraphs: The paper examines creative problem solving through the ability to find connections among words. It draws on cognitive research in which misleading associations can cause people to fixate on an unhelpful solution. The authors argue that this aspect of human-like behavior has received little attention in language-model evaluation.

They introduce the Only Connect Wall dataset from a quiz format containing deliberately misleading clues. Models must group clue words using varied kinds of connections and identify the correct connection within each group. This setting makes an attractive but incorrect association part of the problem, providing a proxy for studying fixation and the Einstellung effect in language models.

The study evaluates selected pretrained language models and LLMs, including GPT models, and creates OCW-Randomized and OCW-WordNet as additional synthetic datasets to investigate its red-herring hypothesis. The title frames the work around model fixation, while the abstract describes the evaluation without numerical outcomes. Its concrete contribution is a dataset and experimental setup for examining how misleading associations interact with connection-based problem solving.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces word-connection datasets to investigate creative problem solving and fixation on misleading associations in language models.

title: Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Exploring Creative Problem Solving and Einstellung Effect using the Only Connect Wall Dataset

abstract: Although existing fMRI-to-image reconstruction methods could predict high-quality images, they do not explicitly consider the semantic gap between training and testing data, resulting in reconstruction with unstable and uncertain semantics. This paper addresses the problem of generalized fMRI-to-image reconstruction by explicitly alleviates the semantic gap. Specifically, we leverage the pre-trained CLIP model to map the training data to a compact feature representation, which essentially extends the sparse semantics of training data to dense ones, thus alleviating the semantic gap of the instances nearby known concepts (i.e., inside the training super-classes). Inspired by the robust low-level representation in fMRI data, which could help alleviate the semantic gap for instances that far from the known concepts (i.e., outside the training super-classes), we leverage structural information as a general cue to guide image reconstruction. Further, we quantify the semantic uncertainty based on probability density estimation and achieve Generalized fMRI-to-image reconstruction by adaptively integrating Expanded Semantics and Structural information (GESS) within a diffusion process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GESS model outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and we propose a generalized scenario split strategy to evaluate the advantage of GESS in closing the semantic gap.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from fMRI data requires recovering its meaning as well as its appearance. Existing methods can produce high-quality images while becoming uncertain about what they depict when test examples differ semantically from training examples. This paper develops GESS to address that gap explicitly during image reconstruction.

GESS combines two sources of guidance. A pretrained CLIP model maps training examples into compact features that expand the coverage of their semantic information, helping with examples near known concepts within the training super-classes. For examples farther from those concepts, the method uses structural information motivated by the robust low-level representations available in fMRI data. These two sources address different degrees of semantic distance.

The method estimates semantic uncertainty using probability density estimation and adaptively combines semantic and structural guidance within a diffusion process. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art reconstruction methods. The authors also propose a data-splitting strategy for evaluating generalized reconstruction, making the semantic gap an explicit part of assessment rather than judging only the quality of images from familiar concepts.
summary.tldr: GESS adaptively combines expanded semantic features and structural guidance to improve fMRI-to-image reconstruction across semantic gaps.

title: Alleviating the Semantic Gap for Generalized fMRI-to-Image Reconstruction

abstract: In a broad class of reinforcement learning applications, stochastic rewards have heavy-tailed distributions, which lead to infinite second-order moments for stochastic (semi)gradients in policy evaluation and direct policy optimization. In such instances, the existing RL methods may fail miserably due to frequent statistical outliers. In this work, we establish that temporal difference (TD) learning with a dynamic gradient clipping mechanism, and correspondingly operated natural actor-critic (NAC), can be provably robustified against heavy-tailed reward distributions. It is shown in the framework of linear function approximation that a favorable tradeoff between bias and variability of the stochastic gradients can be achieved with this dynamic gradient clipping mechanism. In particular, we prove that robust versions of TD learning achieve sample complexities of order $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{p}})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1-\frac{1}{p}})$ with and without the full-rank assumption on the feature matrix, respectively, under heavy-tailed rewards with finite moments of order $(1+p)$ for some $p\in(0,1]$, both in expectation and with high probability. We show that a robust variant of NAC based on Robust TD learning achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4-\frac{2}{p}})$ sample complexity. We corroborate our theoretical results with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed rewards can produce frequent statistical outliers and stochastic learning updates with infinite second moments. Such behavior can undermine reinforcement learning methods used for evaluating or improving policies. This paper shows how dynamic gradient clipping can make temporal-difference learning robust to these rewards, and extends the approach to a natural actor-critic method built on robust temporal-difference learning.

The analysis uses linear function approximation and assumes rewards have a finite moment of order 1+p, for p between zero and one inclusive of one. Clipping controls extreme updates while introducing bias, and the authors establish a favorable balance between that bias and variability. For target error ε, robust temporal-difference learning has sample complexity O(ε^(-1/p)) with a full-rank feature matrix and O(ε^(-1-1/p)) without that assumption.

These bounds hold both in expectation and with high probability. The robust natural actor-critic variant has a sample-complexity bound of Õ(ε^(-4-2/p)), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results. The guarantees explicitly depend on reward moments and feature assumptions, showing how statistical tail behavior affects the amount of data needed for reliable learning.
summary.tldr: Dynamic gradient clipping gives temporal-difference and natural actor-critic methods provable robustness to heavy-tailed rewards under stated moment and approximation assumptions.

title: Provably Robust Temporal Difference Learning for Heavy-Tailed Rewards

abstract: A core principle in statistical learning is that smoothness of target functions allows to break the curse of dimensionality. However, learning a smooth function seems to require enough samples close to one another to get meaningful estimate of high-order derivatives, which would be hard in machine learning problems where the ratio between number of data and input dimension is relatively small. By deriving new lower bounds on the generalization error, this paper formalizes such an intuition, before investigating the role of constants and transitory regimes which are usually not depicted beyond classical learning theory statements while they play a dominant role in practice.

By deriving new lower bounds on the generalization error, this paper formalizes such an intuition, before investigating the role of constants and transitory regimes which are usually not depicted beyond classical learning theory statements while they play a dominant role in practice.

paragraphs: Smooth target functions can make statistical learning less vulnerable to high input dimensionality. This paper examines when a dataset is large enough to benefit from that smoothness. The motivating concern is that useful estimates of higher-order derivatives seem to require observations close together, which can be difficult when the sample count is small relative to dimension.

The authors derive new lower bounds on generalization error to formalize this concern. Lower bounds describe limits on achievable accuracy, making them a way to investigate whether the available samples support the benefits associated with smoothness. The analysis connects the mathematical regularity of a target function to the practical availability of informative observations.

The paper also examines constants and transitional regimes that classical learning-theory statements often leave in the background. These aspects can dominate behavior at practically relevant sample sizes. Its contribution is to sharpen the question of when smoothness becomes useful, bringing attention to the finite-data regime between a theoretical advantage and its realization in a learning problem.
summary.tldr: New generalization-error lower bounds examine how much data is needed before target-function smoothness can deliver its expected learning benefits.

title: How many samples are needed to leverage smoothness?

abstract: We present ProtoConcepts, a method for interpretable image classification combining deep learning and case-based reasoning using prototypical parts. Existing work in prototype-based image classification uses a "this looks like that'' reasoning process, which dissects a test image by finding prototypical parts and combining evidence from these prototypes to make a final classification. However, all of the existing prototypical part-based image classifiers provide only one-to-one comparisons, where a single training image patch serves as a prototype to compare with a part of our test image. With these single-image comparisons, it can often be difficult to identify the underlying concept being compared (e.g., "is it comparing the color or the shape?''). Our proposed method modifies the architecture of prototype-based networks to instead learn prototypical concepts which are visualized using multiple image patches. Having multiple visualizations of the same prototype allows us to more easily identify the concept captured by that prototype (e.g., "the test image and the related training patches are all the same shade of blue''), and allows our model to create richer, more interpretable visual explanations. Our experiments show that our ``this looks like those'' reasoning process can be applied as a modification to a wide range of existing prototypical image classification networks while achieving comparable accuracy on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Prototype-based image classifiers explain predictions by matching parts of a test image to representative training patches. A single matching patch can leave the explanation ambiguous: the similarity might concern color, shape, or another feature. ProtoConcepts addresses this ambiguity by representing a prototypical concept through multiple visual examples.

The method changes the network architecture so that learned concepts can be visualized with several image patches. Viewing what those patches share helps a person identify the basis of the comparison. For example, repeated examples sharing a shade of blue can make a color-based match easier to interpret. Classification still combines evidence from prototypical parts, but each piece of evidence has a richer visual explanation.

Experiments show that the approach can modify a wide range of existing prototype-based classification networks while maintaining comparable benchmark accuracy. The contribution is therefore a change in how model concepts are learned and displayed, with evidence that clearer visual context can be provided without a substantial accuracy tradeoff in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ProtoConcepts explains image classifications with multiple patches per prototype, making shared visual concepts clearer while retaining comparable accuracy.

title: This Looks Like Those: Illuminating Prototypical Concepts Using Multiple Visualizations

abstract: In neural network binarization, BinaryConnect (BC) and its variants are considered the standard. These methods apply the sign function in their forward pass and their respective gradients are backpropagated to update the weights. However, the derivative of the sign function is zero whenever defined, which consequently freezes training. Therefore, implementations of BC (e.g., BNN) usually replace the derivative of sign in the backward computation with identity or other approximate gradient alternatives. Although such practice works well empirically, it is largely a heuristic or ``training trick.'' We aim at shedding some light on these training tricks from the optimization perspective. Building from existing theory on ProxConnect (PC, a generalization of BC), we (1) equip PC with different forward-backward quantizers and obtain ProxConnect++ (PC++) that includes existing binarization techniques as special cases; (2) derive a principled way to synthesize forward-backward quantizers with automatic theoretical guarantees; (3) illustrate our theory by proposing an enhanced binarization algorithm BNN++; (4) conduct image classification experiments on CNNs and vision transformers, and empirically verify that BNN++ generally achieves competitive results on binarizing these models.

paragraphs: Binarized neural networks commonly use a sign function during the forward pass. Its derivative is zero wherever defined, so directly using that derivative prevents useful weight updates. Practical methods replace it during backpropagation with an identity function or another approximation, creating a gap between the forward computation and the gradient used for training.

The paper studies these approximations from an optimization perspective. Building on ProxConnect, a generalization of BinaryConnect, the authors introduce ProxConnect++, which supports different forward and backward quantizers. The framework includes existing binarization techniques as special cases and provides a principled procedure for constructing quantizer pairs with theoretical guarantees.

The authors use the theory to develop BNN++, an enhanced binarization algorithm. Image-classification experiments on convolutional networks and Vision Transformers show that it generally achieves competitive results. The contribution combines an explanation of widely used training heuristics with a method for designing alternatives, and the experiments demonstrate that an algorithm derived from this framework can perform competitively across both evaluated architecture families.
summary.tldr: ProxConnect++ gives an optimization-based framework for forward and backward binarization rules and motivates the competitive BNN++ algorithm.

title: Understanding Neural Network Binarization with Forward and Backward Proximal Quantizers

abstract: We develop a versatile new methodology for multidimensional mechanism design that incorporates side information about agent types to generate high social welfare and high revenue simultaneously. Prominent sources of side information in practice include predictions from a machine-learning model trained on historical agent data, advice from domain experts, and even the mechanism designer's own gut instinct. In this paper we adopt a prior-free perspective that makes no assumptions on the correctness, accuracy, or source of the side information. First, we design a meta-mechanism that integrates input side information with an improvement of the classical VCG mechanism. The welfare, revenue, and incentive properties of our meta-mechanism are characterized by novel constructions we introduce based on the notion of a weakest competitor, which is an agent that has the smallest impact on welfare. We show that our meta-mechanism, when carefully instantiated, simultaneously achieves strong welfare and revenue guarantees parameterized by errors in the side information. When the side information is highly informative and accurate, our mechanism achieves welfare and revenue competitive with the total social surplus, and its performance decays continuously and gradually as the quality of the side information decreases. Finally, we apply our meta-mechanism to a setting where each agent's type is determined by a constant number of parameters. Specifically, agent types lie on constant-dimensional subspaces (of the potentially high-dimensional ambient type space) that are known to the mechanism designer. We use our meta-mechanism to obtain the first known welfare and revenue guarantees in this setting.

title: Bicriteria Multidimensional Mechanism Design with Side Information

abstract: This paper focuses on improving the reconstruction of 2D floorplans from unstructured 3D point clouds. We identify opportunities for enhancement over the existing methods in three main areas: semantic quality, efficient representation, and local geometric details. To address these, we presents SLIBO-Net, an innovative approach to reconstructing 2D floorplans from unstructured 3D point clouds. We propose a novel transformer-based architecture that employs an efficient floorplan representation, providing improved room shape supervision and allowing for manageable token numbers. By incorporating geometric priors as a regularization mechanism and post-processing step, we enhance the capture of local geometric details. We also propose a scale-independent evaluation metric, correcting the discrepancy in error treatment between varying floorplan sizes. Our approach notably achieves a new state-of-the-art on the Structure3D dataset. The resultant floorplans exhibit enhanced semantic plausibility, substantially improving the overall quality and realism of the reconstructions. Our code and dataset are available online.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a two-dimensional floorplan from an unstructured three-dimensional point cloud requires more than recovering an approximate outline. Room shapes must be plausible, the representation must remain manageable, and local geometry must be captured accurately. SLIBO-Net addresses these three aspects together.

The method uses a transformer architecture with a slicing-box floorplan representation. The representation improves room-shape supervision while keeping the number of tokens manageable. Geometric priors enter both as regularization during learning and through post-processing, helping the system recover local details that matter to the quality of the reconstructed plan.

The authors also introduce a scale-independent evaluation metric to address unequal treatment of errors across floorplans of different sizes. On Structure3D, SLIBO-Net achieves a new state-of-the-art result, with reconstructions described as more semantically plausible and realistic. The contribution combines representation, geometric guidance, and evaluation design to improve how floorplans are produced and how their reconstruction quality is assessed.
summary.tldr: SLIBO-Net combines an efficient floorplan representation with geometric guidance to improve reconstruction quality from 3D point clouds.

title: SLIBO-Net: Floorplan Reconstruction via Slicing Box Representation with Local Geometry Regularization

abstract: Extensive experiments have gradually revealed the potential performance bottleneck of modeling Combinatorial Optimization (CO) solving as neural solution prediction tasks. The neural networks, in their pursuit of minimizing the average objective score across the distribution of historical problem instances, diverge from the core target of CO of seeking optimal solutions for every test instance. This calls for an effective search on each problem instance, while the model should serve to provide supporting knowledge that benefits the search. To this end, we propose T2T (Training to Testing) framework that first leverages the generative modeling to estimate the high-quality solution distribution for each instance during training, and then conducts a gradient-based search within the solution space during testing. The proposed neural search paradigm consistently leverages generative modeling, specifically diffusion, for graduated solution improvement. It disrupts the local structure of the given solution by introducing noise and reconstructs a lower-cost solution guided by the optimization objective. Experimental results on Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Maximal Independent Set (MIS) show the significant superiority of T2T, demonstrating an average performance gain of 49.15% for TSP solving and 17.27% for MIS solving compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: A neural solver trained to produce good solutions on average may not sufficiently optimize each new combinatorial problem. T2T addresses that mismatch by giving the learned model a supporting role in a search performed separately for each test instance. Training supplies knowledge of good solutions; testing uses that knowledge to improve a particular solution.

The framework learns a distribution of high-quality solutions through generative modeling, then conducts gradient-based search during testing. Its diffusion-based procedure adds noise to disrupt the local structure of a current solution and reconstructs a lower-cost one under guidance from the optimization objective. This creates a repeated improvement process connecting the learned distribution to instance-specific search.

Experiments on the Traveling Salesman Problem and Maximal Independent Set report average performance gains of 49.15% and 17.27%, respectively, over the previous state of the art. These are the paper’s reported performance gains, without a more specific metric interpretation supplied in the abstract. The results support combining generative learning with explicit test-time optimization for the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: T2T combines diffusion-based learning of good solutions with objective-guided search for each new combinatorial problem.

title: T2T: From Distribution Learning in Training to Gradient Search in Testing for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Efficiently searching for target objects in complex environments that contain various types of furniture, such as shelves, tables, and beds, is crucial for mobile robots, but it poses significant challenges due to various factors such as localization errors, limited field of view, and visual occlusion. To address this problem, we propose a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) formulation with a growing state space for object search in a 3D region. We solve this POMDP by carefully designing a perception module and developing a planning algorithm, called Growing Partially Observable Monte-Carlo Planning (GPOMCP), based on online Monte-Carlo tree search and belief tree reuse with a novel upper confidence bound. We have demonstrated that belief tree reuse is reasonable and achieves good performance when the belief differences are limited. Additionally, we introduce a guessed target object with an updating grid world to guide the search in the information-less and reward-less cases, like the absence of any detected objects. We tested our approach using Gazebo simulations on four scenarios of target finding in a realistic indoor living environment with the Fetch robot simulator. Compared to the baseline approaches, which are based on POMCP, our results indicate that our approach enables the robot to find the target object with a higher success rate faster while using the same computational requirements.

paragraphs: A robot searching an indoor environment must cope with blocked views, limited visibility, and localization errors. The authors model this search as a partially observable decision process whose state space grows as the robot explores a three-dimensional region. This formulation accommodates uncertainty about a scene that is only partly known.

Their planner, GPOMCP, combines online Monte-Carlo tree search with reuse of a belief tree and a new upper confidence bound. Reusing earlier planning work is shown to be reasonable and effective when differences between beliefs are limited. When no objects have been detected and guidance is scarce, a guessed target object and an updating grid world help direct the search.

Evaluation uses the Fetch robot simulator in Gazebo across four target-finding scenarios in a realistic indoor living environment. Compared with POMCP-based baselines, the method finds targets faster and with higher success rates under the same computational requirements. These are simulation findings, and the result concerning belief-tree reuse specifically retains its condition that the belief differences remain limited.
summary.tldr: GPOMCP combines a growing search model, conditional reuse of planning work, and exploratory guidance to improve simulated robot object search.

title: POMDP Planning for Object Search in Partially Unknown Environment

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at implementing code from functionality descriptions but struggle with algorithmic problems that require not only implementation but also identification of the suitable algorithm. Moreover, LLM-generated programs lack guaranteed correctness and require human verification. To address these challenges, we propose ALGO, a framework that synthesizes Algorithmic programs with LLM-Generated Oracles to guide the generation and verify their correctness. ALGO first generates a reference oracle by prompting an LLM to exhaustively enumerate all the combinations of relevant variables. This oracle is then utilized to guide an arbitrary search strategy in exploring the algorithm space and to verify the synthesized algorithms. Our study shows that the LLM-generatedoracles are correct for 88% of the cases. With the oracles as verifiers, ALGO can be integrated with any existing code generation model in a model-agnostic manner to enhance its performance. Experiments show that when equipped with ALGO, we achieve an 8× better one-submission pass rate over the Codex model and a 2.6× better one-submission pass rate over CodeT, the current state-of-the-art model on CodeContests. We can also get 1.3× better pass rate over the ChatGPT Code Interpreter on unseen problems. The problem set we used for testing, the prompts we used, the verifier and solution programs, and the test cases generated by ALGOare available at https://github.com/zkx06111/ALGO.

paragraphs: Algorithmic programming requires both choosing a suitable algorithm and implementing it correctly. ALGO addresses these challenges by asking a language model to generate a reference program, or oracle, that exhaustively enumerates combinations of relevant variables. This oracle supplies a reference against which proposed solutions can be checked.

The framework uses the generated oracle to guide a search through possible algorithms and verify candidate programs. Its design can accommodate different search strategies and existing code generation models. The important separation is between producing a reference answer through exhaustive enumeration and searching for an algorithmic solution that agrees with that reference.

In the study, generated oracles were correct in 88% of cases, so the reference-generation step itself was imperfect. Nevertheless, ALGO produced substantial empirical gains: one-submission pass rates were eight times those of Codex and 2.6 times those of CodeT on CodeContests. It also achieved a 1.3-fold pass-rate improvement over ChatGPT Code Interpreter on unseen problems. These findings support generated verification as a useful aid to algorithm synthesis, while retaining the stated qualification about oracle correctness.
summary.tldr: ALGO uses language-model-generated exhaustive reference programs to guide algorithm synthesis and improve empirical programming pass rates.

title: ALGO: Synthesizing Algorithmic Programs with Generated Oracle Verifiers

abstract: We investigate area convexity [Sherman17], a mysterious tool introduced to tackle optimization problems under the challenging $\ell_\infty$ geometry. We develop a deeper understanding of its relationship with conventional analyses of extragradient methods [Nemirovski04, Nesterov07]. We also give improved solvers for the subproblems required by variants of the [Sherman17] algorithm, designed through the lens of relative smoothness [BBT17, LFN18}.Leveraging these new tools, we give a state-of-the-art first-order algorithm for solving box-simplex games (a primal-dual formulation of $\ell_\infty$ regression) in a $d \times n$ matrix with bounded rows, using $O(\log d \cdot \epsilon^{-1})$ matrix-vector queries. As a consequence, we obtain improved complexities for approximate maximum flow, optimal transport, min-mean-cycle, and other basic combinatorial optimization problems. We also develop a near-linear time algorithm for a matrix generalization of box-simplex games, capturing a family of problems closely related to semidefinite programs recently used as subroutines in robust statistics and numerical linear algebra.

title: Revisiting Area Convexity: Faster Box-Simplex Games and Spectrahedral Generalizations

abstract: Graph contrastive learning (GCL) has emerged as a potent technology for numerous graph learning tasks. It has been successfully applied to real-world recommender systems, where the contrastive loss and the downstream recommendation objectives are always combined to form the overall objective function. Such a strategy is inconsistent with the original GCL paradigm, where graph embeddings are pre-trained without involving downstream training objectives. In this paper, we innovatively propose a prompt-enhanced framework for GCL-based recommender systems, namely CPTPP, which can fully leverage the advantages of the original GCL protocol through prompt tuning. Specifically, we first summarise user profiles in graph recommender systems to automatically generate personalized user prompts. These prompts will then be combined with pre-trained user embeddings to conduct prompt-tuning in downstream tasks, thereby narrowing the distinct targets between pre-training and downstream tasks. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of CPTPP against state-of-the-art baselines. A further visualization experiment demonstrates that user embeddings generated by CPTPP have a more uniform distribution, indicating a better capacity to model the diversity of user preferences.The implementation code is available online to ease reproducibility: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CPTPP-F8F4

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations from graph data, but recommender systems often train its objective together with the recommendation objective. This paper examines a different arrangement: first learn graph representations without the downstream objective, then adapt them for recommendations. The challenge is connecting what pretraining learns with what the recommendation task needs.

The proposed framework, CPTPP, makes that connection through personalized user prompts. It summarizes user profiles to generate prompts automatically, then combines those prompts with pretrained user embeddings during downstream prompt tuning. Here, the prompts help adapt the learned representation to the recommendation task and reduce the mismatch between the two training stages.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets support CPTPP's effectiveness against leading baselines. A visualization also shows more uniformly distributed user embeddings, which the authors interpret as evidence of better representation of diverse preferences. Together, these findings support personalized prompt tuning as a way to use separate graph contrastive pretraining effectively in recommendation systems.
summary.tldr: CPTPP adapts separately pretrained graph representations for recommendations using automatically generated, personalized user prompts.

title: An Empirical Study Towards Prompt-Tuning for Graph Contrastive Pre-Training in Recommendations

abstract: Generating video stories from text prompts is a complex task. In addition to having high visual quality, videos need to realistically adhere to a sequence of text prompts whilst being consistent throughout the frames. Creating a benchmark for video generation requires data annotated over time, which contrasts with the single caption used often in video datasets. To fill this gap, we collect comprehensive human annotations on three existing datasets, and introduce StoryBench: a new, challenging multi-task benchmark to reliably evaluate forthcoming text-to-video models. Our benchmark includes three video generation tasks of increasing difficulty: action execution, where the next action must be generated starting from a conditioning video; story continuation, where a sequence of actions must be executed starting from a conditioning video; and story generation, where a video must be generated from only text prompts. We evaluate small yet strong text-to-video baselines, and show the benefits of training on story-like data algorithmically generated from existing video captions. Finally, we establish guidelines for human evaluation of video stories, and reaffirm the need of better automatic metrics for video generation. StoryBench aims at encouraging future research efforts in this exciting new area.

paragraphs: StoryBench evaluates whether text-to-video models can produce coherent visual stories. A successful video must do more than look convincing: it must follow a sequence of instructions while remaining consistent across frames. The authors address the mismatch between this requirement and video datasets that describe an entire clip with just one caption.

They add comprehensive human annotations over time to three existing datasets and define three increasingly difficult tasks. Action execution generates the next action from a supplied video. Story continuation extends a supplied video through several actions. Story generation starts from text prompts alone. Together, these tasks distinguish continuing an established visual situation from creating a whole story without video context.

The paper evaluates small but strong text-to-video baselines and finds benefits from training on story-like data created algorithmically from existing captions. It also establishes guidelines for human evaluation and highlights the need for better automatic metrics. The benchmark therefore contributes both temporally detailed test material and evaluation practices for studying instruction-following and consistency throughout generated stories.
summary.tldr: StoryBench evaluates coherent video storytelling through temporally annotated data, three generation tasks, and human evaluation guidelines.

title: StoryBench: A Multifaceted Benchmark for Continuous Story Visualization

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering the ground truth ordering (ranking, top-$k$, or others) over a large number of alternatives. The wisdom of crowd is a heuristic approach based on Condorcet's Jury theorem to address this problem through collective opinions.This approach fails to recover the ground truth when the majority of the crowd is misinformed. The \emph{surprisingly popular} (SP) algorithm~\citep{prelec2017solution} is an alternative approach that is able to recover the ground truth even when experts are in minority. The SP algorithm requires the voters to predict other voters' report in the form of a full probability distribution over all rankings of alternatives. However, when the number of alternatives, $m$, is large, eliciting the prediction report or even the vote over $m$ alternatives might be too costly. In this paper, we design a scalable alternative of the SP algorithm which only requires eliciting partial preferences from the voters, and propose new variants of the SP algorithm. In particular, we propose two versions---\emph{Aggregated-SP} and \emph{Partial-SP}---that ask voters to report vote and prediction on a subset of size $k$ ($\ll m$) in terms of top alternative, partial rank, or an approval set. Through a large-scale crowdsourcing experiment on MTurk, we show that both of our approaches outperform conventional preference aggregation algorithms for the recovery of ground truth rankings, when measured in terms of Kendall-Tau distance and Spearman's $\rho$. We further analyze the collected data and demonstrate that voters' behavior in the experiment, including the minority of the experts, and the SP phenomenon, can be correctly simulated by a concentric mixtures of Mallows model. Finally, we provide theoretical bounds on the sample complexity of SP algorithms with partial rankings to demonstrate the theoretical guarantees of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Recovering a correct ranking from a crowd becomes difficult when most voters are misinformed. Surprisingly popular voting uses both voters' answers and their predictions about other voters to help recover information held by a knowledgeable minority. However, requesting full rankings and probability distributions becomes burdensome when there are many alternatives.

The paper introduces Aggregated-SP and Partial-SP to reduce that reporting burden. Voters provide an answer and a prediction for a much smaller subset of alternatives, using a top choice, partial ranking, or approval set. These variants adapt the surprisingly popular approach to partial preferences, making its information requirements more manageable as the number of alternatives grows.

A large MTurk experiment finds that both methods outperform conventional aggregation approaches on ranking recovery, measured by Kendall-Tau distance and Spearman's rho. The authors also show that a concentric mixture of Mallows models can reproduce observed voting behavior, including minority expertise and the surprisingly popular phenomenon. Sample-complexity bounds provide theoretical support for using partial rankings in these methods.
summary.tldr: Two surprisingly popular voting variants use partial preferences to reduce reporting costs while improving ranking recovery in a crowdsourcing experiment.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of SP Voting with Partial Preferences

abstract: Uncertainty quantification in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for applications where safety and reliability are important. In particular, uncertainty can be used to improve the trustworthiness of LLMs by detecting factually incorrect model responses, commonly called hallucinations. Critically, one should seek to capture the model's semantic uncertainty, i.e., the uncertainty over the meanings of LLM outputs, rather than uncertainty over lexical or syntactic variations that do not affect answer correctness.To address this problem, we propose Kernel Language Entropy (KLE), a novel method for uncertainty estimation in white- and black-box LLMs. KLE defines positive semidefinite unit trace kernels to encode the semantic similarities of LLM outputs and quantifies uncertainty using the von Neumann entropy. It considers pairwise semantic dependencies between answers (or semantic clusters), providing more fine-grained uncertainty estimates than previous methods based on hard clustering of answers. We theoretically prove that KLE generalizes the previous state-of-the-art method called semantic entropy and empirically demonstrate that it improves uncertainty quantification performance across multiple natural language generation datasets and LLM architectures.

paragraphs: A language model can express the same answer in many different ways, so variation in wording is not automatically uncertainty about meaning. This paper focuses on semantic uncertainty, which is relevant when trying to detect factually incorrect responses. It proposes Kernel Language Entropy, or KLE, for models accessed either with or without internal visibility.

KLE represents semantic relationships among outputs using positive semidefinite kernels with unit trace, then measures uncertainty through von Neumann entropy. In practical terms, the representation preserves graded pairwise relationships between answers or groups of answers. This provides finer distinctions than assigning answers to hard semantic clusters and treating those assignments as the whole description of their relationships.

The authors prove that KLE generalizes semantic entropy, the previous state-of-the-art method identified in the abstract. Experiments across multiple generation datasets and model architectures show improved uncertainty quantification. The contribution is a richer mathematical treatment of meaning-level variation, supported by empirical gains in uncertainty estimation. Such estimates are relevant to hallucination detection without making uncertainty itself a guarantee of factual correctness.
summary.tldr: Kernel Language Entropy uses graded semantic similarities to improve uncertainty estimates beyond methods based on hard answer clusters.

title: Kernel Language Entropy: Fine-grained Uncertainty Quantification for LLMs from Semantic Similarities

abstract: In this paper, we address the challenges of offline reinforcement learning (RL) under model mismatch, where the agent aims to optimize its performance through an offline dataset that may not accurately represent the deployment environment. We identify two primary challenges under the setting: inaccurate model estimation due to limited data and performance degradation caused by the model mismatch between the dataset-collecting environment and the target deployment one. To tackle these issues, we propose a unified principle of pessimism using distributionally robust Markov decision processes. We carefully construct a robust MDP with a single uncertainty set to tackle both data sparsity and model mismatch, and demonstrate that the optimal robust policy enjoys a near-optimal sub-optimality gap under the target environment across three widely used uncertainty models: total variation, $\chi^2$ divergence, and KL divergence. Our results improve upon or match the state-of-the-art performance under the total variation and KL divergence models, and provide the first result for the $\chi^2$ divergence model.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses an existing dataset to choose how an agent should act. That dataset can create two distinct difficulties: limited observations make the environment hard to estimate, and the environment that produced the data may differ from the one where the agent will operate. The paper develops a single conservative framework for addressing both sources of uncertainty.

The approach uses a distributionally robust Markov decision process. Its central construction is one uncertainty set that accounts for both sparse data and mismatch between the collection and deployment environments. Optimizing the robust policy implements pessimism by accounting for unfavorable possibilities within that set. This ties the treatment of estimation error directly to the treatment of deployment differences.

The authors prove a near-optimal bound on the robust policy's performance gap in the target environment for three uncertainty models: total variation, chi-squared divergence, and KL divergence. Their guarantees match or improve prior results for total variation and KL, and provide the first result for the chi-squared model. The contribution is a unified theoretical treatment across these three ways of describing uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A single robust uncertainty set yields near-optimal offline reinforcement learning guarantees that account for both limited data and deployment mismatch.

title: A Unified Principle of Pessimism for Offline Reinforcement Learning under Model Mismatch

abstract: The field of face recognition (FR) has undergone significant advancements with the rise of deep learning. Recently, the success of unsupervised learning and graph neural networks has demonstrated the effectiveness of data structure information. Considering that the FR task can leverage large-scale training data, which intrinsically contains significant structure information, we aim to investigate how to encode such critical structure information into the latent space. As revealed from our observations, directly aligning the structure information between the input and latent spaces inevitably suffers from an overfitting problem, leading to a structure collapse phenomenon in the latent space. To address this problem, we propose TopoFR, a novel FR model that leverages a topological structure alignment strategy called PTSA and a hard sample mining strategy named SDE. Concretely, PTSA uses persistent homology to align the topological structures of the input and latent spaces, effectively preserving the structure information and improving the generalization performance of FR model. To mitigate the impact of hard samples on the latent space structure, SDE accurately identifies hard samples by automatically computing structure damage score (SDS) for each sample, and directs the model to prioritize optimizing these samples. Experimental results on popular face benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our TopoFR over the state-of-the-art methods. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/modelscope/facechain/tree/main/face_module/TopoFR.

paragraphs: TopoFR investigates how face-recognition models can preserve structural information already present in large training datasets. The authors observe that directly aligning structure between input data and learned representations leads to overfitting and collapse of structure in the latent space. Their method addresses both how structure is aligned and which training examples receive attention.

The first component, PTSA, uses persistent homology to align the topological structures of the input and latent spaces. This provides a way to preserve structural information while improving generalization. The second component, SDE, computes a structure damage score for each sample, identifies difficult examples, and directs the model to prioritize their optimization.

Together, the components connect a global concern—maintaining useful structure in the representation—with attention to individual samples that damage that structure. Experiments on popular face-recognition benchmarks report stronger performance than the state-of-the-art methods considered. The findings support topology alignment and structure-aware hard-sample mining as complementary tools for improving the learned space used in face recognition.
summary.tldr: TopoFR improves face recognition by aligning topological structure and prioritizing samples that damage the learned representation.

title: TopoFR: A Closer Look at Topology Alignment on Face Recognition

abstract: Online Class Incremental Learning (OCIL) aims to train models incrementally, where data arrive in mini-batches, and previous data are not accessible. A major challenge in OCIL is Catastrophic Forgetting, i.e., the loss of previously learned knowledge. Among existing baselines, replay-based methods show competitive results but requires extra memory for storing exemplars, while exemplar-free (i.e., data need not be stored for replay in production) methods are resource friendly but often lack accuracy. In this paper, we propose an exemplar-free approach—Forward-only Online Analytic Learning (F-OAL). Unlike traditional methods, F-OAL does not rely on back-propagation and is forward-only, significantly reducing memory usage and computational time. Cooperating with a pre-trained frozen encoder with Feature Fusion, F-OAL only needs to update a linear classifier by recursive least square. This approach simultaneously achieves high accuracy and low resource consumption. Extensive experiments on bench mark datasets demonstrate F-OAL’s robust performance in OCIL scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/liuyuchen-cz/F-OAL

paragraphs: Online class incremental learning asks a model to learn from successive small batches as new classes arrive, without access to earlier data. A central difficulty is forgetting previously learned knowledge. Storing examples for replay can help, but uses extra memory; methods that avoid storing examples often sacrifice accuracy.

F-OAL combines a pretrained, frozen encoder with feature fusion and an analytically updated linear classifier. The encoder supplies representations while recursive least squares updates the classifier. Because this process does not rely on backpropagation, it reduces the memory and computation associated with training. It also avoids retaining examples for replay in production.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report robust performance in the online class incremental setting, combining high accuracy with low resource consumption. The approach matters because it changes which part of the model must keep learning: a fixed representation supports a classifier that can be updated as batches arrive. The stated results show that this combination can offer a favorable balance between retaining knowledge and limiting training resources.
summary.tldr: F-OAL combines frozen features with recursive classifier updates to support accurate, resource-efficient incremental learning without replay or backpropagation.

title: F-OAL: Forward-only Online Analytic Learning with Fast Training and Low Memory Footprint in Class Incremental Learning

abstract: Large transformer-based foundation models have been commonly used as pre-trained models that can be adapted to different challenging datasets and settings with state-of-the-art generalization performance. Parameter efficient fine-tuning ($\texttt{PEFT}$) provides promising generalization performance in adaptation while incurring minimum computational overhead. However, adaptation of these foundation models through $\texttt{PEFT}$ leads to accurate but severely underconfident models, especially in few-shot learning settings. Moreover, the adapted models lack accurate fine-grained uncertainty quantification capabilities limiting their broader applicability in critical domains. To fill out this critical gap, we develop a novel lightweight {Bayesian Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning} (referred to as $\texttt{Bayesian-PEFT}$) framework for large transformer-based foundation models. The framework integrates state-of-the-art $\texttt{PEFT}$ techniques with two Bayesian components to address the under-confidence issue while ensuring reliable prediction under challenging few-shot settings. The first component performs base rate adjustment to strengthen the prior belief corresponding to the knowledge gained through pre-training, making the model more confident in its predictions; the second component builds an evidential ensemble that leverages belief regularization to ensure diversity among different ensemble components.Our thorough theoretical analysis justifies that the Bayesian components can ensure reliable and accurate few-shot adaptations with well-calibrated uncertainty quantification. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets, few-shot learning scenarios, and multiple $\texttt{PEFT}$ techniques demonstrate the outstanding prediction and calibration performance by $\texttt{Bayesian-PEFT}$.
