paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts large pretrained models with little computational overhead. The authors identify a problem with this adaptation: models can remain accurate while becoming severely underconfident, especially when only a few examples are available. They also lack sufficiently precise uncertainty estimates, so prediction quality alone does not capture how reliably they communicate what they know.

Bayesian-PEFT adds two lightweight Bayesian components to existing fine-tuning techniques. A base rate adjustment strengthens prior belief associated with knowledge learned during pretraining, increasing confidence. An evidential ensemble then combines multiple components, using belief regularization to encourage diversity among them. These mechanisms address both confidence in retained knowledge and the quality of uncertainty estimates.

The paper provides theoretical analysis supporting accurate, reliable adaptation with calibrated uncertainty. Experiments span different datasets, few-shot settings, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, reporting strong prediction and calibration performance. The significance is that adaptation is evaluated on two connected requirements: making correct predictions and assigning confidence that appropriately reflects their reliability.
summary.tldr: Bayesian-PEFT combines prior adjustment and a diverse evidential ensemble to improve confidence calibration and prediction during few-shot adaptation.

title: Be Confident in What You Know: Bayesian Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning of Vision Foundation Models

abstract: Understanding the training dynamics of transformers is important to explain the impressive capabilities behind large language models. In this work, we study the dynamics of training a shallow transformer on a task of recognizing co-occurrence of two designated words. In the literature of studying training dynamics of transformers, several simplifications are commonly adopted such as weight reparameterization, attention linearization, special initialization, and lazy regime. In contrast, we analyze the gradient flow dynamics of simultaneously training three attention matrices and a linear MLP layer from random initialization, and provide a framework of analyzing such dynamics via a coupled dynamical system. We establish near minimum loss and characterize the attention model after training. We discover that gradient flow serves as an inherent mechanism that naturally divide the training process into two phases. In Phase 1, the linear MLP quickly aligns with the two target signals for correct classification, whereas the softmax attention remains almost unchanged. In Phase 2, the attention matrices and the MLP evolve jointly to enlarge the classification margin and reduce the loss to a near minimum value. Technically, we prove a novel property of the gradient flow, termed \textit{automatic balancing of gradients}, which enables the loss values of different samples to decrease almost at the same rate and further facilitates the proof of near minimum training loss. We also conduct experiments to verify our theoretical results.

The authors analyze gradient flow while simultaneously training three attention matrices and a linear MLP from random initialization. Their coupled dynamical-system framework avoids several simplifications commonly used in related analyses, including attention linearization and a lazy training regime.

The analysis identifies two phases. Initially, the linear MLP quickly aligns with the two target signals and enables correct classification, while softmax attention changes very little. Later, attention and the MLP evolve together to enlarge the classification margin and drive the loss close to its minimum.

A key theoretical property is automatic balancing of gradients, which makes different samples' losses decrease at nearly the same rate and helps establish the near-minimum-loss result. The authors also characterize the trained attention model and conduct experiments supporting the theory. Within the studied task, the findings explain how early learning in one component gives way to coordinated improvement across the transformer.
summary.tldr: A gradient-flow analysis reveals two learning phases in a shallow transformer, from early MLP alignment to joint attention and MLP refinement.

title: Training Dynamics of Transformers to Recognize Word Co-occurrence via Gradient Flow Analysis

abstract: Implicit neural networks including deep equilibrium models have achieved superior task performance with better parameter efficiency in various applications. However, it is often at the expense of higher computation costs during inference. In this work, we identify a phenomenon named $\textbf{heterogeneous convergence}$ that exists in deep equilibrium models and other iterative methods. We observe much faster convergence of state activations in certain dimensions therefore indicating the dimensionality of the underlying dynamics of the forward pass is much lower than the defined dimension of the states. We thereby propose to exploit heterogeneous convergence by storing past linear operation results (e.g., fully connected and convolutional layers) and only propagating the state activation when its change exceeds a threshold. Thus, for the already converged dimensions, the computations can be skipped. We verified our findings and reached 84\% FLOPs reduction on the implicit neural representation task, 73\% on the Sintel and 76\% on the KITTI datasets for the optical flow estimation task while keeping comparable task accuracy with the models that perform the full update.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models can achieve strong performance with relatively few parameters, but their iterative inference can require substantial computation. DeltaDEQ investigates a useful unevenness in those iterations: some dimensions of the model’s state settle much earlier than others. The authors call this heterogeneous convergence and also observe it in other iterative methods.

The proposed method stores previous results of linear operations, including fully connected and convolutional layers. It propagates a state activation only when its change exceeds a threshold. Dimensions that have already settled can therefore avoid repeated computation, concentrating updates on the parts of the state that are still changing meaningfully.

The authors report reductions in floating-point operations of 84% for an implicit neural representation task, 73% on Sintel, and 76% on KITTI for optical flow estimation. Task accuracy remains comparable to models that update the full state. These results show how exploiting uneven convergence can substantially reduce arithmetic work without requiring all state dimensions to finish converging together.
summary.tldr: DeltaDEQ skips updates to already settled state dimensions, substantially reducing computation while preserving comparable accuracy in tested tasks.

title: DeltaDEQ: Exploiting Heterogeneous Convergence for Accelerating Deep Equilibrium Iterations

abstract: Procedure learning refers to the task of identifying the key-steps and determining their logical order, given several videos of the same task. For both third-person and first-person (egocentric) videos, state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods aim at finding correspondences across videos in time to accomplish procedure learning. However, to establish temporal relationships within the sequences, these methods often rely on frame-to-frame mapping, or assume monotonic alignment of video pairs, leading to sub-optimal results. To this end, we propose to treat the video frames as samples from an unknown distribution, enabling us to frame their distance calculation as an optimal transport (OT) problem. Notably, the OT-based formulation allows us to relax the previously mentioned assumptions. To further improve performance, we enhance the OT formulation by introducing two regularization terms. The first, inverse difference moment regularization, promotes transportation between instances that are homogeneous in the embedding space as well as being temporally closer. The second, regularization based on the KL-divergence with an exponentially decaying prior smooths the alignment while enforcing conformity to the optimality (alignment obtained from vanilla OT optimization) and temporal priors. The resultant optimal transport guided procedure learning framework (`OPEL') significantly outperforms the SOTA on benchmark datasets. Specifically, we achieve 22.4\% (IoU) and 26.9\% (F1) average improvement compared to the current SOTA on large scale egocentric benchmark, EgoProceL. Furthermore, for the third person benchmarks (ProCeL and CrossTask), the proposed approach obtains 46.2\% (F1) average enhancement over SOTA.

paragraphs: Procedure learning identifies the key steps of a task and their logical order from multiple videos. Existing approaches often compare frames directly or assume video pairs can be aligned monotonically in time. OPEL instead treats frames as samples from unknown distributions and uses optimal transport to compare them, relaxing those alignment assumptions.

The method adds two forms of regularization to this transport problem. One favors correspondence between frames that are similar in their learned representations and close in time. The other uses KL divergence with an exponentially decaying prior to smooth the alignment while preserving guidance from both the unregularized transport solution and temporal information.

OPEL reports substantial improvements on first-person and third-person procedure-learning benchmarks. On EgoProceL, the average improvements over the current leading method are 22.4% in intersection over union and 26.9% in F1. Across ProCeL and CrossTask, the reported average F1 improvement is 46.2%. These results support combining a more flexible distributional alignment with explicit preferences for visual similarity and temporal coherence.
summary.tldr: OPEL uses regularized optimal transport to align task videos more flexibly and improves procedure learning on egocentric and third-person benchmarks.

title: OPEL: Optimal Transport Guided ProcedurE Learning

abstract: Through an uncertainty quantification (UQ) perspective, we show that score-based generative models (SGMs) are provably robust to the multiple sources of error in practical implementation. Our primary tool is the Wasserstein uncertainty propagation (WUP) theorem, a *model-form UQ* bound that describes how the $L^2$ error from learning the score function propagates to a Wasserstein-1 ($\mathbf{d}_1$) ball around the true data distribution under the evolution of the Fokker-Planck equation. We show how errors due to (a) finite sample approximation, (b) early stopping, (c) score-matching objective choice, (d) score function parametrization expressiveness, and (e) reference distribution choice, impact the quality of the generative model in terms of a $\mathbf{d}_1$ bound of computable quantities. The WUP theorem relies on Bernstein estimates for Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman partial differential equations (PDE) and the regularizing properties of diffusion processes. Specifically, *PDE regularity theory* shows that *stochasticity* is the key mechanism ensuring SGM algorithms are provably robust. The WUP theorem applies to integral probability metrics beyond $\mathbf{d}_1$, such as the total variation distance and the maximum mean discrepancy. Sample complexity and generalization bounds in $\mathbf{d}_1$ follow directly from the WUP theorem. Our approach requires minimal assumptions, is agnostic to the manifold hypothesis and avoids absolute continuity assumptions for the target distribution. Additionally, our results clarify the *trade-offs* among multiple error sources in SGMs.

paragraphs: Practical score-based generative models face several errors at once: limited samples, imperfect learned scores, early stopping, and choices about training objectives and reference distributions. This paper develops a mathematical framework for tracking how such errors affect the generated distribution. Robustness here means bounding their distributional consequences.

The central Wasserstein uncertainty propagation theorem connects squared score-learning error to a Wasserstein-1 bound around the true data distribution under Fokker-Planck evolution. The resulting bounds use computable quantities and expose trade-offs between error sources. The proof draws on partial differential equation regularity and identifies the smoothing effect of stochastic diffusion as the mechanism supporting robustness.

The framework also extends to other distribution comparisons, including total variation and maximum mean discrepancy. Sample-complexity and generalization bounds follow from the theorem. The approach requires minimal assumptions, does not rely on the manifold hypothesis, and avoids requiring absolute continuity of the target distribution. This broadens the distributions covered by the analysis while providing a unified account of implementation errors.
summary.tldr: A new uncertainty-propagation theorem bounds how practical errors affect score-based generators and identifies stochastic diffusion as the robustness mechanism.

title: Score-based generative models are provably robust: an uncertainty quantification perspective

abstract: Many training data attribution (TDA) methods aim to estimate how a model's behavior would change if one or more data points were removed from the training set. Methods based on implicit differentiation, such as influence functions, can be made computationally efficient, but fail to account for underspecification, the implicit bias of the optimization algorithm, or multi-stage training pipelines. By contrast, methods based on unrolling address these issues but face scalability challenges. In this work, we connect the implicit-differentiation-based and unrolling-based approaches and combine their benefits by introducing Source, an approximate unrolling-based TDA method that is computed using an influence-function-like formula. While being computationally efficient compared to unrolling-based approaches, Source is suitable in cases where implicit-differentiation-based approaches struggle, such as in non-converged models and multi-stage training pipelines. Empirically, Source outperforms existing TDA techniques in counterfactual prediction, especially in settings where implicit-differentiation-based approaches fall short.

By contrast, methods based on unrolling address these issues but face scalability challenges. In this work, we connect the implicit-differentiation-based and unrolling-based approaches and combine their benefits by introducing Source, an approximate unrolling-based TDA method that is computed using an influence-function-like formula. While being computationally efficient compared to unrolling-based approaches, Source is suitable in cases where implicit-differentiation-based approaches struggle, such as in non-converged models and multi-stage training pipelines. Empirically, Source outperforms existing TDA techniques in counterfactual prediction, especially in settings where implicit-differentiation-based approaches fall short.

paragraphs: Training-data attribution estimates how a model's behavior would change if particular training examples were removed. Efficient methods based on implicit differentiation can miss the effects of the optimization algorithm, multiple possible fitted solutions, or training pipelines with several stages. Methods that unroll the training process address these issues, but become difficult to scale.

Source connects these two approaches through approximate unrolling. It accounts for the training process using an approximation that can be evaluated with a formula resembling an influence function. The goal is to retain useful information about how training produced the model while avoiding the computational burden of directly unrolling that process.

The authors describe Source as suitable for cases that challenge implicit-differentiation methods, including models that have not converged and pipelines with multiple training stages. Experiments show better counterfactual prediction than existing attribution methods, especially in those difficult settings. These findings support incorporating training history into attribution efficiently: the relevant question is how removing data would affect the trained model through its learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Source uses approximate training unrolling to estimate data-removal effects efficiently, improving attribution for non-converged models and multistage training.

title: Training Data Attribution via Approximate Unrolling

abstract: While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has proven beneficial for efficiently fine-tuning large models, LoRA fine-tuned text-to-image diffusion models lack diversity in the generated images, as the model tends to copy data from the observed training samples. This effect becomes more pronounced at higher values of adapter strength and for adapters with higher ranks which are fine-tuned on smaller datasets. To address these challenges, we present FouRA, a novel low-rank method that learns projections in the Fourier domain along with learning a flexible input-dependent adapter rank selection strategy. Through extensive experiments and analysis, we show that FouRA successfully solves the problems related to data copying and distribution collapse while significantly improving the generated image quality. We demonstrate that FouRA enhances the generalization of fine-tuned models thanks to its adaptive rank selection. We further show that the learned projections in the frequency domain are decorrelated and prove effective when merging multiple adapters. While FouRA is motivated for vision tasks, we also demonstrate its merits for language tasks on commonsense reasoning and GLUE benchmarks.

FouRA addresses this behavior through a different adaptation design.

title: FouRA: Fourier Low-Rank Adaptation

abstract: While significant progress has been made on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), a comprehensive comparison of these methods across a wide range of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) is still lacking. This study introduces PINNacle, a benchmarking tool designed to fill this gap. PINNacle provides a diverse dataset, comprising over 20 distinct PDEs from various domains, including heat conduction, fluid dynamics, biology, and electromagnetics. These PDEs encapsulate key challenges inherent to real-world problems, such as complex geometry, multi-scale phenomena, nonlinearity, and high dimensionality. PINNacle also offers a user-friendly toolbox, incorporating about 10 state-of-the-art PINN methods for systematic evaluation and comparison. We have conducted extensive experiments with these methods, offering insights into their strengths and weaknesses. In addition to providing a standardized means of assessing performance, PINNacle also offers an in-depth analysis to guide future research, particularly in areas such as domain decomposition methods and loss reweighting for handling multi-scale problems and complex geometry. To the best of our knowledge, it is the largest benchmark with a diverse and comprehensive evaluation that will undoubtedly foster further research in PINNs.

paragraphs: PINNacle provides a common testing framework for physics-informed neural networks used to solve partial differential equations. Although many PINN methods have been developed, their performance has lacked a broad, systematic comparison across different equations. The benchmark addresses that gap by putting varied problems and methods into a shared evaluation setting.

Its dataset includes more than twenty distinct PDEs spanning heat conduction, fluid dynamics, biology, and electromagnetics. The problems incorporate challenges such as complicated geometry, behavior at multiple scales, nonlinearity, and high dimensionality. A toolbox containing about ten state-of-the-art PINN methods supports systematic comparisons across this range, making it possible to examine how methods behave under different kinds of difficulty.

The authors conduct extensive experiments and analyze the methods’ strengths and weaknesses. Their discussion points toward research on domain decomposition and loss reweighting for problems involving multiple scales and complex geometry. PINNacle’s contribution is therefore both an evaluation resource and an analysis of where existing approaches need improvement, helping connect future method development to a wider range of PDE challenges.
summary.tldr: PINNacle benchmarks about ten physics-informed neural network methods on more than twenty diverse PDEs and analyzes their strengths and weaknesses.

title: PINNacle: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving PDEs

abstract: RNA plays a pivotal role in translating genetic instructions into functional outcomes, underscoring its importance in biological processes and disease mechanisms. Despite the emergence of numerous deep learning approaches for RNA, particularly universal RNA language models, there remains a significant lack of standardized benchmarks to assess the effectiveness of these methods. In this study, we introduce the first comprehensive RNA benchmark BEACON **BE**nchm**A**rk for **CO**mprehensive R**N**A Task and Language Models).First, BEACON comprises 13 distinct tasks derived from extensive previous work covering structural analysis, functional studies, and engineering applications, enabling a comprehensive assessment of the performance of methods on various RNA understanding tasks. Second, we examine a range of models, including traditional approaches like CNNs, as well as advanced RNA foundation models based on language models, offering valuable insights into the task-specific performances of these models. Third, we investigate the vital RNA language model components from the tokenizer and positional encoding aspects. Notably, our findings emphasize the superiority of single nucleotide tokenization and the effectiveness of Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi) over traditional positional encoding methods. Based on these insights, a simple yet strong baseline called BEACON-B is proposed, which can achieve outstanding performance with limited data and computational resources. The datasets and source code of our benchmark are available at https://github.com/terry-r123/RNABenchmark.

paragraphs: RNA learning methods address questions about molecular structure, biological function, and sequence engineering, but comparing them requires a common evaluation framework. BEACON supplies such a framework through 13 tasks drawn from previous research. Its breadth allows methods to be assessed across several kinds of RNA understanding rather than through a single task.

The authors evaluate both traditional neural approaches, including convolutional networks, and RNA foundation models built around language modeling. They also examine two basic design decisions: how RNA sequences are divided into input tokens and how models represent position. These comparisons expose task-specific performance and help connect model design choices to observed results.

The findings favor treating each nucleotide as its own token and using Attention with Linear Biases, or ALiBi, over the traditional positional encodings examined. Based on these observations, the authors propose BEACON-B, a simple baseline that achieves strong performance with limited data and computation. The benchmark therefore contributes both a standardized assessment framework and an empirically motivated model design.
summary.tldr: BEACON evaluates RNA models across 13 tasks and uses its findings to build a strong baseline with limited data and computation.

title: BEACON: Benchmark for Comprehensive RNA Tasks and Language Models

abstract: Real-world Image Dehazing (RID) aims to alleviate haze-induced degradation in real-world settings. This task remains challenging due to the complexities in accurately modeling real haze distributions and the scarcity of paired real-world data. To address these challenges, we first introduce a cooperative unfolding network that jointly models atmospheric scattering and image scenes, effectively integrating physical knowledge into deep networks to restore haze-contaminated details. Additionally, we propose the first RID-oriented iterative mean-teacher framework, termed the Coherence-based Label Generator, to generate high-quality pseudo labels for network training. Specifically, we provide an optimal label pool to store the best pseudo-labels during network training, leveraging both global and local coherence to select high-quality candidates and assign weights to prioritize haze-free regions. We verify the effectiveness of our method, with experiments demonstrating that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on RID tasks. Code will be available at https://github.com/cnyvfang/CORUN-Colabator.

paragraphs: Removing haze from real photographs is difficult because real haze distributions are complex and paired training examples are scarce. This paper addresses both the restoration model and the training supervision. Its cooperative unfolding network jointly models atmospheric scattering and image scenes, incorporating physical knowledge into a deep network to recover details obscured by haze.

To provide training targets, the authors introduce an iterative mean-teacher framework called the Coherence-based Label Generator. It produces pseudo labels and maintains a pool of the best candidates encountered during training. Both global and local coherence guide candidate selection, while weighting gives priority to haze-free regions.

The two components serve complementary purposes: the network incorporates knowledge of how haze affects images, and the label generator improves the supervision available when paired real-world data are scarce. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on real-world dehazing tasks. The stated findings support combining physically informed restoration with selective pseudo-label generation as a way to address the modeling and data challenges together.
summary.tldr: A physically informed restoration network and coherence-based pseudo labels jointly improve real-world image dehazing.

title: Real-world Image Dehazing with Coherence-based Pseudo Labeling and Cooperative Unfolding Network

abstract: Physically realistic materials are pivotal in augmenting the realism of 3D assets across various applications and lighting conditions. However, existing 3D assets and generative models often lack authentic material properties. Manual assignment of materials using graphic software is a tedious and time-consuming task. In this paper, we exploit advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly GPT-4V, to present a novel approach, Make-it-Real: 1) We demonstrate that GPT-4V can effectively recognize and describe materials, allowing the construction of a detailed material library. 2) Utilizing a combination of visual cues and hierarchical text prompts, GPT-4V precisely identifies and aligns materials with the corresponding components of 3D objects. 3) The correctly matched materials are then meticulously applied as reference for the new SVBRDF material generation according to the original albedo map, significantly enhancing their visual authenticity. Make-it-Real offers a streamlined integration into the 3D content creation workflow, showcasing its utility as an essential tool for developers of 3D assets.

paragraphs: A 3D object's realism depends on its material properties as well as its visible colors. Materials determine how its appearance responds to lighting, yet existing assets and generative models often lack authentic material information. Make-it-Real addresses the time-consuming task of assigning suitable materials manually by using a multimodal language model to support that process.

The approach first uses GPT-4V's ability to recognize and describe materials to construct a detailed material library. It then combines visual evidence with hierarchical text prompts to match materials to the appropriate components of a 3D object. This links the model's interpretation of an object's parts to references that can guide material creation.

The matched materials serve as references for generating spatially varying reflectance properties, using the object's original albedo map. The authors report that this process substantially improves visual authenticity and can fit into a 3D content-creation workflow. The contribution connects material understanding, component-level matching, and material generation into a pipeline intended to reduce the burden of producing realistically surfaced 3D assets.
summary.tldr: Make-it-Real uses GPT-4V to identify and match materials to 3D object parts, guiding the generation of more realistic surface properties.

title: Make-it-Real: Unleashing Large Multimodal Model for Painting 3D Objects with Realistic Materials

abstract: We present DC-Gaussian, a new method for generating novel views from in-vehicle dash cam videos. While neural rendering techniques have made significant strides in driving scenarios, existing methods are primarily designed for videos collected by autonomous vehicles. However, these videos are limited in both quantity and diversity compared to dash cam videos, which are more widely used across various types of vehicles and capture a broader range of scenarios. Dash cam videos often suffer from severe obstructions such as reflections and occlusions on the windshields, which significantly impede the application of neural rendering techniques. To address this challenge, we develop DC-Gaussian based on the recent real-time neural rendering technique 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Our approach includes an adaptive image decomposition module to model reflections and occlusions in a unified manner. Additionally, we introduce illumination-aware obstruction modeling to manage reflections and occlusions under varying lighting conditions. Lastly, we employ a geometry-guided Gaussian enhancement strategy to improve rendering details by incorporating additional geometry priors. Experiments on self-captured and public dash cam videos show that our method not only achieves state-of-the-art performance in novel view synthesis, but also accurately reconstructing captured scenes getting rid of obstructions.

paragraphs: Dash cameras record driving scenes across many vehicles and environments, making their videos an appealing source for reconstructing scenes and rendering new viewpoints. A major obstacle is the windshield: reflections and occlusions can obscure the outside world. The paper addresses these effects directly instead of treating dash-camera footage as equivalent to the video typically collected by autonomous vehicles.

DC-Gaussian builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting and introduces an adaptive image decomposition module that models reflections and occlusions together. An illumination-aware component accounts for how these obstructions change under different lighting conditions. A further enhancement uses geometric guidance to improve the details represented by the Gaussians. These components address both unwanted image content and the quality of the underlying scene reconstruction.

Experiments use both self-captured and public dash-camera videos. The authors report state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis performance and accurate reconstructions with obstructions removed. The stated findings support adapting neural rendering to the specific visual interference in windshield footage, helping make this widely available video source useful for scene reconstruction.
summary.tldr: DC-Gaussian models windshield interference and lighting changes to improve scene reconstruction and novel-view rendering from dash-camera videos.

title: DC-Gaussian: Improving 3D Gaussian Splatting for Reflective Dash Cam Videos

abstract: Achieving robust 3D perception in the face of corrupted data presents an challenging hurdle within 3D vision research. Contemporary transformer-based point cloud recognition models, albeit advanced, tend to overfit to specific patterns, consequently undermining their robustness against corruption. In this work, we introduce the Target-Guided Adversarial Point Cloud Transformer, termed APCT, a novel architecture designed to augment global structure capture through an adversarial feature erasing mechanism predicated on patterns discerned at each step during training. Specifically, APCT integrates an Adversarial Significance Identifier and a Target-guided Promptor. The Adversarial Significance Identifier, is tasked with discerning token significance by integrating global contextual analysis, utilizing a structural salience index algorithm alongside an auxiliary supervisory mechanism. The Target-guided Promptor, is responsible for accentuating the propensity for token discard within the self-attention mechanism, utilizing the value derived above, consequently directing the model attention towards alternative segments in subsequent stages. By iteratively applying this strategy in multiple steps during training, the network progressively identifies and integrates an expanded array of object-associated patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple corruption benchmarks.

paragraphs: Point cloud recognition models can rely too heavily on particular patterns and become less robust when their inputs are corrupted. APCT addresses this by erasing significant features during training, encouraging the model to capture a broader range of object structure. The features targeted for erasure depend on the patterns identified at each training step.

An Adversarial Significance Identifier estimates token importance using global context, a structural salience index, and auxiliary supervision. A Target-guided Promptor then uses those importance values to increase the tendency to discard tokens within self-attention. This directs later processing toward alternative parts of the object representation.

Repeating the process over multiple training steps encourages the network to identify and integrate additional object-related patterns. The mechanism aims to strengthen global structure capture by making familiar cues less dependable during training. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on multiple corruption benchmarks, supporting this strategy for improving recognition robustness in the evaluated corrupted point cloud settings.
summary.tldr: APCT repeatedly suppresses important point-cloud features during training to learn broader object structure and improve corruption robustness.

title: Target-Guided Adversarial Point Cloud Transformer Towards Recognition Against Real-world Corruptions

abstract: Many studies have proposed attack methods to generate adversarial patterns for evading pedestrian detection, alarming the computer vision community about the need for more attention to the robustness of detectors. However, adversarial patterns optimized by these methods commonly have limited performance at medium to long distances in the physical world. To overcome this limitation, we identify two main challenges. First, in existing methods, there is commonly an appearance gap between simulated distant adversarial patterns and their physical world counterparts, leading to incorrect optimization. Second, there exists a conflict between adversarial losses at different distances, which causes difficulties in optimization. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a Full Distance Attack (FDA) method. Our physical world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our FDA patterns across various detection models like YOLOv5, Deformable-DETR, and Mask RCNN. Codes available at https://github.com/zhicheng2T0/Full-Distance-Attack.git

paragraphs: Adversarial visual patterns can cause pedestrian detectors to miss people, making them useful for studying detector robustness. Existing patterns often become less effective at medium and long viewing distances in physical settings. This paper investigates why performance changes with distance and introduces Full Distance Attack, or FDA, to address the identified problems.

The authors distinguish two challenges. First, a simulated view of a distant pattern can differ from how the physical pattern actually appears, so optimization may improve the wrong visual representation. Second, the adversarial objectives associated with different distances can conflict. A change that helps at one distance can therefore complicate optimization across the full set of distances.

FDA is designed to address both challenges. Physical-world experiments demonstrate effective patterns across several detector architectures, including YOLOv5, Deformable-DETR, and Mask RCNN. The findings show why robustness evaluation needs to consider viewing distance and the match between simulation and physical appearance. The reported evidence establishes effectiveness in the tested settings, rather than a guarantee of evasion at every possible distance or against every detector.
summary.tldr: FDA addresses simulation mismatch and conflicting distance-specific objectives to improve physical adversarial patterns across viewing distances.

title: Full-Distance Evasion of Pedestrian Detectors in the Physical World

abstract: In most practical applications such as recommendation systems, display advertising, and so forth, the collected data often contains missing values and those missing values are generally missing-not-at-random, which deteriorates the prediction performance of models. Some existing estimators and regularizers attempt to achieve unbiased estimation to improve the predictive performance. However, variances and generalization bound of these methods are generally unbounded when the propensity scores tend to zero, compromising their stability and robustness. In this paper, we first theoretically reveal that limitations of regularization techniques. Besides, we further illustrate that, for more general estimators, unbiasedness will inevitably lead to unbounded variance. These general laws inspire us that the estimator designs is not merely about eliminating bias, reducing variance, or simply achieve a bias-variance trade-off. Instead, it involves a quantitative joint optimization of bias and variance. Then, we develop a systematic fine-grained dynamic learning framework to jointly optimize bias and variance, which adaptively selects an appropriate estimator for each user-item pair according to the predefined objective function. With this operation, the generalization bounds and variances of models are reduced and bounded with theoretical guarantees. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify the theoretical results and the effectiveness of the proposed dynamic learning framework.

paragraphs: In recommendation and advertising data, missing observations often reflect a selective collection process. Methods that correct this selection can become unstable when propensity scores, which describe observation probabilities, approach zero. This paper examines why pursuing unbiased estimates in that setting can produce unbounded variance and unbounded generalization guarantees.

The authors first analyze limitations of regularization and then establish a broader connection between unbiasedness and unbounded variance in the setting they study. Their response is to optimize bias and variance quantitatively together. They introduce a dynamic framework that selects an estimator separately for each user-item pair according to a predefined objective.

This pair-specific choice lets the learning process adapt its estimation strategy at a finer level than choosing one estimator for all observations. The paper provides theoretical guarantees that the resulting variances and generalization bounds are reduced and bounded. Extensive experiments support the analysis and the framework's effectiveness, showing the value of explicitly accounting for both sources of estimation error.
summary.tldr: The framework selects estimators for individual user-item pairs to jointly control bias and variance when observations are missing nonrandomly.

title: Fine-Grained Dynamic Framework for Bias-Variance Joint Optimization on Data Missing Not at Random

abstract: We introduce FlexCap, a vision-language model that generates region-specific descriptions of varying lengths. FlexCap is trained to produce length-conditioned captions for input boxes, enabling control over information density, with descriptions ranging from concise object labels to detailed captions. To achieve this, we create large-scale training datasets of image region descriptions with varying lengths from captioned web images. We demonstrate FlexCap’s effectiveness in several applications: first, it achieves strong performance in dense captioning tasks on the Visual Genome dataset. Second, we show how FlexCap’s localized descriptions can serve as input to a large language model to create a visual question answering (VQA) system, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on multiple VQA benchmarks. Our experiments illustrate FlexCap’s utility for tasks including image labeling, object attribute recognition, and visual dialog. Project webpage: https://flex-cap.github.io.

paragraphs: FlexCap describes selected regions of an image while allowing control over how much detail each description contains. Given a box around a region, it can produce text ranging from a short object label to a fuller caption. The central capability is control over information density for a particular part of an image.

The model is trained on captions conditioned on their requested length. To support this training, the authors construct large datasets of region descriptions at different lengths using captioned images from the web. This gives the model training examples that connect the same kind of localized visual input with different levels of verbal detail.

FlexCap shows strong dense-captioning performance on Visual Genome. Its local descriptions can also be passed to a language model to build a visual question answering system, which achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on multiple benchmarks. Additional experiments demonstrate uses in image labeling, recognizing object attributes, and visual dialogue. Together, these applications show how adjustable regional descriptions can support broader image-understanding tasks.
summary.tldr: FlexCap generates descriptions of selected image regions at controllable lengths and supports tasks including visual question answering.

title: FlexCap: Describe Anything in Images in Controllable Detail

abstract: We describe a family of architectures to support transductive inference by allowing memory to grow to a finite but a-priori unknown bound while making efficient use of finite resources for inference. Current architectures use such resources to represent data either eidetically over a finite span ('context' in Transformers), or fading over an infinite span (in State Space Models, or SSMs). Recent hybrid architectures have combined eidetic and fading memory, but with limitations that do not allow the designer or the learning process to seamlessly modulate the two, nor to extend the eidetic memory span. We leverage ideas from Stochastic Realization Theory to develop a class of models called B'MOJO to seamlessly combine eidetic and fading memory within an elementary composable module. The overall architecture can be used to implement models that can access short-term eidetic memory 'in-context,' permanent structural memory 'in-weights,' fading memory 'in-state,' and long-term eidetic memory 'in-storage' by natively incorporating retrieval from an asynchronously updated memory. We show that Transformers, existing SSMs such as Mamba, and hybrid architectures such as Jamba are special cases of B'MOJO and describe a basic implementation that can be stacked and scaled efficiently in hardware. We test B'MOJO on transductive inference tasks, such as associative recall, where it outperforms existing SSMs and Hybrid models; as a baseline, we test ordinary language modeling where B'MOJO achieves perplexity comparable to similarly-sized Transformers and SSMs up to 1.4B parameters, while being up to 10% faster to train. Finally, we test whether models trained inductively on a-priori bounded sequences (up to 8K tokens) can still perform transductive inference on sequences many-fold longer. B'MOJO's ability to modulate eidetic and fading memory results in better inference on longer sequences tested up to 32K tokens, four-fold the length of the longest sequences seen during training.

Transformer context and state-space models emphasize different forms of memory. The proposed architecture makes them adjustable within one composable module, while allowing memory to grow to a finite size that need not be specified beforehand.

Drawing on Stochastic Realization Theory, the framework accommodates short-term context, learned weights, recurrent state, and long-term storage with asynchronous retrieval. The authors show that Transformers, Mamba, and Jamba fit within the framework as special cases. They also describe an implementation designed to stack and scale efficiently on hardware.

In associative recall and related tasks, B'MOJO outperforms the tested state-space and hybrid models. summary.tldr: B'MOJO combines explicit and fading memory, improving tested recall and longer-sequence inference while maintaining competitive language modeling.

title: B'MOJO: Hybrid State Space Realizations of Foundation Models with Eidetic and Fading Memory

abstract: Binarization, which converts weight parameters to binary values, has emerged as an effective strategy to reduce the size of large language models (LLMs). However, typical binarization techniques significantly diminish linguistic effectiveness of LLMs.To address this issue, we introduce a novel binarization technique called Mixture of Scales (BinaryMoS). Unlike conventional methods, BinaryMoS employs multiple scaling experts for binary weights, dynamically merging these experts for each token to adaptively generate scaling factors. This token-adaptive approach boosts the representational power of binarized LLMs by enabling contextual adjustments to the values of binary weights. Moreover, because this adaptive process only involves the scaling factors rather than the entire weight matrix, BinaryMoS maintains compression efficiency similar to traditional static binarization methods. Our experimental results reveal that BinaryMoS surpasses conventional binarization techniques in various natural language processing tasks and even outperforms 2-bit quantization methods, all while maintaining similar model size to static binarization techniques.

paragraphs: Converting language-model weights to binary values can greatly reduce model size, but conventional binarization damages language performance. BinaryMoS addresses this tradeoff by making the scaling of binary weights depend on the token being processed. The binary representation remains compact while its effective values can adjust to context.

The method uses several scaling experts and dynamically combines them for each token. Their combination produces adaptive scaling factors, increasing the representational flexibility available to the binarized model. Because this adaptation operates on the scaling factors rather than on the entire weight matrix, the approach retains compression efficiency similar to static binarization.

Experiments across natural-language-processing tasks show BinaryMoS outperforming conventional binarization methods and even the compared two-bit quantization methods. Its model size remains similar to that of static binary approaches. The results suggest that allocating flexibility to token-dependent scales can recover useful language capability without giving up the compact storage associated with binary weights.
summary.tldr: BinaryMoS improves binarized language models through token-dependent scaling while retaining model sizes similar to static binarization.

title: Mixture of Scales: Memory-Efficient Token-Adaptive Binarization for Large Language Models

abstract: Many causal inference frameworks rely on a staticity assumption, where repeated interventions are expected to yield consistent outcomes, often summarized by metrics like the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). This assumption, however, frequently fails in dynamic environments where interventions can alter the system's underlying causal structure, rendering traditional `static' ATE insufficient or misleading. Recent works on meta-causal models (MCM) offer a promising avenue by enabling qualitative reasoning over evolving relationships. In this work, we propose a specific class of MCM with desirable properties for explicitly modeling and predicting intervention outcomes under meta-causal dynamics, together with a first method for meta-causal analysis. Through expository examples in high-impact domains of medical treatment and judicial decision-making, we highlight the severe consequences that arise when system dynamics are neglected and demonstrate the successful application of meta-causal strategies to navigate these challenges.

paragraphs: An intervention can change more than an immediate outcome: it can also change how the system responds to later interventions. This paper studies settings where causal relationships themselves evolve. Under those conditions, treating repeated interventions as having stable effects can make a static average treatment effect insufficient or misleading.

The authors build on meta-causal models, which support reasoning about changing causal relationships. They propose a particular class of these models with properties intended to support explicit modeling and prediction of intervention outcomes under such dynamics. They also introduce a method for meta-causal analysis, moving from qualitative recognition of evolving relationships toward analyzing interventions within the proposed framework.

Expository examples concern medical treatment and judicial decision-making. They illustrate serious consequences of neglecting system dynamics and demonstrate how meta-causal strategies can navigate the modeled situations. The contribution is a framework and analysis method for interventions that may reshape their own future effects. The examples establish the intended reasoning use cases, rather than reporting clinical or judicial deployment outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper develops meta-causal models and an analysis method for interventions that can change a system’s underlying causal relationships.

title: When Causal Dynamics Matter: Adapting Causal Strategies through Meta-Aware Interventions

abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) offers unprecedented opportunities to reimagine peer review beyond the constraints of traditional workflows. Despite these opportunities, prior efforts have largely focused on replicating traditional review workflows with LLMs serving as direct substitutes for human reviewers, while limited attention has been given to exploring new paradigms that fundamentally rethink how LLMs can participate in the academic review process. In this paper, we introduce and explore a novel mechanism that employs LLM agents to perform pairwise comparisons among manuscripts instead of individual scoring. By aggregating outcomes from substantial pairwise evaluations, this approach enables a more accurate and robust measure of relative manuscript quality. Our experiments demonstrate that this comparative approach significantly outperforms traditional rating-based methods in identifying high-impact papers. However, our analysis also reveals emergent biases in the selection process, notably a reduced novelty in research topics and an increased institutional imbalance. These findings highlight both the transformative potential of rethinking peer review with LLMs and critical challenges that future systems must address to ensure equity and diversity.

paragraphs: Using language models for peer review creates an opportunity to change the review process itself. This paper explores a mechanism in which model agents compare two manuscripts at a time, instead of assigning each manuscript an individual score. The goal is to build a more accurate and robust assessment of relative manuscript quality.

The method aggregates outcomes from many pairwise evaluations. Each comparison contributes evidence about the manuscripts’ relative standing, and the combined results form the broader assessment. In the reported experiments, this comparative approach significantly outperforms traditional rating-based methods at identifying high-impact papers, supporting the value of redesigning the evaluation task around relative judgments.

The analysis also finds consequential selection biases: selected research topics become less novel, and institutional imbalance increases. These findings qualify the performance gain because better identification of high-impact papers does not resolve questions about diversity and equity. The paper therefore presents pairwise comparison as a promising review mechanism whose selection behavior needs attention alongside its ability to identify impactful work.
summary.tldr: Pairwise LLM manuscript comparisons better identify high-impact papers in experiments but increase institutional imbalance and reduce topic novelty.

title: From Replication to Redesign: Exploring Pairwise Comparisons for LLM-Based Peer Review

abstract: Recent research shows that large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to hijacking attacks under the scenario of in-context learning (ICL) where LLMs demonstrate impressive capabilities in performing tasks by conditioning on a sequence of in-context examples (ICEs) (i.e., prompts with task-specific input-output pairs). Adversaries can manipulate the provided ICEs to steer the model toward attacker-specified outputs, effectively ''hijacking'' the model's decision-making process. Unlike traditional adversarial attacks targeting single inputs, hijacking attacks in LLMs aim to subtly manipulate the initial few examples to influence the model's behavior across a range of subsequent inputs, which requires distributed and stealthy perturbations. However, existing approaches overlook how to effectively allocate the perturbation budget across ICEs. We argue that fixed budgets miss the potential of dynamic reallocation to improve attack success while maintaining high stealthiness and text quality. In this paper, we propose BAM-ICL, a novel **b**udgeted **a**dversarial **m**anipulation hijacking attack framework for in-context learning. We also consider a more practical yet stringent scenario where ICEs arrive sequentially and only the current ICE can be perturbed. BAM-ICL mainly consists of two stages: In the offline stage, where we assume the adversary has access to data drawn from the same distribution as the target task, we develop a global gradient-based attack to learn optimal budget allocations across ICEs. In the online stage, where ICEs arrive sequentially, perturbations are generated progressively according to the learned budget profile. We evaluate BAM-ICL on diverse LLMs and datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that it achieves superior attack success rates and stealthiness, and the adversarial ICEs are highly transferable to other models.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from examples included in its prompt. Those examples can also become an attack surface: manipulated demonstrations may steer the model toward an attacker's preferred outputs on subsequent inputs. This paper studies how to distribute a limited amount of manipulation across multiple examples.

BAM-ICL uses an offline stage to learn how the perturbation budget should be allocated. This stage assumes the attacker has data from the same distribution as the target task and uses a global gradient-based attack to learn an allocation profile. The central idea is that different examples can warrant different amounts of modification.

The online stage applies that learned profile as examples arrive sequentially, under the restriction that only the current example can be changed. This makes allocation relevant even when earlier examples cannot be revisited. Across the evaluated models and datasets, the authors report stronger attack success and stealthiness, along with transfer to other models. These results identify budget allocation as an important component of attacks on demonstration-based learning.
summary.tldr: BAM-ICL learns how to allocate limited changes across prompt examples to improve the success and stealthiness of in-context learning attacks.

title: BAM-ICL: Causal Hijacking In-Context Learning with Budgeted Adversarial Manipulation

abstract: Watermarking is a promising defense against the misuse of large language models (LLMs), yet it remains vulnerable to scrubbing and spoofing attacks. This vulnerability stems from an inherent trade-off governed by watermark window size: smaller windows resist scrubbing better but are easier to reverse-engineer, enabling low-cost statistics-based spoofing attacks. This work expands the trade-off boundary by introducing a novel mechanism, equivalent texture keys, where multiple tokens within a watermark window can independently support the detection. Based on the redundancy, we propose a watermark scheme with **S**ub-vocabulary decomposed **E**quivalent t**E**xture **K**ey (**SEEK**). It achieves a Pareto improvement, increasing the resilience against scrubbing attacks without compromising robustness to spoofing. Our code will be available at [https://github.com/Hearum/SeekWM](https://github.com/Hearum/SeekWM).

paragraphs: Text watermarking faces two opposing threats: scrubbing removes evidence of a watermark, while spoofing imitates that evidence. The paper identifies watermark window size as a source of tension between them. Smaller windows provide greater resistance to scrubbing, but they are easier to reverse-engineer, making inexpensive statistical spoofing attacks more feasible.

The proposed mechanism, equivalent texture keys, introduces redundancy inside a watermark window. Multiple tokens can each independently support watermark detection. This changes how detection evidence is distributed within the window, giving the scheme another way to improve resilience beyond adjusting window size. The authors incorporate the mechanism into SEEK, a watermarking scheme based on sub-vocabulary decomposition.

The paper reports a Pareto improvement: greater resilience against scrubbing without sacrificing robustness to spoofing. That is a claim about improving the trade-off between the two attack types, rather than eliminating either threat. The contribution matters because it targets the structure of the detection signal itself, showing how redundant support can improve one protection dimension while preserving the other.
summary.tldr: SEEK adds redundant watermark evidence to improve resistance to scrubbing without reducing robustness to spoofing.

title: Enhancing LLM Watermark Resilience Against Both Scrubbing and Spoofing Attacks

abstract: Zero-shot optimization aims to achieve both generalization and performance gains on solving previously unseen black-box optimization problems over SOTA methods without task-specific tuning. Pre-trained optimization models (POMs) address this challenge by learning a general mapping from task features to optimization strategies, enabling direct deployment on new tasks. In this paper, we identify three essential components that determine the effectiveness of POMs: (1) task feature modeling, which captures structural properties of optimization problems; (2) optimization strategy representation, which defines how new candidate solutions are generated; and (3) the feature-to-strategy mapping mechanism learned during pre-training. However, existing POMs often suffer from weak feature representations, rigid strategy modeling, and unstable training. To address these limitations, we propose EPOM, an enhanced framework for pre-trained optimization. EPOM enriches task representations using a cross-attention-based tokenizer, improves strategy diversity through deformable attention, and stabilizes training by replacing non-differentiable operations with a differentiable crossover mechanism. Together, these enhancements yield better generalization, faster convergence, and more reliable performance in zero-shot black-box optimization.

paragraphs: Zero-shot black-box optimization asks a pretrained optimizer to solve unfamiliar problems without task-specific tuning. Such a model must recognize useful problem features and turn them into strategies for generating candidate solutions. The paper organizes this challenge around three components: task representations, strategy representations, and the learned mapping connecting the two.

EPOM improves each part of that pipeline. A tokenizer based on cross-attention builds richer task representations, while deformable attention increases the diversity of optimization strategies. A differentiable crossover mechanism replaces non-differentiable operations to make training more stable. These changes target weak representations, rigid candidate-generation strategies, and unstable learning identified in existing pretrained optimization models.

The authors report better generalization, faster convergence, and more reliable performance on zero-shot black-box optimization. The approach matters because deployment on new tasks depends on both recognizing unfamiliar structure and responding with a suitable strategy. EPOM treats these abilities, together with training stability, as connected design problems for an optimizer intended to transfer without additional tuning.
summary.tldr: EPOM improves pretrained black-box optimizers through richer task features, more flexible strategies, and differentiable training operations.

title: Enhancing Zero-Shot Black-Box Optimization via Pretrained Models with Efficient Population Modeling, Interaction, and Stable Gradient Approximation

abstract: Current evaluation paradigms for large language models (LLMs) represent a critical blind spot in AI research—relying on opaque numerical metrics that conceal fundamental limitations in spatial reasoning while providing no intuitive understanding of model capabilities. This deficiency creates a dangerous disconnect between reported performance and practical abilities, particularly for applications requiring physical world understanding. We introduce LTD-Bench, a breakthrough benchmark that transforms LLM evaluation from abstract scores to directly observable visual outputs by requiring models to generate drawings through dot matrices or executable code. This approach makes spatial reasoning limitations immediately apparent even to non-experts, bridging the fundamental gap between statistical performance and intuitive assessment. LTD-Bench implements a comprehensive methodology with complementary generation tasks (testing spatial imagination) and recognition tasks (assessing spatial perception) across three progressively challenging difficulty levels, methodically evaluating both directions of the critical language-spatial mapping. Our extensive experiments with state-of-the-art models expose an alarming capability gap: even LLMs achieving impressive results on traditional benchmarks demonstrate profound deficiencies in establishing bidirectional mappings between language and spatial concepts—a fundamental limitation that undermines their potential as genuine world models. Furthermore, LTD-Bench's visual outputs enable powerful diagnostic analysis, offering a potential approach to investigate model similarity. Our dataset and codes are available at https://github.com/walktaster/LTD-Bench.

paragraphs: LTD-Bench evaluates language models through drawings that people can inspect directly. Models produce visual outputs using dot matrices or executable code. The motivation is that numerical benchmark scores can obscure weaknesses in spatial reasoning, whereas a drawing can make a model's interpretation of spatial concepts immediately visible.

The benchmark tests both directions of the connection between language and space. Generation tasks examine spatial imagination, while recognition tasks assess spatial perception. Three progressively harder levels organize these complementary tasks. Together, they probe whether a model can express spatial concepts visually and understand the corresponding spatial information.

Experiments find substantial weaknesses in these bidirectional mappings even among models that perform strongly on traditional benchmarks. The results therefore challenge using those benchmark scores alone as evidence of physical-world understanding. The authors also propose that patterns in the drawings could help investigate similarities between models. This diagnostic use is presented as a potential application, while the observed spatial-reasoning gaps are the benchmark's central empirical finding.
summary.tldr: LTD-Bench uses drawing and recognition tasks to make language models' spatial-reasoning weaknesses directly observable.

title: LTD-Bench: Evaluating Large Language Models by Letting Them Draw

abstract: Large language model (LLM) decoding suffers from high latency due to fragmented execution across operators and heavy reliance on off-chip memory for data exchange and reduction. This execution model limits opportunities for fusion and incurs significant memory traffic and kernel launch overhead. While modern architectures such as NVIDIA Hopper provide distributed shared memory and low-latency intra-cluster interconnects, they expose only low-level data movement instructions, lacking structured abstractions for collective on-chip communication. To bridge this software-hardware gap, we introduce two cluster-level communication primitives, ClusterReduce and ClusterGather, which abstract common communication patterns and enable structured, high-speed data exchange and reduction between thread blocks within a cluster, allowing intermediate results to be on-chip without involving off-chip memory. Building on these abstractions, we design ClusterFusion, an execution framework that schedules communication and computation jointly to expand operator fusion scope by composing decoding stages such as QKV Projection, Attention, and Output Projection into a single fused kernels. Evaluations on H100 GPUs show that ClusterFusion outperforms state-of-the-art inference frameworks by $1.61\times$ on average in end-to-end latency across different models and configurations.

When those operations execute separately, exchanging data through off-chip memory and launching additional kernels can increase latency. This paper addresses that fragmentation by making communication within a GPU thread-block cluster easier to organize and combine with computation.

The authors introduce ClusterReduce and ClusterGather, two primitives for common communication patterns among thread blocks in the same cluster. They use hardware facilities such as distributed shared memory and low-latency cluster interconnects to keep intermediate results on-chip. The result connects broader operator fusion with measured gains across the tested models and configurations.
summary.tldr: ClusterFusion uses structured on-chip communication to fuse more LLM decoding operations, achieving an average 1.61-fold speedup on H100 evaluations.

title: ClusterFusion: Expanding Operator Fusion Scope for LLM Inference via Cluster-Level Collective Primitive

abstract: Deep learning-based image stitching methods have achieved promising performance on conventional stitching datasets. However, real-world scenarios may introduce challenges such as complex weather conditions, illumination variations, and dynamic scene motion, which severely degrade image quality and lead to significant misalignment in stitching results. To solve this problem, we propose an adverse condition-tolerant image stitching network, dubbed ACDIS. We first introduce a bidirectional consistency learning framework, which ensures reliable alignment through an iterative optimization paradigm that integrates differentiable image restoration and Gaussian-distribute encoded homography estimation. Subsequently, we incorporate motion constraints into the seamless composition network to produce robust stitching results without interference from moving scenes. We further propose the first adverse scene image stitching dataset, which covers diverse parallax and scenes under low-light, haze, and underwater environments. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method can generate visually pleasing stitched images under adverse conditions, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Image stitching depends on aligning overlapping views and combining them into a coherent image. Poor lighting, haze, and other difficult conditions can damage the visual evidence needed for alignment, while moving objects introduce additional inconsistencies. This paper develops ACDIS to address these problems within a single stitching framework.

Its bidirectional consistency learning procedure iteratively combines differentiable image restoration with homography estimation, which estimates a geometric alignment between views. The homography component uses a Gaussian-distribution encoding. By placing restoration and alignment inside the same iterative process, the method addresses degraded image appearance together with the geometric matching problem.

For the final composition, the authors add motion constraints to reduce interference from moving scene content. They also introduce a benchmark covering varied parallax and low-light, hazy, and underwater scenes, making adverse conditions an explicit part of evaluation. Experiments report visually pleasing stitched images and better results than state-of-the-art methods. The contribution links an adverse-condition stitching method with a dataset designed to test the environmental and motion challenges motivating it.
summary.tldr: ACDIS combines iterative restoration, geometric alignment, and motion-aware composition to improve image stitching under adverse conditions.

title: Image Stitching in Adverse Condition: A Bidirectional-Consistency Learning Framework and Benchmark

abstract: Benchmarking models is a key factor for the rapid progress in machine learning (ML) research. Thus, further progress depends on improving benchmarking metrics. A standard metric to measure the behavioral alignment between ML models and human observers is error consistency (EC). EC allows for more fine-grained comparisons of behavior than other metrics such as accuracy, and has been used in the influential Brain-Score benchmark to rank different DNNs by their behavioral consistency with humans. Previously, EC values have been reported without confidence intervals. However, empirically measured EC values are typically noisy - thus, without confidence intervals, valid benchmarking conclusions are problematic. Here we improve on standard EC in two ways: First, we show how to obtain confidence intervals for EC using a bootstrapping technique, allowing us to derive significance tests for EC. Second, we propose a new computational model relating the EC between two classifiers to the implicit probability that one of them copies responses from the other. This view of EC allows us to give practical guidance to scientists regarding the number of trials required for sufficiently powerful, conclusive experiments. Finally, we use our methodology to revisit popular NeuroAI-results. We find that while the general trend of behavioral differences between humans and machines holds up to scrutiny, many reported differences between deep vision models are statistically insignificant. Our methodology enables researchers to design adequately powered experiments that can reliably detect behavioral differences between models, providing a foundation for more rigorous benchmarking of behavioral alignment.

The methodology supports both more cautious comparisons and better-powered experimental designs.

title: Quantifying Uncertainty in Error Consistency: Towards Reliable Behavioral Comparison of Classifiers

abstract: Image classifiers play a critical role in detecting diseases in medical imaging and identifying anomalies in manufacturing processes. However, their predefined behaviors after extensive training make post hoc model editing difficult, especially when it comes to forgetting specific classes or adapting to distribution shifts. Existing classifier editing methods either focus narrowly on correcting errors or incur extensive retraining costs, creating a bottleneck for flexible editing. Moreover, such editing has seen limited investigation in image classification. To overcome these challenges, we introduce class vectors, which capture class-specific representation adjustments during fine-tuning. Whereas task vectors encode task-level changes in weight space, class vectors disentangle each class’s adaptation in the latent space. We show that class vectors capture each class’s semantic shift and that classifier editing can be achieved either by steering latent features along these vectors or by mapping them into weight space to update the decision boundaries. We also demonstrate that the inherent linearity and orthogonality of class vectors support efficient, flexible, and high-level concept editing via simple class arithmetic. Finally, we validate their utility in applications such as unlearning, environmental adaptation, adversarial defense, and adversarial trigger optimization.

The authors show two ways to use them for editing. One steers internal features along the vectors; the other maps the vectors into weight space to change decision boundaries.

Together, these results present class-specific representation changes as practical editing tools, offering more targeted flexibility than treating every modification as an undifferentiated change to the whole task.
summary.tldr: Class vectors capture class-specific representation changes that can be combined and applied to edit trained image classifiers.

title: Exploring and Leveraging Class Vectors for Classifier Editing

abstract: Proper initialization is critical for Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly in long-range reasoning tasks, where repeated application of the same weight matrix can cause vanishing or exploding signals. A common baseline for linear recurrences is Glorot initialization, designed to ensure stable signal propagation---but derived under the infinite-width, fixed-length regime—an unrealistic setting for RNNs processing long sequences. In this work, we show that Glorot initialization is in fact unstable: small positive deviations in the spectral radius are amplified through time and cause the hidden state to explode. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that sequences of length $t = O(\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ is the hidden width, are sufficient to induce instability. To address this, we propose a simple, dimension-aware rescaling of Glorot that shifts the spectral radius slightly below one, preventing rapid signal explosion or decay. These results suggest that standard initialization schemes may break down in the long-sequence regime, motivating a separate line of theory for stable recurrent initialization.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks repeatedly apply the same weight matrix, so small imbalances can accumulate over long sequences. Glorot initialization is intended to preserve stable signals, but its derivation assumes infinite width and a fixed sequence length. This paper examines what happens when a finite-width linear recurrence instead processes increasingly long sequences.

The authors show that small positive deviations in the matrix's spectral radius can grow through repeated application and cause the hidden state to explode. Their theoretical analysis finds that sequence lengths on the order of the square root of hidden width are sufficient to induce instability. This is a sufficient scale for the demonstrated instability, rather than a claim that every shorter sequence is stable.

To address the problem, the paper proposes a width-aware rescaling of Glorot initialization that places the spectral radius slightly below one, preventing rapid signal growth or decay. The results suggest that initialization theory based on fixed sequence lengths may fail to capture long-range recurrent behavior, motivating theory that explicitly accounts for sequence length and model width together.
summary.tldr: The paper shows long-sequence instability in Glorot-initialized linear recurrences and proposes a width-aware rescaling to control signal growth and decay.

title: Revisiting Glorot Initialization for Long-Range Linear Recurrences

abstract: Spatial conditioning in pretrained text-to-image diffusion models has significantly improved fine-grained control over the structure of generated images. However, existing control adapters exhibit limited adaptability and incur high training costs when encountering novel spatial control conditions that differ substantially from the training tasks. To address this limitation, we propose Universal Few-Shot Control (UFC), a versatile few-shot control adapter capable of generalizing to novel spatial conditions. Given a few image-condition pairs of an unseen task and a query condition, UFC leverages the analogy between query and support conditions to construct task-specific control features, instantiated by a matching mechanism and an update on a small set of task-specific parameters. Experiments on six novel spatial control tasks show that UFC, fine-tuned with only 30 annotated examples of novel tasks, achieves fine-grained control consistent with the spatial conditions. Notably, when fine-tuned with 0.1\% of the full training data, UFC achieves competitive performance with the fully supervised baselines in various control tasks. We also show that UFC is applicable agnostically to various diffusion backbones and demonstrate its effectiveness on both UNet and DiT architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/kietngt00/UFC.
