Universal Few-Shot Control addresses this problem by learning to use a small set of examples from a new control task. The goal is fine-grained structural control with much less task-specific training data.

Given example image–condition pairs and a query condition, UFC uses analogies between the query and supporting conditions to construct control features. A matching mechanism supplies this comparison, together with an update to a small set of task-specific parameters. These components allow the adapter to tailor its guidance to an unseen task.

Across six novel spatial control tasks, fine-tuning with 30 annotated examples produces images consistent with the supplied conditions. Using 0.1% of full training data, UFC achieves competitive performance with fully supervised baselines on various tasks. The authors also demonstrate it on both UNet and DiT diffusion architectures, supporting its applicability across different backbone designs.
summary.tldr: UFC adapts diffusion models to new spatial control tasks using a small example set and task-specific matching.

title: Universal Few-shot Spatial Control for Diffusion Models

abstract: Generalization in robot manipulation is essential for deploying robots in open-world environments and advancing toward artificial general intelligence. While recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models leverage large pre-trained understanding models for perception and instruction following, their ability to generalize to novel tasks, objects, and settings remains limited. In this work, we present VideoVLA, a simple approach that explores the potential of transforming large video generation models into robotic VLA manipulators. Given a language instruction and an image, VideoVLA predicts an action sequence as well as the future visual outcomes. Built on a multi-modal Diffusion Transformer, VideoVLA jointly models video, language, and action modalities, using pre-trained video generative models for joint visual and action forecasting. Our experiments show that high-quality imagined futures correlate with reliable action predictions and task success, highlighting the importance of visual imagination in manipulation. VideoVLA demonstrates strong generalization, including imitating other embodiments' skills and handling novel objects. This dual-prediction strategy—forecasting both actions and their visual consequences—explores a paradigm shift in robot learning and unlocks generalization capabilities in manipulation systems.

paragraphs: VideoVLA investigates whether pretrained video generators can provide a useful foundation for robot manipulation. Given a language instruction and an image, it predicts both a sequence of actions and the future visual outcomes. This connects the robot's proposed behavior to an imagined account of what that behavior will look like.

The system uses a multimodal Diffusion Transformer to model video, language, and actions together. Pretrained video-generation capability supports joint visual and action forecasting. The central design choice is to learn these predictions together, bringing the ability to anticipate visual change into the same framework that produces manipulation actions.

Experiments find that higher-quality imagined futures correlate with more reliable action predictions and greater task success. They also show strong generalization, including handling unfamiliar objects and imitating skills from other embodiments. The correlation supports the relevance of visual forecasting without by itself establishing that better imagery causes successful manipulation. Overall, the findings support joint prediction of actions and consequences as a promising route to more generalizable robotic behavior.
summary.tldr: VideoVLA jointly predicts robot actions and future video, showing generalization to novel objects and skills from other embodiments.

title: VideoVLA: Video Generators Can Be Generalizable Robot Manipulators

abstract: A Computer-Aided Design (CAD) model encodes an object in two coupled forms: a \emph{parametric construction sequence} and its resulting \emph{visible geometric shape}. During iterative design, adjustments to the geometric shape inevitably require synchronized edits to the underlying parametric sequence, called \emph{geometry-driven parametric CAD editing}. The task calls for 1) preserving the original sequence’s structure, 2) ensuring each edit's semantic validity, and 3) maintaining high shape fidelity to the target shape, all under scarce editing data triplets. We present \emph{CADMorph}, an iterative \emph{plan–generate–verify} framework that orchestrates pretrained domain-specific foundation models during inference: a \emph{parameter-to-shape} (P2S) latent diffusion model and a \emph{masked-parameter-prediction} (MPP) model. In the planning stage, cross-attention maps from the P2S model pinpoint the segments that need modification and offer editing masks. The MPP model then infills these masks with semantically valid edits in the generation stage. During verification, the P2S model embeds each candidate sequence in shape-latent space, measures its distance to the target shape, and selects the closest one. The three stages leverage the inherent geometric consciousness and design knowledge in pretrained priors, and thus tackle structure preservation, semantic validity, and shape fidelity respectively. Besides, both P2S and MPP models are trained without triplet data, bypassing the data-scarcity bottleneck. CADMorph surpasses GPT-4o and specialized CAD baselines, and supports downstream applications such as iterative editing and reverse-engineering enhancement.

paragraphs: A parametric CAD object has both a visible shape and a construction sequence that produces it. Editing the shape therefore requires appropriate changes to that sequence. CADMorph addresses three linked requirements: retaining the original sequence structure, making valid parameter edits, and matching the desired geometry, despite scarce examples of complete editing tasks.

A masked-parameter model fills those segments with candidate edits. During verification, the parameter-to-shape model represents each candidate in a shape space and selects the one closest to the target.

This division gives each stage a concrete responsibility while drawing on geometric and design knowledge already learned by the models. Both models are trained without editing triplets, addressing the stated data bottleneck. The authors report improvements over GPT-4o and specialized CAD baselines, along with applications to repeated editing and reverse-engineering enhancement.
summary.tldr: CADMorph edits parametric CAD sequences through a plan–generate–verify loop using pretrained models that do not require editing-triplet training data.

title: CADMorph: Geometry‑Driven Parametric CAD Editing via a Plan–Generate–Verify Loop

abstract: The detection of ligand binding sites for proteins is a fundamental step in Structure-Based Drug Design. Despite notable advances in recent years, existing methods, datasets, and evaluation metrics are confronted with several key challenges: (1) current datasets and methods are centered on individual protein–ligand complexes and neglect that diverse binding sites may exist across multiple complexes of the same protein, introducing significant statistical bias; (2) ligand binding site detection is typically modeled as a discontinuous workflow, employing binary segmentation and subsequent clustering algorithms; (3) traditional evaluation metrics do not adequately reflect the actual performance of different binding site prediction methods. To address these issues, we first introduce UniSite-DS, the first UniProt (Unique Protein)-centric ligand binding site dataset, which contains 4.81 times more multi-site data and 2.08 times more overall data compared to the previously most widely used datasets. We then propose UniSite, the first end-to-end ligand binding site detection framework supervised by set prediction loss with bijective matching. In addition, we introduce Average Precision based on Intersection over Union (IoU) as a more accurate evaluation metric for ligand binding site prediction. Extensive experiments on UniSite-DS and several representative benchmark datasets demonstrate that IoU-based Average Precision provides a more accurate reflection of prediction quality, and that UniSite outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in ligand binding site detection. The dataset and codes will be made publicly available at https://github.com/quanlin-wu/unisite.

The paper argues that organizing data around individual protein–ligand complexes overlooks binding sites observed in other complexes of the same protein. It also identifies problems with separating detection into segmentation and clustering, and with evaluation measures that inadequately reflect prediction quality.

The UniSite model predicts binding sites end to end, using a set prediction loss with one-to-one matching to connect predicted sites with supervision.

The authors also introduce Average Precision based on intersection over union, measuring prediction quality through overlap. Experiments on UniSite-DS and other representative benchmarks support this metric as a more accurate reflection of prediction quality and show UniSite outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution links more complete protein-level data, unified prediction, and improved evaluation.
summary.tldr: UniSite combines a protein-centric binding-site dataset, end-to-end set prediction, and overlap-based evaluation to improve ligand binding-site detection.

title: UniSite: The First Cross-Structure Dataset and Learning Framework for End-to-End Ligand Binding Site Detection

abstract: We study safe linear bandits (SLBs), where an agent selects actions from a convex set to maximize an unknown linear objective subject to unknown linear constraints in each round. Existing methods for SLBs provide strong regret guarantees, but require solving expensive optimization problems (e.g., second-order cones, NP hard programs). To address this, we propose Constrained Linear Thompson Sampling (COLTS), a sampling-based framework that selects actions by solving perturbed linear programs, which significantly reduces computational costs while matching the regret and risk of prior methods. We develop two main variants: S-COLTS, which ensures zero risk and ${\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d^3 T})}$ regret given a safe action, and R-COLTS, which achieves ${\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d^3 T})}$ regret and risk with no instance information. In simulations, these methods match or outperform state of the art SLB approaches while substantially improving scalability. On the technical front, we introduce a novel coupled noise design that ensures frequent 'local optimism' about the true optimum, and a scaling-based analysis to handle the per-round variability of constraints.

paragraphs: Safe linear bandits describe repeated decisions in which both the reward objective and the constraints are unknown. An agent must learn which actions perform well while managing constraint violations. Existing approaches offer strong regret guarantees, but their action-selection steps can require expensive optimization, making computational cost a central obstacle.

COLTS selects actions by solving linear programs with added perturbations. The framework has two variants with different information requirements. Given a safe action, S-COLTS guarantees zero risk and regret bounded by approximately the square root of d cubed times T, apart from logarithmic factors. R-COLTS needs no instance information and obtains that same order for both regret and risk, where d is dimension and T is the number of rounds.

The analysis uses coupled noise to produce frequent local optimism about the optimum, together with a scaling argument for changing constraints across rounds. Simulations report performance matching or exceeding existing safe-bandit methods with substantially better scalability. The result offers less expensive action selection while preserving the stated guarantees, with the zero-risk guarantee specifically depending on access to a safe action.
summary.tldr: COLTS uses perturbed linear programs for efficient safe-bandit decisions, offering distinct guarantees with and without a known safe action.

title: Constrained Linear Thompson Sampling

abstract: Antimicrobial peptides have emerged as promising molecules to combat antimicrobial resistance. However, fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and the lack of standardized benchmarks hinder computational approaches and slow down the discovery of new candidates. To address these challenges, we present the Expanded Standardized Collection for Antimicrobial Peptide Evaluation (ESCAPE), an experimental framework integrating over 80.000 peptides from 27 validated repositories. Our dataset separates antimicrobial peptides from negative sequences and incorporates their functional annotations into a biologically coherent multilabel hierarchy, capturing activities across antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, and antiparasitic classes. Building on ESCAPE, we propose a transformer-based model that leverages sequence and structural information to predict multiple functional activities of peptides. Our method achieves up to a 2.56% relative average improvement in mean Average Precision over the second-best method adapted for this task, establishing a new state-of-the-art multilabel peptide classification. ESCAPE provides a comprehensive and reproducible evaluation framework to advance AI-driven antimicrobial peptide research.

summary.tldr: ESCAPE standardizes multilabel antimicrobial peptide evaluation and pairs it with a transformer that improves functional activity prediction.

title: A Standardized Benchmark for Multilabel Antimicrobial Peptide Classification

abstract: Classical image filters, such as those for averaging or differencing, are carefully normalized to ensure consistency, interpretability, and to avoid artifacts like intensity shifts, halos, or ringing. In contrast, convolutional filters learned end-to-end in deep networks lack such constraints. Although they may resemble wavelets and blob/edge detectors, they are not normalized in the same or any way. Consequently, when images undergo atmospheric transfer, their responses become distorted, leading to incorrect outcomes. We address this limitation by proposing filter normalization, followed by learnable scaling and shifting, akin to batch normalization. This simple yet effective modification ensures that the filters are atmosphere-equivariant, enabling co-domain symmetry. By integrating classical filtering principles into deep learning (applicable to both convolutional neural networks and convolution-dependent vision transformers), our method achieves significant improvements on artificial and natural intensity variation benchmarks. Our ResNet34 could even outperform CLIP by a large margin. Our analysis reveals that unnormalized filters degrade performance, whereas filter normalization regularizes learning, promotes diversity, and improves robustness and generalization.

paragraphs: Classical image filters use normalization to keep their responses consistent and avoid unwanted visual effects. Learned convolutional filters usually lack comparable constraints, even when they resemble familiar edge or blob detectors. This paper argues that this omission distorts filter responses when images undergo atmospheric transfer, contributing to incorrect model outputs.

The proposed modification normalizes filters and then applies learnable scaling and shifting, in a pattern analogous to batch normalization. The authors state that this makes the filters atmosphere-equivariant: their responses respect the relevant transformation relationship. The method applies to convolutional networks and vision transformers that depend on convolution, bringing a classical filtering principle into learned vision architectures.

Experiments show significant gains on benchmarks involving artificial and natural intensity variation. The authors also report a setting where their ResNet34 substantially outperforms CLIP. Their analysis links unnormalized filters to degraded performance and finds that normalization regularizes learning, encourages filter diversity, and improves robustness and generalization in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Normalizing learned image filters improves robustness to intensity variation by incorporating consistency principles from classical image processing.

title: Normalize Filters! Classical Wisdom for Deep Vision

abstract: Diffusion models can be improved with additional guidance towards more effective representations of input. Indeed, prior empirical work has already shown that aligning internal representations of the diffusion model with those of pre-trained models improves generation quality. In this paper, we present a systematic framework for incorporating representation guidance into diffusion models. We provide alternative decompositions of denoising models along with their associated training criteria, where the decompositions determine when and how the auxiliary representations are incorporated. Guided by our theoretical insights, we introduce two new strategies for enhancing representation alignment in diffusion models. First, we pair examples with target representations either derived from themselves or arisen from different synthetic modalities, and subsequently learn a joint model over the multimodal pairs. Second, we design an optimal training curriculum that balances representation learning and data generation. Our experiments across image, protein sequence, and molecule generation tasks demonstrate superior performance as well as accelerated training. In particular, on the class-conditional ImageNet $256\times 256$ benchmark, our guidance results in $23.3$ times faster training than the original SiT-XL as well as four times speedup over the state-of-the-art method REPA.

The framework motivates two strategies. title: Learning Diffusion Models with Flexible Representation Guidance

abstract: Lens flare occurs when shooting towards strong light sources, significantly degrading the visual quality of images. Due to the difficulty in capturing flare-corrupted and flare-free image pairs in the real world, existing datasets are typically synthesized in 2D by overlaying artificial flare templates onto background images. However, the lack of flare diversity in templates and the neglect of physical principles in the synthesis process hinder models trained on these datasets from generalizing well to real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a new physics-informed method for flare data generation, which consists of three stages: parameterized template creation, the laws of illumination-aware 2D synthesis, and physical engine-based 3D rendering, which finally gives us a mixed flare dataset that incorporates both 2D and 3D perspectives, namely FlareX. This dataset offers 9,500 2D templates derived from 95 flare patterns and 3,000 flare image pairs rendered from 60 3D scenes. Furthermore, we design a masking approach to obtain real-world flare-free images from their corrupted counterparts to measure the performance of the model on real-world images. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and dataset.

FlareX addresses these weaknesses through a three-stage data-generation process. The contribution links the realism and diversity of training examples to the challenge of making flare removal work outside synthetic data.
summary.tldr: FlareX combines illumination-aware 2D synthesis and physical 3D rendering to create more varied, physically informed training data for lens-flare removal.

title: FlareX: A Physics-Informed Dataset for Lens Flare Removal via 2D Synthesis and 3D Rendering

abstract: Despite their many successes, transformer-based large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with tasks that require complex reasoning over large parts of their input. We argue that these failures arise due to capacity limits on the accurate flow of information within LLMs. To formalize this issue, we introduce the bounded attention prefix oracle (BAPO) model, a new computational framework that models bandwidth constraints on attention heads, the mechanism for internal communication in LLMs. We show that several important reasoning problems like graph reachability require high communication bandwidth for BAPOs to solve; we call these problems BAPO-hard. Our experiments corroborate our theoretical predictions: GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini succeed on BAPO-easy tasks and fail even on relatively small BAPO-hard tasks. BAPOs also reveal another benefit of chain of thought (CoT): we prove that breaking down a task using CoT can turn any BAPO-hard problem into a BAPO-easy one. Our results offer principled explanations for key LLM failures and suggest directions for architectures and inference methods that mitigate bandwidth limits.

paragraphs: Language models can struggle when a task requires combining information from many parts of an input. The authors argue that limited capacity for accurate internal communication helps explain these failures. They introduce the bounded attention prefix oracle, or BAPO, as a computational model of bandwidth constraints on attention heads.

Within this framework, some reasoning problems require substantial communication bandwidth. Graph reachability is one example of what the authors call a BAPO-hard problem. Experiments with GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini align with the theoretical predictions: the models succeed on BAPO-easy tasks but fail on even relatively small instances of BAPO-hard tasks.

summary.tldr: A bandwidth-limited model of attention explains observed global-reasoning failures and formalizes how chain-of-thought decomposition can ease communication demands.

title: Lost in Transmission: When and Why LLMs Fail to Reason Globally

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in learning algorithms, evaluations, and optimization tasks. Recent studies have shown that using LLM-based optimizers to automatically optimize model prompts, demonstrations, predictions themselves, or other components can significantly enhance the performance of AI systems, as demonstrated by frameworks such as DSPy and TextGrad. However, optimizers built on language models themselves are usually designed by humans with manual design choices; optimizers themselves are not optimized. Moreover, these optimizers are general purpose by design, to be useful to a broad audience, and are not tailored for specific tasks. To address these challenges, we propose metaTextGrad, which focuses on designing a meta-optimizer to further enhance existing optimizers and align them to be good optimizers for a given task. Our approach consists of two key components: a meta prompt optimizer and a meta structure optimizer. The combination of these two significantly improves performance across multiple benchmarks, achieving an average absolute performance improvement of up to 6% compared to the best baseline.

paragraphs: metaTextGrad addresses an extra layer of design in language-model optimization. Frameworks such as DSPy and TextGrad use language models to improve prompts, demonstrations, predictions, or other system components. Yet the optimizers that make those improvements are generally designed by people and intended to work across many tasks, leaving their own design choices outside the optimization process.

The paper proposes a meta-optimizer that improves an existing optimizer for a particular task. It combines two components: a meta prompt optimizer and a meta structure optimizer. Together, these target both the prompts used by the optimizer and its structure, making the optimization procedure itself something that can be adapted to the task.

Across multiple benchmarks, the combined approach significantly improves performance, with average absolute gains of up to 6% over the best baseline. These findings support treating the optimizer as another adaptable component of an AI system. The practical significance is that a general-purpose language-model optimizer can be further tailored, rather than assuming its initial human-designed configuration is the best fit for each task.
summary.tldr: metaTextGrad improves language-model optimizers themselves by adapting their prompts and structure to specific tasks.

title: metaTextGrad: Automatically optimizing language model optimizers

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) node detection in graphs is a critical yet challenging task. Most existing approaches rely heavily on fine-grained labeled data to obtain a pre-trained supervised classifier, inherently assuming the existence of a well-defined pretext classification task. However, when such a task is ill-defined or absent, their applicability becomes severely limited. To overcome this limitation, there is an urgent need to propose a more scalable OOD detection method that is independent of both pretext tasks and label supervision. We harness a new phenomenon called **Feature Resonance**, focusing on the feature space rather than the label space. We observe that, ideally, during the optimization of known ID samples, unknown ID samples undergo more significant representation changes than OOD samples, even when the model is trained to align arbitrary targets. The rationale behind it is that even without gold labels, the local manifold may still exhibit smooth resonance. Based on this, we further develop a novel graph OOD framework, dubbed **R**esonance-based **S**eparation and **L**earning (**RSL**), which comprises two core modules: (i)-a more practical micro-level proxy of feature resonance that measures the movement of feature vectors in one training step. (ii)-integrate with a synthetic OOD node strategy to train an effective OOD classifier. Theoretically, we derive an error bound showing the superior separability of OOD nodes during the resonance period. Extensive experiments on a total of thirteen real-world graph datasets empirically demonstrate that RSL achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar nodes in a graph often depends on a classifier trained with detailed labels. That creates a problem when there is no suitable classification task or label set. This paper instead examines how node representations change during training, aiming to distinguish in-distribution and out-of-distribution nodes without relying on that supervised setup.

The motivating phenomenon is feature resonance. Ideally, optimizing known in-distribution examples causes larger representation changes in other in-distribution examples than in unfamiliar ones, even when training targets are arbitrary. The authors connect this behavior to local smoothness in the feature space. Their RSL framework measures feature movement over one training step as a practical proxy and combines it with synthetic out-of-distribution nodes to train a detector.

A theoretical error bound supports stronger separation during the resonance period. Experiments on thirteen real-world graph datasets report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is a detection signal based on responses to training rather than predefined class meanings. Its theoretical interpretation specifically concerns the period when resonance provides the stated separation.
summary.tldr: RSL detects unfamiliar graph nodes through differences in feature movement during training, without requiring a supervised pretext classification task.

title: Harnessing Feature Resonance under Arbitrary Target Alignment for Out-of-Distribution Node Detection

abstract: Efficient sampling from the Boltzmann distribution given its energy function is a key challenge for modeling complex physical systems such as molecules. Boltzmann Generators address this problem by leveraging continuous normalizing flows to transform a simple prior into a distribution that can be reweighted to match the target using sample likelihoods. Despite the elegance of this approach, obtaining these likelihoods requires computing costly Jacobians during integration, which is impractical for large molecular systems. To overcome this difficulty, we train an energy-based model (EBM) to approximate likelihoods using both noise contrastive estimation (NCE) and score matching, which we show outperforms the use of either objective in isolation. On 2D synthetic systems where failure can be easily visualized, NCE improves mode weighting relative to score matching alone. On alanine dipeptide, our method yields free energy profiles and energy distributions that closely match those obtained using exact likelihoods while achieving $100\times$ faster inference. By training on multiple dipeptide systems, we show that our approach also exhibits effective transfer learning, generalizing to new systems at inference time and achieving at least a $6\times$ speedup over standard MD with only a bit of fine-tuning. While many recent efforts in generative modeling have prioritized models with fast sampling, our work demonstrates the design of models with accelerated likelihoods, enabling the application of reweighting schemes that ensure unbiased Boltzmann statistics at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/RishalAggarwal/BoltzNCE.

The contribution focuses on accelerating likelihood evaluation so that reweighting remains practical, with the reported physical agreement demonstrated on the studied systems.
summary.tldr: BoltzNCE learns approximate likelihoods that accelerate molecular sample reweighting while closely reproducing exact-likelihood results on the studied systems.

title: BoltzNCE: Learning likelihoods for Boltzmann Generation with Stochastic Interpolants and Noise Contrastive Estimation

abstract: We present LrcSSM, a $\textit{non-linear}$ recurrent model that processes long sequences as fast as today's linear state-space layers. By forcing its Jacobian matrix to be diagonal, the full sequence can be solved in parallel, giving $\mathcal{O}(TD)$ computational work and memory and only $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ sequential depth, for input-sequence length $T$ and a state dimension $D$. Moreover, LrcSSM offers a formal gradient-stability guarantee that other input-varying systems such as Liquid-S4 and Mamba do not provide. Importantly, the diagonal Jacobian structure of our model results in no performance loss compared to the original model with dense Jacobian, and the approach can be generalized to other non-linear recurrent models, demonstrating broader applicability. On a suite of long-range forecasting tasks, we demonstrate that LrcSSM outperforms Transformers, LRU, S5, and Mamba.

paragraphs: Nonlinear recurrent models offer expressive sequence processing, but their recurrence creates a challenge for efficient computation over long inputs. LrcSSM is designed to retain nonlinear dynamics while processing long sequences as quickly as contemporary linear state-space layers. Its central structural choice is to constrain the model's Jacobian matrix to be diagonal.

That restriction allows the full sequence to be solved in parallel. For sequence length T and state dimension D, the method requires O(TD) computational work and memory, with only O(log T) sequential depth. The paper also provides a formal gradient-stability guarantee, addressing how learning signals behave through the recurrent computation.

The authors report no performance loss from the diagonal Jacobian compared with the original dense-Jacobian model. On the evaluated long-range forecasting tasks, LrcSSM outperforms Transformers, LRU, S5, and Mamba. They also describe the approach as generalizable to other nonlinear recurrent models. The findings support structured nonlinear recurrence as a way to combine parallel computation, stable gradients, and strong forecasting performance.
summary.tldr: LrcSSM uses a diagonal Jacobian to parallelize nonlinear recurrence while providing gradient stability and strong long-range forecasting results.

title: Parallelization of Non-linear State-Space Models: Scaling Up Liquid-Resistance Liquid-Capacitance Networks for Efficient Sequence Modeling

abstract: Probability distributions and histograms are natural representations for product ratings, traffic measurements, and other data considered in many machine learning applications. Thus, this paper introduces a technique for graph-based semi-supervised learning of histograms, derived from the theory of optimal transportation. Our method has several properties making it suitable for this application; in particular, its behavior can be characterized by the moments and shapes of the histograms at the labeled nodes. In addition, it can be used for histograms on non-standard domains like circles, revealing a strategy for manifold-valued semi-supervised learning. We also extend this technique to related problems such as smoothing distributions on graph nodes.

paragraphs: Some learning problems attach entire histograms or probability distributions to observations, rather than single labels. Product ratings and traffic measurements are examples mentioned in this paper. The authors develop graph-based semi-supervised learning for such data, using known histograms at labeled nodes to support learning elsewhere on the graph.

The method is derived from optimal transportation theory. Its behavior can be characterized through the moments and shapes of the labeled histograms, connecting the propagation process to meaningful properties of the distributions being learned. This gives a way to describe how the supplied distributional information affects the method, beyond treating each histogram as an undifferentiated collection of numbers.

The approach also accommodates histograms on nonstandard domains such as circles. That extension reveals a strategy for semi-supervised learning with values on manifolds. The authors further extend the technique to smoothing distributions attached to graph nodes. The contribution is thus a distribution-aware graph learning method with both structural characterizations and related extensions.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein propagation uses optimal transportation to learn and smooth graph-associated histograms, including distributions on circular domains.

title: Wasserstein Propagation for Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We present an approach for learning simple algorithms such as copying, multi-digit addition and single digit multiplication directly from examples. Our framework consists of a set of interfaces, accessed by a controller. Typical interfaces are 1-D tapes or 2-D grids that hold the input and output data. For the controller, we explore a range of neural network-based models which vary in their ability to abstract the underlying algorithm from training instances and generalize to test examples with many thousands of digits. The controller is trained using Q-learning with several enhancements and we show that the bottleneck is in the capabilities of the controller rather than in the search incurred by Q-learning.

paragraphs: The paper investigates learning simple procedures directly from examples, including copying, addition of multi-digit numbers, and single-digit multiplication. The central question is whether a learned model can extract an underlying algorithm that continues to work on much longer inputs. The study therefore emphasizes generalization beyond the individual examples used for training.

The framework separates a controller from interfaces that hold input and output data. These interfaces can take the form of one-dimensional tapes or two-dimensional grids. The authors explore several neural-network controllers, comparing their ability to learn the procedure and apply it to test examples containing many thousands of digits.

Training uses Q-learning with several enhancements. The authors find that the main bottleneck lies in the controller’s capabilities rather than in the search carried out by Q-learning. This finding directs attention to the model that operates the interfaces: different controllers differ in their ability to represent and generalize the required procedure. The contribution combines an interface-based framework with evidence about what constrains algorithm learning.
summary.tldr: Neural controllers learn simple algorithms through data interfaces, with controller capability identified as the main bottleneck to generalization.

title: Learning Simple Algorithms from Examples

abstract: An algorithm for stochastic (convex or nonconvex) optimization is presented. The algorithm is variable-metric in the sense that, in each iteration, the step is computed through the product of a symmetric positive definite scaling matrix and a stochastic (mini-batch) gradient of the objective function, where the sequence of scaling matrices is updated dynamically by the algorithm. A key feature of the algorithm is that it does not overly restrict the manner in which the scaling matrices are updated. Rather, the algorithm exploits fundamental self-correcting properties of BFGS-type updating—properties that have been over-looked in other attempts to devise quasi-Newton methods for stochastic optimization. Numerical experiments illustrate that the method and a limited memory variant of it are stable and outperform (mini-batch) stochastic gradient and other quasi-Newton methods when employed to solve a few machine learning problems.

A key feature of the algorithm is that it does not overly restrict the manner in which the scaling matrices are updated. Rather, the algorithm exploits fundamental self-correcting properties of BFGS-type updating—properties that have been over-looked in other attempts to devise quasi-Newton methods for stochastic optimization. paragraphs: This paper presents an optimization algorithm for objectives that may be convex or nonconvex and whose gradients are estimated from mini-batches. At each iteration, it multiplies the stochastic gradient by a symmetric positive definite scaling matrix. Updating this matrix over time lets the algorithm change how it scales and combines gradient directions.

The central design choice is to avoid imposing overly restrictive rules on those matrix updates. Instead, the method draws on self-correcting properties of BFGS-type updates. The authors argue that these properties had been overlooked in other efforts to adapt quasi-Newton optimization to stochastic settings. They use them as the basis for a dynamically changing metric.

Experiments on a few machine learning problems found that both the main algorithm and a limited-memory version were stable and outperformed mini-batch stochastic gradient and other quasi-Newton methods. The results support the practical usefulness of the design on those problems. The contribution is an approach to stochastic curvature adaptation that makes self-correction central to its update strategy.
summary.tldr: A stochastic variable-metric optimizer uses BFGS self-correction and performed well on several machine learning problems.

title: A Self-Correcting Variable-Metric Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Solving systems of quadratic equations is a central problem in machine learning and signal processing. One important example is phase retrieval, which aims to recover a signal from only magnitudes of its linear measurements. This paper focuses on the situation when the measurements are corrupted by arbitrary outliers, for which the recently developed non-convex gradient descent Wirtinger flow (WF) and truncated Wirtinger flow (TWF) algorithms likely fail. We develop a novel median-TWF algorithm that exploits robustness of sample median to resist arbitrary outliers in the initialization and the gradient update in each iteration. We show that such a non-convex algorithm provably recovers the signal from a near-optimal number of measurements composed of i.i.d. Gaussian entries, up to a logarithmic factor, even when a constant portion of the measurements are corrupted by arbitrary outliers. We further show that median-TWF is also robust when measurements are corrupted by both arbitrary outliers and bounded noise. Our analysis of performance guarantee is accomplished by development of non-trivial concentration measures of median-related quantities, which may be of independent interest. We further provide numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

One important example is phase retrieval, which aims to recover a signal from only magnitudes of its linear measurements. This paper focuses on the situation when the measurements are corrupted by arbitrary outliers, for which the recently developed non-convex gradient descent Wirtinger flow (WF) and truncated Wirtinger flow (TWF) algorithms likely fail. We develop a novel median-TWF algorithm that exploits robustness of sample median to resist arbitrary outliers in the initialization and the gradient update in each iteration. We show that such a non-convex algorithm provably recovers the signal from a near-optimal number of measurements composed of i.i.d. Gaussian entries, up to a logarithmic factor, even when a constant portion of the measurements are corrupted by arbitrary outliers. We further show that median-TWF is also robust when measurements are corrupted by both arbitrary outliers and bounded noise. Our analysis of performance guarantee is accomplished by development of non-trivial concentration measures of median-related quantities, which may be of independent interest. We further provide numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from the magnitudes of its linear measurements. This paper studies the harder situation in which some measurements contain arbitrary outliers. Such corruption can undermine the nonconvex Wirtinger flow and truncated Wirtinger flow methods that motivate the work.

The authors introduce median-TWF, which uses the robustness of the sample median both when forming the initial estimate and during gradient updates. Protecting both stages matters to the proposed approach: an outlier-resistant starting point is followed by updates designed to continue resisting corrupted observations. The resulting algorithm retains a nonconvex optimization formulation.

The recovery guarantee assumes measurements with independent, identically distributed Gaussian entries. Under that setting, median-TWF tolerates a constant fraction of arbitrary outliers using a measurement count that is near optimal up to a logarithmic factor. The authors also establish robustness when bounded noise accompanies the outliers. Their analysis develops concentration results for median-related quantities, and numerical experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Median-TWF robustifies phase retrieval and provides recovery guarantees under Gaussian measurements with a constant fraction of arbitrary outliers.

title: Provable Non-convex Phase Retrieval with Outliers: Median TruncatedWirtinger Flow

abstract: Instability and variability of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms tend to adversely affect their performance. Averaged-DQN is a simple extension to the DQN algorithm, based on averaging previously learned Q-values estimates, which leads to a more stable training procedure and improved performance by reducing approximation error variance in the target values. To understand the effect of the algorithm, we examine the source of value function estimation errors and provide an analytical comparison within a simplified model. We further present experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment benchmark that demonstrate significantly improved stability and performance due to the proposed extension.

To understand the effect of the algorithm, we examine the source of value function estimation errors and provide an analytical comparison within a simplified model. paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can be unstable, with variability in learning reducing performance. Averaged-DQN addresses this problem through a simple modification to DQN: it averages previously learned estimates of Q-values. These estimates describe the values of actions, so variation in them can affect the targets used to train the learning system.

The proposed averaging reduces the variance of approximation errors in those target values. The intended effect is a steadier training signal and, consequently, a more stable learning procedure. To explain the mechanism, the authors examine sources of value-estimation error and develop an analytical comparison within a simplified model.

Experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment show significantly improved stability and performance from the extension. The analysis and experiments serve different roles: the simplified model helps explain why averaging can help, while the benchmark demonstrates its effect in the tested setting. The contribution is a small change to the value-estimation procedure with both analytical motivation and empirical evidence of improved learning.
summary.tldr: Averaged-DQN averages earlier Q-value estimates to reduce target-error variance and improve learning stability and benchmark performance.

title: Averaged-DQN: Variance Reduction and Stabilization for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Curating labeled training data has become the primary bottleneck in machine learning. Recent frameworks address this bottleneck with generative models to synthesize labels at scale from weak supervision sources. The generative model’s dependency structure directly affects the quality of the estimated labels, but selecting a structure automatically without any labeled data is a distinct challenge. We propose a structure estimation method that maximizes the l1-regularized marginal pseudolikelihood of the observed data. Our analysis shows that the amount of unlabeled data required to identify the true structure scales sublinearly in the number of possible dependencies for a broad class of models. Simulations show that our method is 100x faster than a maximum likelihood approach and selects 1/4 as many extraneous dependencies. We also show that our method provides an average of 1.5 F1 points of improvement over existing, user-developed information extraction applications on real-world data such as PubMed journal abstracts.

paragraphs: Weak supervision sources can supply training labels at scale, but their dependencies affect the quality of labels inferred by a generative model. Choosing those dependencies is difficult when no labeled data are available to guide the choice. This paper proposes a way to estimate the model’s dependency structure using only unlabeled observations.

The method maximizes a marginal pseudolikelihood objective with l1 regularization, combining a structure-estimation criterion with a preference for sparsity. For a broad class of models, the authors show that the amount of unlabeled data needed to identify the true structure grows sublinearly with the number of possible dependencies. This gives a theoretical reason that examining a large space of dependencies need not require proportionally more data.

In simulations, the method is reported to be 100 times faster than a maximum-likelihood approach and to select one quarter as many extraneous dependencies. On real information-extraction applications, including PubMed abstracts, it improves existing user-developed systems by an average of 1.5 F1 points. These findings connect structure estimation to practical label quality.
summary.tldr: Sparse dependency estimation from unlabeled data improves generative weak-supervision models, with theoretical sample guarantees and practical gains.

title: Learning the Structure of Generative Models without Labeled Data

abstract: We propose and systematically evaluate three strategies for training dynamically-routed artificial neural networks: graphs of learned transformations through which different input signals may take different paths. Though some approaches have advantages over others, the resulting networks are often qualitatively similar. We find that, in dynamically-routed networks trained to classify images, layers and branches become specialized to process distinct categories of images. Additionally, given a fixed computational budget, dynamically-routed networks tend to perform better than comparable statically-routed networks.
originalAbstract: We propose and systematically evaluate three strategies for training dynamically-routed artificial neural networks: graphs of learned transformations through which different input signals may take different paths. Though some approaches have advantages over others, the resulting networks are often qualitatively similar. We find that, in dynamically-routed networks trained to classify images, layers and branches become specialized to process distinct categories of images. Additionally, given a fixed computational budget, dynamically-routed networks tend to perform better than comparable statically-routed networks.

paragraphs: A dynamically routed neural network can send different inputs through different sequences of learned transformations. The network is a graph with multiple possible paths, so its computation depends on the signal being processed. This paper proposes and systematically evaluates three strategies for training networks with that kind of input-dependent routing.

The comparison finds that some training approaches have advantages over others, but their resulting networks are often qualitatively similar. In image classification, layers and branches specialize in different image categories. This finding gives a concrete interpretation of the learned paths: different parts of the network develop distinct processing roles associated with the inputs they receive.

The authors also compare performance under a fixed computational budget. Dynamically routed networks tend to outperform comparable networks with static routing in that setting. The stated finding is a tendency, rather than a universal guarantee. Together, the results connect input-dependent computation with observed specialization and suggest that routing can improve how a network uses limited computation.
summary.tldr: Dynamically routed networks develop specialized branches and tend to improve image classification under a fixed computational budget.

title: Deciding How to Decide: Dynamic Routing in Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: We propose to study equivariance in deep neural networks through parameter symmetries. In particular, given a group G that acts discretely on the input and output of a standard neural network layer, we show that its equivariance is linked to the symmetry group of network parameters. We then propose two parameter-sharing scheme to induce the desirable symmetry on the parameters of the neural network. Under some conditions on the action of G, our procedure for tying the parameters achieves G-equivariance and guarantees sensitivity to all other permutation groups outside of G.
originalAbstract: We propose to study equivariance in deep neural networks through parameter symmetries. In particular, given a group G that acts discretely on the input and output of a standard neural network layer, we show that its equivariance is linked to the symmetry group of network parameters. We then propose two parameter-sharing scheme to induce the desirable symmetry on the parameters of the neural network. Under some conditions on the action of G, our procedure for tying the parameters achieves G-equivariance and guarantees sensitivity to all other permutation groups outside of G.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to make a neural network layer respond predictably to transformations of its inputs. The desired property is equivariance: when an input is transformed, the output changes according to the corresponding transformation. Here, the transformations form a group acting discretely on the layer's inputs and outputs.

The authors connect this behavior to symmetries in the network parameters. They propose two schemes for sharing parameters so that the parameters acquire the desired symmetry. This turns the design of an equivariant layer into a question about which parameters should be tied together, providing a structural route to controlling the layer's response.

Under conditions on how the transformation group acts, the construction guarantees equivariance to that group. It also guarantees sensitivity to permutation groups outside it. This second property matters because imposing parameter sharing can otherwise raise questions about whether the resulting symmetry is broader than intended. The result is conditional, but it provides a precise relationship between the chosen sharing pattern and the symmetry the layer expresses.
summary.tldr: Two parameter-sharing schemes induce desired network equivariances and, under stated conditions, avoid unintended permutation symmetries.

title: Equivariance Through Parameter-Sharing

abstract: Rapid learning requires flexible representations to quickly adopt to new evidence. We develop a novel class of models called Attentive Recurrent Comparators (ARCs) that form representations of objects by cycling through them and making observations. Using the representations extracted by ARCs, we develop a way of approximating a dynamic representation space and use it for one-shot learning. In the task of one-shot classification on the Omniglot dataset, we achieve the state of the art performance with an error rate of 1.5\%. This represents the first super-human result achieved for this task with a generic model that uses only pixel information.
originalAbstract: Rapid learning requires flexible representations to quickly adopt to new evidence. We develop a novel class of models called Attentive Recurrent Comparators (ARCs) that form representations of objects by cycling through them and making observations. Using the representations extracted by ARCs, we develop a way of approximating a dynamic representation space and use it for one-shot learning. In the task of one-shot classification on the Omniglot dataset, we achieve the state of the art performance with an error rate of 1.5\%. This represents the first super-human result achieved for this task with a generic model that uses only pixel information.

paragraphs: Learning from very little evidence puts pressure on how a model represents the objects it compares. This paper introduces Attentive Recurrent Comparators, or ARCs, with the aim of forming representations that can respond flexibly to new evidence. The model builds those representations by repeatedly cycling through objects and making observations.

The repeated observation process supplies representations that the authors use to approximate a dynamic representation space. They then apply that construction to one-shot learning, where classification must work from a single example of a class. The important connection is between the way objects are examined and the representation subsequently used to make the classification.

On the Omniglot one-shot classification task, the method achieves a reported error rate of 1.5%, establishing state-of-the-art performance in the paper's comparison. The authors also describe it as the first result exceeding human performance on that task from a generic model using only pixels. This is a task-specific empirical finding supporting the proposed representation approach for learning from very limited examples.
summary.tldr: Attentive Recurrent Comparators build representations through repeated observations and achieve 1.5% error on Omniglot one-shot classification.

title: Attentive Recurrent Comparators

abstract: MAP perturbation models have emerged as a powerful framework for inference in structured prediction. Such models provide a way to efficiently sample from the Gibbs distribution and facilitate predictions that are robust to random noise. In this paper, we propose a provably polynomial time randomized algorithm for learning the parameters of perturbed MAP predictors. Our approach is based on minimizing a novel Rademacher-based generalization bound on the expected loss of a perturbed MAP predictor, which can be computed in polynomial time. We obtain conditions under which our randomized learning algorithm can guarantee generalization to unseen examples.
originalAbstract: MAP perturbation models have emerged as a powerful framework for inference in structured prediction. Such models provide a way to efficiently sample from the Gibbs distribution and facilitate predictions that are robust to random noise. In this paper, we propose a provably polynomial time randomized algorithm for learning the parameters of perturbed MAP predictors. Our approach is based on minimizing a novel Rademacher-based generalization bound on the expected loss of a perturbed MAP predictor, which can be computed in polynomial time. We obtain conditions under which our randomized learning algorithm can guarantee generalization to unseen examples.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires choosing an output with interconnected parts. MAP perturbation models introduce randomness into maximum-a-posteriori prediction, providing a framework for efficient Gibbs-distribution sampling and predictions robust to random noise. This paper addresses how to learn the parameters of those perturbed predictors with a provable computational guarantee.

The authors develop a randomized learning algorithm that runs in polynomial time. Its objective comes from a new Rademacher-based generalization bound on a perturbed predictor's expected loss. The bound can itself be computed in polynomial time, so it provides a tractable quantity to minimize while explicitly connecting the learning procedure to performance on unseen data.

The paper also derives conditions under which the randomized algorithm guarantees generalization to new examples. Its contribution therefore joins two questions: whether parameter learning is computationally manageable and when the learned predictor is expected to extend beyond its training examples. The generalization result is conditional, while the stated algorithmic contribution is a provably polynomial-time procedure for learning the perturbed model's parameters.
summary.tldr: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm learns perturbed MAP predictors by minimizing a computable generalization bound.

title: Learning Maximum-A-Posteriori Perturbation Models for Structured Prediction in Polynomial Time

abstract: In this paper, we make an important step towards the black-box machine teaching by considering the cross-space machine teaching, where the teacher and the learner use different feature representations and the teacher can not fully observe the learner’s model. In such scenario, we study how the teacher is still able to teach the learner to achieve faster convergence rate than the traditional passive learning. We propose an active teacher model that can actively query the learner (i.e., make the learner take exams) for estimating the learner’s status and provably guide the learner to achieve faster convergence. The sample complexities for both teaching and query are provided. In the experiments, we compare the proposed active teacher with the omniscient teacher and verify the effectiveness of the active teacher model.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we make an important step towards the black-box machine teaching by considering the cross-space machine teaching, where the teacher and the learner use different feature representations and the teacher can not fully observe the learner’s model. In such scenario, we study how the teacher is still able to teach the learner to achieve faster convergence rate than the traditional passive learning. We propose an active teacher model that can actively query the learner (i.e., make the learner take exams) for estimating the learner’s status and provably guide the learner to achieve faster convergence. The sample complexities for both teaching and query are provided. In the experiments, we compare the proposed active teacher with the omniscient teacher and verify the effectiveness of the active teacher model.

paragraphs: Machine teaching asks how a teacher can guide a learner toward a desired model efficiently. This paper studies a difficult version in which teacher and learner use different feature representations and the teacher cannot fully inspect the learner’s model. That mismatch makes the learner’s current status something the teacher must estimate.

The proposed active teacher queries the learner through exam-like interactions. Responses provide information about the learner’s status, which the teacher then uses to guide subsequent teaching. The authors prove that this process can achieve faster convergence than traditional passive learning and provide sample-complexity results for both teaching and querying.

Experiments compare the active teacher with an omniscient teacher and verify the active model’s effectiveness. The contribution is a way to make progress toward black-box teaching despite differing representations and incomplete visibility. Its mechanism depends on active access to the learner through queries: the teacher can gather evidence about learning progress even when it cannot directly observe the full internal model.
summary.tldr: An active teacher uses learner queries to guide faster convergence despite different feature representations and incomplete access to the learner’s model.

title: Towards Black-box Iterative Machine Teaching

abstract: We formalize the problem of selecting the optimal set of options for planning as that of computing the smallest set of options so that planning converges in less than a given maximum of value-iteration passes. We first show that the problem is $\NP$-hard, even if the task is constrained to be deterministic—the first such complexity result for option discovery. We then present the first polynomial-time boundedly suboptimal approximation algorithm for this setting, and empirically evaluate it against both the optimal options and a representative collection of heuristic approaches in simple grid-based domains.
originalAbstract: We formalize the problem of selecting the optimal set of options for planning as that of computing the smallest set of options so that planning converges in less than a given maximum of value-iteration passes. We first show that the problem is $\NP$-hard, even if the task is constrained to be deterministic—the first such complexity result for option discovery. We then present the first polynomial-time boundedly suboptimal approximation algorithm for this setting, and empirically evaluate it against both the optimal options and a representative collection of heuristic approaches in simple grid-based domains.

paragraphs: Options provide extended actions that a planner can use alongside individual steps. This paper asks how to choose them specifically to accelerate planning. It defines a precise objective: find the smallest collection of options that lets planning converge within a prescribed limit on the number of value-iteration passes.

This formulation makes two resources explicit. The planner should use few options, but those options must reduce the required planning iterations enough to satisfy the chosen budget. The authors prove that finding the optimal collection is NP-hard even when the task is deterministic. Thus, removing randomness from the environment does not remove the computational difficulty of optimal option selection.

The paper then presents a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a bound on its suboptimality, described as the first such algorithm for this setting. It evaluates the method in simple grid domains against optimal options and representative heuristics. The contribution combines a formal planning-speed objective, a hardness result, and a computationally tractable approximation; the abstract reports the evaluation without specifying its comparative outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes compact option selection for faster planning, proves it NP-hard, and provides a bounded polynomial-time approximation.

title: Finding Options that Minimize Planning Time

abstract: We introduce the implicit processes (IPs), a stochastic process that places implicitly defined multivariate distributions over any finite collections of random variables. IPs are therefore highly flexible implicit priors over functions , with examples including data simulators, Bayesian neural networks and non-linear transformations of stochastic processes. A novel and efficient approximate inference algorithm for IPs, namely the variational implicit processes (VIPs), is derived using generalised wake-sleep updates. This method returns simple update equations and allows scalable hyper-parameter learning with stochastic optimization. Experiments show that VIPs return better uncertainty estimates and lower errors over existing inference methods for challenging models such as Bayesian neural networks, and Gaussian processes.
originalAbstract: We introduce the implicit processes (IPs), a stochastic process that places implicitly defined multivariate distributions over any finite collections of random variables. This method returns simple update equations and allows scalable hyper-parameter learning with stochastic optimization. paragraphs: Implicit processes provide a flexible way to specify prior distributions over functions. They define joint distributions for finite collections of random variables implicitly, allowing examples such as data simulators, Bayesian neural networks, and nonlinear transformations of stochastic processes. The paper introduces this framework and addresses how to perform inference within it.

The proposed inference method, variational implicit processes, uses generalized wake-sleep updates. It produces simple update equations and supports scalable hyperparameter learning through stochastic optimization. This is the computational counterpart to the modeling framework: flexible implicit function priors become usable through an efficient approximate inference procedure.

Experiments involving challenging models, including Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, show lower errors and better uncertainty estimates than existing inference methods. These findings support both predictive accuracy and the quality of uncertainty produced by the approach. The contribution combines a broad class of function priors with a practical learning method, connecting implicit model definitions to scalable approximate inference and experimentally improved predictions.
summary.tldr: Variational implicit processes enable scalable approximate inference for flexible implicit function priors, with improved errors and uncertainty estimates in experiments.

title: Variational Implicit Processes

abstract: There is growing interest in studying the languages that emerge when neural agents are jointly trained to solve tasks requiring communication through a discrete channel. We investigate here the information-theoretic complexity of such languages, focusing on the basic two-agent, one-exchange setup. We find that, under common training procedures, the emergent languages are subject to an entropy minimization pressure that has also been detected in human language, whereby the mutual information between the communicating agent’s inputs and the messages is minimized, within the range afforded by the need for successful communication. That is, emergent languages are (nearly) as simple as the task they are developed for allow them to be. This pressure is amplified as we increase communication channel discreteness. Further, we observe that stronger discrete-channel-driven entropy minimization leads to representations with increased robustness to overfitting and adversarial attacks. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the study of natural and artificial communication systems.

We find that, under common training procedures, the emergent languages are subject to an entropy minimization pressure that has also been detected in human language, whereby the mutual information between the communicating agent’s inputs and the messages is minimized, within the range afforded by the need for successful communication. paragraphs: When neural agents learn a task that requires exchanging discrete messages, they can develop their own communication system. This paper examines the information-theoretic complexity of those systems in a setup with two agents and one exchange. The question is how much information the learned messages retain about the sender's input.

Under common training procedures, the authors find pressure to minimize that information while preserving successful communication. The resulting languages are nearly as simple as their tasks permit. Increasing the discreteness of the communication channel strengthens this pressure, linking a property of the channel to the complexity of the representations that emerge.

The authors also observe that stronger entropy minimization driven by channel discreteness accompanies greater robustness to overfitting and adversarial attacks. These findings connect task-sufficient communication with useful properties of learned representations. They concern the studied training procedures and communication setup, while also motivating discussion of similar entropy pressures in human language and of how communication constraints shape artificial languages.
summary.tldr: Discrete communication pressures learned languages toward task-sufficient simplicity, with stronger pressure associated with more robust representations.

title: Entropy Minimization In Emergent Languages

abstract: A graph generative model takes a graph as input and is supposed to generate new graphs that “look like” the input graph. While most classical models focus on few, hand-selected graph statistics and are too simplistic to reproduce real-world graphs, NetGAN recently emerged as an attractive alternative: by training a GAN to learn the random walk distribution of the input graph, the algorithm is able to reproduce a large number of important network patterns simultaneously, without explicitly specifying any of them. In this paper, we investigate the implicit bias of NetGAN. We find that the root of its generalization properties does not lie in the GAN architecture, but in an inconspicuous low-rank approximation of the logits random walk transition matrix. Step by step we can strip NetGAN of all unnecessary parts, including the GAN, and obtain a highly simplified reformulation that achieves comparable generalization results, but is orders of magnitudes faster and easier to adapt. Being much simpler on the conceptual side, we reveal the implicit inductive bias of the algorithm — an important step towards increasing the interpretability, transparency and acceptance of machine learning systems.

While most classical models focus on few, hand-selected graph statistics and are too simplistic to reproduce real-world graphs, NetGAN recently emerged as an attractive alternative: by training a GAN to learn the random walk distribution of the input graph, the algorithm is able to reproduce a large number of important network patterns simultaneously, without explicitly specifying any of them. paragraphs: A graph generator should reproduce meaningful patterns in an input network without needing every pattern specified by hand. NetGAN approaches this by training a generative adversarial network to learn the input graph's random-walk distribution. This paper investigates which part of that system actually accounts for its ability to generalize.

The authors identify a low-rank approximation of the logits of the random-walk transition matrix as the source of the relevant inductive bias. They progressively simplify NetGAN, removing components including the adversarial network itself. The resulting formulation makes the structural assumption behind the method more explicit and easier to understand.

The simplified approach achieves comparable generalization results while running orders of magnitude faster and being easier to adapt. The finding changes the explanation of NetGAN's success: the essential mechanism identified by this study is a matrix approximation embedded in the procedure. Making that mechanism visible provides both a computational simplification and a clearer account of how the graph model generalizes.
summary.tldr: A low-rank matrix reformulation preserves NetGAN-like generalization while removing the GAN and greatly reducing computation.

title: NetGAN without GAN: From Random Walks to Low-Rank Approximations

abstract: Exploration in reinforcement learning (RL) suffers from the curse of dimensionality when the state-action space is large. A common practice is to parameterize the high-dimensional value and policy functions using given features. However existing methods either have no theoretical guarantee or suffer a regret that is exponential in the planning horizon $H$.In this paper, we propose an online RL algorithm, namely the MatrixRL, that leverages ideas from linear bandit to learn a low-dimensional representation of the probability transition model while carefully balancing the exploitation-exploration tradeoff. We show that MatrixRL achieves a regret bound ${O}\big(H^2d\log T\sqrt{T}\big)$ where $d$ is the number of features, independent with the number of state-action pairs. MatrixRL has an equivalent kernelized version, which is able to work with an arbitrary kernel Hilbert space without using explicit features. In this case, the kernelized MatrixRL satisfies a regret bound ${O}\big(H^2\wt{d}\log T\sqrt{T}\big)$, where $\wt{d}$ is the effective dimension of the kernel space.

A common practice is to parameterize the high-dimensional value and policy functions using given features. However existing methods either have no theoretical guarantee or suffer a regret that is exponential in the planning horizon $H$.In this paper, we propose an online RL algorithm, namely the MatrixRL, that leverages ideas from linear bandit to learn a low-dimensional representation of the probability transition model while carefully balancing the exploitation-exploration tradeoff. We show that MatrixRL achieves a regret bound ${O}\big(H^2d\log T\sqrt{T}\big)$ where $d$ is the number of features, independent with the number of state-action pairs. MatrixRL has an equivalent kernelized version, which is able to work with an arbitrary kernel Hilbert space without using explicit features. In this case, the kernelized MatrixRL satisfies a regret bound ${O}\big(H^2\wt{d}\log T\sqrt{T}\big)$, where $\wt{d}$ is the effective dimension of the kernel space.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an agent must explore a large collection of state-action pairs. Feature representations offer a way to reduce that complexity, but the paper notes that existing methods can lack guarantees or have regret growing exponentially with the planning horizon. MatrixRL addresses exploration through a compact representation of the transition model.

The algorithm adapts ideas from linear bandits to learn that representation while balancing exploration with the use of already acquired knowledge. Its reported regret bound is O(H² d log(T) √T), where H is the planning horizon and d is the number of features. The bound is independent of the number of state-action pairs and has polynomial dependence on H.

The paper also provides an equivalent kernelized algorithm that operates in a kernel Hilbert space without explicit features. Its bound replaces d with the kernel space’s effective dimension. These results identify representation dimension as the relevant complexity measure in the stated guarantees, showing how feature-based and kernel-based transition modeling can support theoretically controlled online exploration.
summary.tldr: MatrixRL learns transition dynamics in feature or kernel space with regret bounds that depend on representation dimension rather than state-action count.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Feature Space: Matrix Bandit, Kernels, and Regret Bound

abstract: The linear contextual bandit literature is mostly focused on the design of efficient learning algorithms for a given representation. However, a contextual bandit problem may admit multiple linear representations, each one with different characteristics that directly impact the regret of the learning algorithm. In particular, recent works showed that there exist “good” representations for which constant problem-dependent regret can be achieved. In this paper, we first provide a systematic analysis of the different definitions of “good” representations proposed in the literature. We then propose a novel selection algorithm able to adapt to the best representation in a set of $M$ candidates. We show that the regret is indeed never worse than the regret obtained by running \textsc{LinUCB} on best representation (up to a $\ln M$ factor). As a result, our algorithm achieves constant regret if a “good” representation is available in the set. Furthermore, we show the algorithm may still achieve constant regret by implicitly constructing a “good” representation, even when none of the initial representations is “good”. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings in a number of standard contextual bandit problems.
