paragraphs: A linear contextual bandit chooses actions using a representation of the available context. The same problem can have several valid linear representations, and that choice can strongly affect regret—the cumulative cost of decisions relative to the benchmark. This paper studies how a learner can benefit from favorable representations without being given the best one in advance.

The authors first organize and analyze existing definitions of a good representation. They then propose an algorithm that selects among M candidates. Its regret is no worse than running LinUCB with the best candidate, up to a logarithmic factor in M. Consequently, when the candidate set contains a good representation, the algorithm achieves constant problem-dependent regret.

A further result shows that constant regret may still be possible when no initial candidate is individually good: the algorithm can implicitly construct a good representation. This is a possibility established by the analysis, not a claim for every candidate set. Experiments on standard contextual bandit problems validate the theoretical findings and highlight representation selection as part of the learning problem.
summary.tldr: A representation-selection algorithm approaches the best candidate’s regret and achieves constant regret when suitable representation structure is available.

title: Leveraging Good Representations in Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: The ability to plan into the future while utilizing only raw high-dimensional observations, such as images, can provide autonomous agents with broad and general capabilities. However, realistic tasks require performing temporally extended reasoning, and cannot be solved with only myopic, short-sighted planning. Recent work in model-based reinforcement learning (RL) has shown impressive results on tasks that require only short-horizon reasoning. In this work, we study how the long-horizon planning abilities can be improved with an algorithm that optimizes over sequences of states, rather than actions, which allows better credit assignment. To achieve this, we draw on the idea of collocation and adapt it to the image-based setting by leveraging probabilistic latent variable models, resulting in an algorithm that optimizes trajectories over latent variables. Our latent collocation method (LatCo) provides a general and effective visual planning approach, and significantly outperforms prior model-based approaches on challenging visual control tasks with sparse rewards and long-term goals. See the videos on the supplementary website \url{https://sites.google.com/view/latco-mbrl/.}

paragraphs: Planning from images requires an agent to reason about future outcomes using high-dimensional observations. The challenge becomes sharper when rewards are sparse and goals take many steps to reach. This paper studies how model-based reinforcement learning can improve its long-horizon planning by changing what the planner directly optimizes.

The proposed method, LatCo, optimizes sequences of states rather than sequences of actions, which the authors argue allows better credit assignment. It adapts collocation to visual planning through probabilistic latent-variable models. These models provide latent variables over which the planner can optimize trajectories, bringing state-sequence optimization into a setting where the observations themselves are images.

The authors report that LatCo significantly outperforms prior model-based approaches on challenging visual-control tasks involving sparse rewards and long-term goals. These results support the value of its planning formulation for temporally extended reasoning. The central contribution is the combination of latent representations and trajectory optimization, enabling an agent to plan over future states when its observations are high-dimensional.
summary.tldr: LatCo improves long-horizon visual planning by optimizing latent state trajectories rather than action sequences.

title: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning via Latent-Space Collocation

abstract: Neural networks are known to suffer from catastrophic forgetting when trained on sequential datasets. While there have been numerous attempts to solve this problem in large-scale supervised classification, little has been done to overcome catastrophic forgetting in few-shot classification problems. We demonstrate that the popular gradient-based model-agnostic meta-learning algorithm (MAML) indeed suffers from catastrophic forgetting and introduce a Bayesian online meta-learning framework that tackles this problem. Our framework utilises Bayesian online learning and meta-learning along with Laplace approximation and variational inference to overcome catastrophic forgetting in few-shot classification problems. The experimental evaluations demonstrate that our framework can effectively achieve this goal in comparison with various baselines. As an additional utility, we also demonstrate empirically that our framework is capable of meta-learning on sequentially arriving few-shot tasks from a stationary task distribution.

paragraphs: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when learning from new datasets damages a neural network’s previously learned capabilities. This paper examines that problem in few-shot classification, where models must learn tasks from small amounts of labeled data. The authors show that MAML, a widely used method for learning an adaptable model initialization, also suffers from forgetting when learning proceeds sequentially.

Their response is a Bayesian online meta-learning framework. It combines learning across tasks with Bayesian updates as new information arrives, using Laplace approximation and variational inference as part of the framework. The aim is to carry useful information forward through sequential learning while retaining the ability to adapt to few-shot classification tasks.

Experiments show that the framework effectively addresses forgetting compared with the tested baselines. The authors also demonstrate another capability: meta-learning from few-shot tasks that arrive sequentially from a stationary task distribution. That additional result concerns a setting where the underlying distribution of tasks stays fixed. Together, the findings connect resistance to forgetting with the practical ability to learn across a continuing stream of small tasks.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian online meta-learning framework reduces catastrophic forgetting in sequential few-shot classification experiments.

title: Addressing Catastrophic Forgetting in Few-Shot Problems

abstract: Given a learning task where the data is distributed among several parties, communication is one of the fundamental resources which the parties would like to minimize. We present a distributed boosting algorithm which is resilient to a limited amount of noise. Our algorithm is similar to classical boosting algorithms, although it is equipped with a new component, inspired by Impagliazzo’s hard-core lemma (Impagliazzo, 1995), adding a robustness quality to the algorithm. We also complement this result by showing that resilience to any asymptotically larger noise is not achievable by a communication-efficient algorithm.

paragraphs: When training data is divided among several parties, learning must account for the information they exchange as well as the predictions they produce. This paper studies distributed boosting with communication efficiency as a central goal. It asks how such learning can remain effective when the problem also contains a limited amount of noise.

The proposed algorithm follows the general structure of classical boosting but introduces an additional component designed to provide robustness. That component draws inspiration from Impagliazzo’s hard-core lemma. The contribution therefore joins two objectives within one distributed learning procedure: limiting communication between parties and tolerating some noise.

The paper also establishes an impossibility result that puts the resilience guarantee in context. A communication-efficient algorithm cannot withstand noise that is asymptotically larger than the level addressed by the result. This connects the proposed algorithm to a fundamental constraint on the problem: stronger noise tolerance cannot simply be assumed compatible with efficient communication. The finding concerns that asymptotic tradeoff, rather than claiming resilience to arbitrary noise.
summary.tldr: A distributed boosting algorithm tolerates limited noise, while a complementary lower bound rules out asymptotically greater resilience with efficient communication.

title: A Resilient Distributed Boosting Algorithm

abstract: Score-based generative models have excellent performance in terms of generation quality and likelihood. They model the data distribution by matching a parameterized score network with first-order data score functions. The score network can be used to define an ODE (“score-based diffusion ODE”) for exact likelihood evaluation. However, the relationship between the likelihood of the ODE and the score matching objective is unclear. In this work, we prove that matching the first-order score is not sufficient to maximize the likelihood of the ODE, by showing a gap between the maximum likelihood and score matching objectives. To fill up this gap, we show that the negative likelihood of the ODE can be bounded by controlling the first, second, and third-order score matching errors; and we further present a novel high-order denoising score matching method to enable maximum likelihood training of score-based diffusion ODEs. Our algorithm guarantees that the higher-order matching error is bounded by the training error and the lower-order errors. We empirically observe that by high-order score matching, score-based diffusion ODEs achieve better likelihood on both synthetic data and CIFAR-10, while retaining the high generation quality.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models learn score functions and can use the resulting network to define a diffusion ordinary differential equation, or ODE, with exact likelihood evaluation. This paper examines whether the usual first-order score-matching objective is sufficient to maximize that ODE’s likelihood. The authors prove that it is not, identifying a gap between the two objectives.

They then show that the ODE’s negative likelihood can be bounded by controlling score-matching errors of the first, second, and third orders. This result motivates a higher-order denoising score-matching method for maximum-likelihood training. The algorithm also guarantees a bound on higher-order matching error in terms of training error and lower-order errors, connecting the new training procedure to the quantities needed by the analysis.

Experiments on synthetic data and CIFAR-10 show improved likelihood while retaining high generation quality. The contribution therefore distinguishes the ability to evaluate likelihood exactly from having a training objective that appropriately controls it. The theoretical bounds explain why higher-order matching is relevant, while the empirical results show that this change can improve likelihood without sacrificing the reported quality of generated samples.
summary.tldr: Higher-order denoising score matching addresses a proven gap between first-order score matching and maximum-likelihood training of diffusion ODEs.

title: Maximum Likelihood Training for Score-based Diffusion ODEs by High Order Denoising Score Matching

abstract: We study the stochastic shortest path (SSP) problem in reinforcement learning with linear function approximation, where the transition kernel is represented as a linear mixture of unknown models. We call this class of SSP problems as linear mixture SSPs. We propose a novel algorithm with Hoeffding-type confidence sets for learning the linear mixture SSP, which can attain an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d B_{\star}^{1.5}\sqrt{K/c_{\min}})$ regret. Here $K$ is the number of episodes, $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping in the mixture model, $B_{\star}$ bounds the expected cumulative cost of the optimal policy, and $c_{\min}>0$ is the lower bound of the cost function. Our algorithm also applies to the case when $c_{\min} = 0$, and an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{2/3})$ regret is guaranteed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm with a sublinear regret guarantee for learning linear mixture SSP. Moreover, we design a refined Bernstein-type confidence set and propose an improved algorithm, which provably achieves an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d B_{\star}\sqrt{K/c_{\min}})$ regret. In complement to the regret upper bounds, we also prove a lower bound of $\Omega(dB_{\star} \sqrt{K})$. Hence, our improved algorithm matches the lower bound up to a $1/\sqrt{c_{\min}}$ factor and poly-logarithmic factors, achieving a near-optimal regret guarantee.

paragraphs: A stochastic shortest-path learner must reach a goal while controlling accumulated cost in an uncertain environment. This paper studies environments whose transition dynamics have a linear-mixture representation. That structure allows the analysis to depend on the feature dimension rather than treating every possible transition as an unrelated unknown.

The first algorithm uses Hoeffding-style confidence sets to manage uncertainty. When every cost has a positive lower bound, its regret grows with the square root of the number of episodes, alongside factors involving feature dimension, optimal expected cost, and the minimum cost. It also applies when costs can be zero, with a weaker but still sublinear episode dependence of two-thirds power.

A refined algorithm uses Bernstein-style confidence sets and improves dependence on the optimal expected cumulative cost from power one-and-a-half to linear. The authors also prove a regret lower bound. The improved upper bound matches it apart from logarithmic factors and an inverse-square-root minimum-cost factor, making the near-optimality claim explicitly qualified by that remaining gap.
summary.tldr: Confidence-based algorithms achieve sublinear regret for linear-mixture shortest-path learning, with a refined bound approaching the proven lower bound.

title: Learning Stochastic Shortest Path with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty. However, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity of large-scale architectures and datasets. Node-based BNNs have recently been introduced as scalable alternatives, which induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying each hidden node with latent random variables, while learning a point-estimate of the weights. In this paper, we interpret these latent noise variables as implicit representations of simple and domain-agnostic data perturbations during training, producing BNNs that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions. We observe that the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables, and propose a straightforward approach to increase the entropy of these variables during training. We evaluate the method on out-of-distribution image classification benchmarks, and show improved uncertainty estimation of node-based BNNs under covariate shift due to input perturbations. As a side effect, the method also provides robustness against noisy training labels.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to represent uncertainty about what a model has learned, which can help when test inputs differ from training inputs. Placing uncertainty over network weights can be computationally expensive. Node-based alternatives instead learn fixed weight estimates and multiply hidden nodes by latent random variables, providing a more scalable source of epistemic uncertainty.

This paper interprets those random variables as implicitly applying simple, domain-agnostic perturbations to training data. From that perspective, node randomness helps explain performance when covariate shift comes from corrupted inputs. The authors observe that the diversity of these implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables, and propose increasing that entropy during training.

The method also provides robustness to noisy training labels as a side effect. The work connects an internal probabilistic mechanism to a concrete data-perturbation interpretation, then uses that interpretation to motivate a straightforward change to training.
summary.tldr: Increasing latent-node entropy improves uncertainty estimation under input corruption by diversifying implicit training perturbations in Bayesian neural networks.

title: Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks

abstract: We study the problem of classifier derandomization in machine learning: given a stochastic binary classifier $f: X \to [0,1]$, sample a deterministic classifier $\hat{f}: X \to \{0,1\}$ that approximates the output of $f$ in aggregate over any data distribution. Recent work revealed how to efficiently derandomize a stochastic classifier with strong output approximation guarantees, but at the cost of individual fairness — that is, if $f$ treated similar inputs similarly, $\hat{f}$ did not. In this paper, we initiate a systematic study of classifier derandomization with metric fairness guarantees. We show that the prior derandomization approach is almost maximally metric-unfair, and that a simple “random threshold” derandomization achieves optimal fairness preservation but with weaker output approximation. We then devise a derandomization procedure that provides an appealing tradeoff between these two: if $f$ is $\alpha$-metric fair according to a metric $d$ with a locality-sensitive hash (LSH) family, then our derandomized $\hat{f}$ is, with high probability, $O(\alpha)$-metric fair and a close approximation of $f$. We also prove generic results applicable to all (fair and unfair) classifier derandomization procedures, including a bias-variance decomposition and reductions between various notions of metric fairness.

paragraphs: A stochastic binary classifier assigns probabilities, while a deterministic classifier assigns a fixed binary outcome to each input. This paper studies how to sample a deterministic classifier that preserves the original model’s aggregate outputs and individual fairness. The fairness concern is whether inputs considered similar by a chosen metric continue to receive similar treatment.

The authors show that an earlier method with strong output-approximation guarantees is almost maximally unfair under metric fairness. A simple random-threshold method preserves fairness optimally, but provides weaker output approximation. These results expose a tradeoff: faithfully matching aggregate behavior does not automatically retain the way a classifier treats similar individuals.

The proposed procedure balances these goals when the original classifier is alpha-metric fair and the metric admits a locality-sensitive hash family. With high probability, the resulting classifier is O(alpha)-metric fair and closely approximates the original. The paper also develops a bias-variance decomposition and connections between fairness notions, supplying tools for analyzing derandomization procedures more generally.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a conditional, high-probability tradeoff between preserving metric fairness and matching a stochastic classifier’s aggregate outputs after derandomization.

title: Metric-Fair Classifier Derandomization

abstract: We study distributed contextual linear bandits with stochastic contexts, where $N$ agents/learners act cooperatively to solve a linear bandit-optimization problem with $d$-dimensional features over the course of $T$ rounds. For this problem, we derive the first ever information-theoretic lower bound $\Omega(dN)$ on the communication cost of any algorithm that performs optimally in a regret minimization setup. We then propose a distributed batch elimination version of the LinUCB algorithm, DisBE-LUCB, where the agents share information among each other through a central server. We prove that the communication cost of DisBE-LUCB, matches our lower bound up to logarithmic factors. In particular, for scenarios with known context distribution, the communication cost of DisBE-LUCB is only $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(dN)$ and its regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{dNT})$, which is of the same order as that incurred by an optimal single-agent algorithm for $NT$ rounds. We also provide similar bounds for practical settings where the context distribution can only be estimated. Therefore, our proposed algorithm is nearly minimax optimal in terms of both regret and communication cost . Finally, we propose DecBE-LUCB, a fully decentralized version of DisBE-LUCB, which operates without a central server, where agents share information with their immediate neighbors through a carefully designed consensus procedure.

paragraphs: When multiple agents learn which actions are rewarding, sharing observations can improve their decisions but requires communication. This paper studies that tradeoff for contextual linear bandits with stochastic contexts. There are N cooperating agents, d-dimensional features, and T rounds, with performance measured by regret: the reward lost relative to the relevant benchmark.

The authors first prove that algorithms achieving optimal regret must incur communication cost at least proportional to dN. They then introduce DisBE-LUCB, which eliminates candidate actions in batches and coordinates information through a central server. When the context distribution is known, its communication cost matches that lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

In the same setting, its regret scales as the square root of dNT, also up to logarithmic factors. This matches the order achieved by an optimal single learner operating for NT rounds. The paper gives similar guarantees when the context distribution must be estimated. It also proposes a decentralized version in which neighboring agents exchange information through a consensus procedure, extending the design beyond central-server coordination.
summary.tldr: A distributed linear-bandit algorithm achieves nearly optimal regret while matching a fundamental communication lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Distributed Contextual Linear Bandits with Minimax Optimal Communication Cost

abstract: Since the control of the Lipschitz constant has a great impact on the training stability, generalization, and robustness of neural networks, the estimation of this value is nowadays a real scientific challenge. In this paper we introduce a precise, fast, and differentiable upper bound for the spectral norm of convolutional layers using circulant matrix theory and a new alternative to the Power iteration. Called the Gram iteration, our approach exhibits a superlinear convergence. First, we show through a comprehensive set of experiments that our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, computational cost, and scalability. Then, it proves highly effective for the Lipschitz regularization of convolutional neural networks, with competitive results against concurrent approaches.

paragraphs: A layer’s Lipschitz constant describes how strongly changes in its input can affect its output. Controlling this sensitivity is relevant to neural network training stability, generalization, and robustness. This paper focuses on estimating a related quantity for convolutional layers: their spectral norm.

The authors introduce an upper bound that is precise, fast to compute, and differentiable. Their method combines circulant matrix theory with Gram iteration, a new alternative to power iteration. Gram iteration has superlinear convergence, making its convergence behavior a central part of the proposed computational advantage. Differentiability also makes the bound useful within an optimization procedure, beyond evaluating an already trained layer.

Experiments compare the approach with other leading methods and report advantages in precision, computational cost, and scalability. The authors then apply it to Lipschitz regularization of convolutional neural networks, obtaining competitive results against concurrent approaches. These findings connect the estimation method to a concrete training use: efficiently computing a usable sensitivity bound can help make sensitivity control practical during neural network optimization.
summary.tldr: Gram iteration provides a fast, differentiable spectral-norm upper bound that supports practical Lipschitz regularization of convolutional networks.

title: Efficient Bound of Lipschitz Constant for Convolutional Layers by Gram Iteration

abstract: We propose a theoretical framework to analyze semi-supervised classification under the low density separation assumption in a high-dimensional regime. In particular, we introduce QLDS, a linear classification model, where the low density separation assumption is implemented via quadratic margin maximization. The algorithm has an explicit solution with rich theoretical properties, and we show that particular cases of our algorithm are the least-square support vector machine in the supervised case, the spectral clustering in the fully unsupervised regime, and a class of semi-supervised graph-based approaches. As such, QLDS establishes a smooth bridge between these supervised and unsupervised learning methods. Using recent advances in the random matrix theory, we formally derive a theoretical evaluation of the classification error in the asymptotic regime. As an application, we derive a hyperparameter selection policy that finds the best balance between the supervised and the unsupervised terms of our learning criterion. Finally, we provide extensive illustrations of our framework, as well as an experimental study on several benchmarks to demonstrate that QLDS, while being computationally more efficient, improves over cross-validation for hyperparameter selection, indicating a high promise of the usage of random matrix theory for semi-supervised model selection.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised classification must balance information from labeled examples with structure in unlabeled data. This paper studies that balance in high dimensions under the low density separation assumption, which favors separating classes through regions containing little data. It introduces QLDS, a linear classifier that expresses this assumption through quadratic margin maximization.

QLDS has an explicit solution and connects several established approaches within one formulation. Particular cases recover least-square support vector machines, spectral clustering, and a class of graph-based semi-supervised methods. This connection makes the relative emphasis on supervised and unsupervised information a central feature of the model.

Using random matrix theory, the authors derive an asymptotic evaluation of classification error. They turn that analysis into a hyperparameter-selection policy for balancing the two parts of the learning criterion. Benchmark experiments report better hyperparameter selection than cross-validation with greater computational efficiency. The theoretical prediction is asymptotic, while the experiments provide evidence that the resulting selection strategy is useful in the evaluated finite-data settings.
summary.tldr: QLDS uses random matrix theory to choose the balance between labeled and unlabeled information under a low density separation assumption.

title: Random Matrix Analysis to Balance between Supervised and Unsupervised Learning under the Low Density Separation Assumption

abstract: Many practical problems involve solving similar tasks. In recommender systems, the tasks can be users with similar preferences; in search engines, the tasks can be items with similar affinities. To learn statistically efficiently, the tasks can be organized in a hierarchy, where the task affinity is captured using an unknown latent parameter. We study the problem of off-policy learning for similar tasks from logged bandit feedback. To solve the problem, we propose a hierarchical off-policy optimization algorithm HierOPO. The key idea is to estimate the task parameters using the hierarchy and then act pessimistically with respect to them. To analyze the algorithm, we develop novel Bayesian error bounds. Our bounds are the first in off-policy learning that improve with a more informative prior and capture statistical gains due to hierarchical models. Therefore, they are of a general interest. HierOPO also performs well in practice. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of using the hierarchy over solving each task independently.

The key idea is to estimate the task parameters using the hierarchy and then act pessimistically with respect to them. To analyze the algorithm, we develop novel Bayesian error bounds. Our bounds are the first in off-policy learning that improve with a more informative prior and capture statistical gains due to hierarchical models. Therefore, they are of a general interest. HierOPO also performs well in practice. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of using the hierarchy over solving each task independently.

paragraphs: Related decision tasks can contain useful information about one another. This paper studies how to exploit those relationships when learning policies from logged bandit feedback, where the available records describe actions already taken and their observed outcomes. Its motivating settings include users with similar preferences and items with similar affinities.

The proposed algorithm, HierOPO, organizes tasks in a hierarchy whose shared relationships are captured through an unknown latent parameter. It estimates task parameters using this structure and then chooses actions pessimistically with respect to those estimates. This combines information sharing across tasks with caution about what the estimated parameters support.

The authors develop Bayesian error bounds that improve as the prior becomes more informative and explicitly capture statistical gains from the hierarchy. They describe these as the first off-policy bounds with those properties. Experiments also demonstrate benefits over solving each task independently. The theoretical and empirical contributions align around the same idea: related tasks can improve learning efficiency when their shared structure is represented in the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: HierOPO shares information through a task hierarchy and acts pessimistically, with Bayesian bounds and experiments supporting improved off-policy learning.

title: Multi-Task Off-Policy Learning from Bandit Feedback

abstract: This paper proposes a new loss function for adversarial training. Since adversarial training has difficulties, e.g., necessity of high model capacity, focusing on important data points by weighting cross-entropy loss has attracted much attention. However, they are vulnerable to sophisticated attacks, e.g., Auto-Attack. This paper experimentally reveals that the cause of their vulnerability is their small margins between logits for the true label and the other labels. Since neural networks classify the data points based on the logits, logit margins should be large enough to avoid flipping the largest logit by the attacks. Importance-aware methods do not increase logit margins of important samples but decrease those of less-important samples compared with cross-entropy loss. To increase logit margins of important samples, we propose switching one-vs-the-rest loss (SOVR), which switches from cross-entropy to one-vs-the-rest loss for important samples that have small logit margins. We prove that one-vs-the-rest loss increases logit margins two times larger than the weighted cross-entropy loss for a simple problem. We experimentally confirm that SOVR increases logit margins of important samples unlike existing methods and achieves better robustness against Auto-Attack than importance-aware methods.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can be demanding, motivating methods that assign greater importance to selected training examples. This paper finds that weighting cross-entropy can leave these methods vulnerable to strong attacks. The authors experimentally connect that vulnerability to small logit margins: narrow gaps between the score for the true class and competing class scores.

Their analysis finds that existing importance-aware methods do not enlarge margins for important examples relative to cross-entropy, while reducing margins for less-important examples. The proposed switching one-vs-the-rest loss, SOVR, targets important examples with small margins. For those examples, it switches from cross-entropy to a one-vs-the-rest loss intended to increase separation from competing classes.

For a simple problem, the authors prove that one-vs-the-rest loss increases margins by twice as much as weighted cross-entropy. Experiments show that SOVR enlarges important examples' margins and achieves better robustness against Auto-Attack than the compared importance-aware methods. The theoretical factor of two is specific to the simple analyzed problem; the broader robustness finding is empirical.
summary.tldr: SOVR switches losses for important, small-margin examples to improve class-score separation and empirical adversarial robustness.

title: One-vs-the-Rest Loss to Focus on Important Samples in Adversarial Training

abstract: Vision Transformer (ViT) is an attention-based model architecture that has demonstrated superior performance on many computer vision tasks. However, its security properties, in particular, the robustness against adversarial attacks, are yet to be thoroughly studied. Recent works have shown that ViT is vulnerable to attention-based adversarial patch attacks, which cover 1-3% area of the input image using adversarial patches and degrades the model accuracy to 0%. This work provides a generic study targeting the attention-based patch attack. First, we experimentally observe that adversarial patches only activate in a few layers and become lazy during attention updating. According to experiments, we study the theory of how a small adversarial patch perturbates the whole model. Based on understanding adversarial patch attacks, we propose a simple but efficient defense that correctly detects more than 95% of adversarial patches.

paragraphs: Small adversarial patches can severely disrupt a vision transformer even when they cover little of an image. The abstract cites earlier attention-based attacks that cover 1–3% of the image and reduce model accuracy to zero. This paper studies how such localized changes affect attention and develops a defense from that understanding.

The authors experimentally observe that adversarial patches are active in only a few layers and become relatively inactive during attention updates. They use these observations to guide a theoretical study of how a small patch can perturb the wider model. The focus is on tracing the attack’s internal behavior rather than considering only its final effect on predictions.

Based on that analysis, the paper proposes a simple, efficient defense and reports correctly detecting more than 95% of adversarial patches. That figure describes patch detection performance. Together, the behavioral observations, theoretical investigation, and detector show how understanding where an attack acts inside a transformer can inform a targeted defense.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how small adversarial patches disrupt vision-transformer attention and develops a defense that detects more than 95% of patches.

title: Understanding and Defending Patched-based Adversarial Attacks for Vision Transformer

abstract: The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is one of the most widely used statistical models for sequential data analysis. One of the key reasons for this versatility is the ability of HMM to deal with missing data. However, standard HMM learning algorithms rely crucially on the assumption that the positions of the missing observations within the observation sequence are known. In the natural sciences, where this assumption is often violated, special variants of HMM, commonly known as Silent-state HMMs (SHMMs), are used. Despite their widespread use, these algorithms strongly rely on specific structural assumptions of the underlying chain, such as acyclicity, thus limiting the applicability of these methods. Moreover, even in the acyclic case, it has been shown that these methods can lead to poor reconstruction. In this paper we consider the general problem of learning an HMM from data with unknown missing observation locations. We provide reconstruction algorithms that do not require any assumptions about the structure of the underlying chain, and can also be used with limited prior knowledge, unlike SHMM. We evaluate and compare the algorithms in a variety of scenarios, measuring their reconstruction precision, and robustness under model miss-specification. Notably, we show that under proper specifications one can reconstruct the process dynamics as well as if the missing observations positions were known.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models are widely used to analyze sequences, including sequences with missing data. Standard learning methods, however, rely on knowing where the observations are missing. This paper tackles the harder case in which both the missing values and their positions are unknown, a situation that arises in the natural sciences.

Silent-state HMM methods address related problems but can depend on structural restrictions such as an acyclic underlying chain. The authors develop reconstruction algorithms that require no assumptions about the chain's structure and can operate with limited prior knowledge. Removing that structural requirement expands the kinds of sequential processes the algorithms can address.

The evaluation examines reconstruction precision across multiple scenarios and robustness when the model is misspecified. Under proper specifications, the authors show that process dynamics can be reconstructed as well as when the missing positions are known. The qualification matters: the finding identifies circumstances where unknown deletion locations need not degrade reconstruction, alongside an investigation of behavior when the model specification is imperfect.
summary.tldr: New HMM reconstruction algorithms handle unknown missing-observation locations without structural assumptions on the underlying chain.

title: Learning Hidden Markov Models When the Locations of Missing Observations are Unknown

abstract: Self-supervised learning on large-scale Vision Transformers (ViTs) as pre-training methods has achieved promising downstream performance. Yet, how much these pre-training paradigms promote lightweight ViTs’ performance is considerably less studied. In this work, we develop and benchmark several self-supervised pre-training methods on image classification tasks and some downstream dense prediction tasks. We surprisingly find that if proper pre-training is adopted, even vanilla lightweight ViTs show comparable performance to previous SOTA networks with delicate architecture design. It breaks the recently popular conception that vanilla ViTs are not suitable for vision tasks in lightweight regimes. We also point out some defects of such pre-training, e.g., failing to benefit from large-scale pre-training data and showing inferior performance on data-insufficient downstream tasks. Furthermore, we analyze and clearly show the effect of such pre-training by analyzing the properties of the layer representation and attention maps for related models. Finally, based on the above analyses, a distillation strategy during pre-training is developed, which leads to further downstream performance improvement for MAE-based pre-training. Code is available at https://github.com/wangsr126/mae-lite.

paragraphs: Self-supervised pretraining has produced strong results for large vision transformers, but its value for smaller versions is less established. This paper develops and compares several pretraining methods for lightweight vision transformers, evaluating them on image classification and downstream tasks that require predictions across an image.

The central finding is that suitable pretraining allows even plain lightweight transformers to match the performance of earlier leading networks with carefully engineered architectures. This challenges the view that standard transformer designs are inherently unsuitable at small sizes. However, the authors also identify shortcomings: the studied pretraining does not benefit from larger pretraining datasets and performs less well when downstream data are scarce.

To understand these outcomes, the authors examine representations within network layers and the models’ attention maps. Those analyses motivate a distillation strategy applied during pretraining. It further improves downstream performance for masked-autoencoder-based pretraining. Together, the results show that pretraining choices deserve attention alongside architecture design, while identifying specific settings where the studied methods remain less effective.
summary.tldr: Suitable self-supervised pretraining makes plain lightweight vision transformers competitive, and an analysis-guided distillation strategy further improves masked-autoencoder pretraining.

title: A Closer Look at Self-Supervised Lightweight Vision Transformers

abstract: Optimization problems are pervasive in sectors from manufacturing and distribution to healthcare. However, most such problems are still solved heuristically by hand rather than optimally by state-of-the-art solvers because the expertise required to formulate and solve these problems limits the widespread adoption of optimization tools and techniques. This paper introduces OptiMUS, a Large Language Model (LLM)-based agent designed to formulate and solve (mixed integer) linear programming problems from their natural language descriptions. OptiMUS can develop mathematical models, write and debug solver code, evaluate the generated solutions, and improve its model and code based on these evaluations. OptiMUS utilizes a modular structure to process problems, allowing it to handle problems with long descriptions and complex data without long prompts. Experiments demonstrate that OptiMUS outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on easy datasets by more than $20$% and on hard datasets (including a new dataset, NLP4LP, released with this paper that features long and complex problems) by more than $30$%. The implementation and the datasets are available at https://github.com/teshnizi/OptiMUS.

paragraphs: Powerful optimization solvers are difficult to use without expertise in translating practical problems into mathematical models. OptiMUS addresses that barrier with a language-model-based agent that takes natural-language descriptions of linear and mixed-integer linear programming problems. Its purpose is to carry the description through the modeling and solving process.

The agent develops a mathematical formulation, writes and debugs solver code, evaluates the resulting solutions, and uses those evaluations to improve both model and code. A modular structure lets it handle lengthy descriptions and complex data without relying on long prompts. The workflow therefore includes revision after evaluation, rather than ending with an initial formulation.

The authors report performance improvements over existing leading methods exceeding 20% on easy datasets and 30% on hard datasets. The hard evaluations include NLP4LP, a newly released dataset containing long and complex problems. These results support the usefulness of a modular, iterative agent for the evaluated optimization-modeling tasks, especially where substantial descriptions and data complicate the translation into solver-ready form.
summary.tldr: OptiMUS turns natural-language optimization problems into mathematical models and solver code, then evaluates and revises its solutions.

title: OptiMUS: Scalable Optimization Modeling with (MI)LP Solvers and Large Language Models

abstract: In this study, we consider the realm of covariance matrices in machine learning, particularly focusing on computing Fréchet means on the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices, commonly referred to as Karcher or geometric means. Such means are leveraged in numerous machine learning tasks. Relying on advanced statistical tools, we introduce a random matrix theory based method that estimates Fréchet means, which is particularly beneficial when dealing with low sample support and a high number of matrices to average. Our experimental evaluation, involving both synthetic and real-world EEG and hyperspectral datasets, shows that we largely outperform state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Covariance matrices appear in many machine learning tasks, and combining them calls for an appropriate notion of an average. This paper studies the Fréchet mean on the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, also known as the Karcher or geometric mean. The object being estimated is therefore a mean defined through the geometry of this matrix space.

The authors introduce an estimator based on random matrix theory and advanced statistical tools. They identify a particularly useful setting: there is limited sample support, but many matrices need to be averaged. The method addresses estimation of the geometric mean in this regime, where the quantity of matrices and the sample support behind them are separate considerations.

Evaluation uses synthetic data as well as real EEG and hyperspectral datasets. The authors report substantially better performance than state-of-the-art methods in these experiments. The contribution is an improved statistical approach to a matrix-averaging operation used across machine learning, with empirical evidence from both controlled data and two different real-world data types.
summary.tldr: A random matrix theory estimator improves geometric averaging of covariance matrices, especially with low sample support and many matrices.

title: Random matrix theory improved Fréchet mean of symmetric positive definite matrices

abstract: Many multi-agent systems in practice are decentralized and have dynamically varying dependencies. There has been a lack of attempts in the literature to analyze these systems theoretically. In this paper, we propose and theoretically analyze a decentralized model with dynamically varying dependencies called the Locally Interdependent Multi-Agent MDP. This model can represent problems in many disparate domains such as cooperative navigation, obstacle avoidance, and formation control. Despite the intractability that general partially observable multi-agent systems suffer from, we propose three closed-form policies that are theoretically near-optimal in this setting and can be scalable to compute and store. Consequentially, we reveal a fundamental property of Locally Interdependent Multi-Agent MDP’s that the partially observable decentralized solution is exponentially close to the fully observable solution with respect to the visibility radius. We then discuss extensions of our closed-form policies to further improve tractability. We conclude by providing simulations to investigate some long horizon behaviors of our closed-form policies.

paragraphs: Decentralized multi-agent systems often have relationships that change as agents move or interact. This paper introduces the Locally Interdependent Multi-Agent MDP to study such changing dependencies theoretically. The framework can represent settings including cooperative navigation, obstacle avoidance, and formation control, where relevant interactions need not remain fixed over time.

General partially observable multi-agent problems can be intractable, but the authors exploit the structure of this setting to propose three closed-form policies. These policies have theoretical near-optimality guarantees and can be scalable to compute and store. The analysis also relates limited local visibility to the performance available when the entire system is observable.

Specifically, the decentralized, partially observable solution is exponentially close to the fully observable solution as a function of visibility radius within this framework. This quantifies how expanding local visibility narrows the performance gap. The paper also discusses extensions aimed at improving tractability and uses simulations to investigate long-horizon policy behavior, connecting the theoretical policies with their behavior over extended operation.
summary.tldr: A framework for locally interacting decentralized agents yields near-optimal policies and an exponentially shrinking gap to full observability as visibility grows.

title: Locally Interdependent Multi-Agent MDP: Theoretical Framework for Decentralized Agents with Dynamic Dependencies

abstract: Approaches to predicting neuronal spike responses commonly use a Poisson learning objective. This objective quantizes responses into spike counts within a fixed summation interval, typically on the order of 10 to 100 milliseconds in duration; however, neuronal responses are often time accurate down to a few milliseconds, and Poisson models struggle to precisely model them at these timescales. We propose the concept of a spike distance function that maps points in time to the temporal distance to the nearest spike. We show that neural networks can be trained to approximate spike distance functions, and we present an efficient algorithm for inferring spike trains from the outputs of these models. Using recordings of chicken and frog retinal ganglion cells responding to visual stimuli, we compare the performance of our approach to that of Poisson models trained with various summation intervals. We show that our approach outperforms the use of Poisson models at spike train inference.

paragraphs: Predicting neural activity often means predicting when individual spikes occur. A common Poisson training objective instead represents activity as spike counts within fixed time intervals, typically 10 to 100 milliseconds. This can be a poor fit when neuronal responses carry timing precision down to a few milliseconds, where those models struggle.

The paper introduces a spike distance function: at every time point, its value is the temporal distance to the nearest spike. Neural networks are trained to approximate this function, making proximity to spike events the learning target. An efficient inference algorithm then converts the network’s predicted distance function into a spike train.

The authors evaluate the approach using recordings from chicken and frog retinal ganglion cells responding to visual stimuli. They compare it with Poisson models trained using different counting intervals and report better spike-train inference. The finding supports changing the target representation when precise event timing matters: learning distances to events provides a useful alternative to learning counts aggregated over intervals.
summary.tldr: Learning the temporal distance to the nearest neural spike improves spike-train inference over Poisson models on the evaluated retinal recordings.

title: Spike Distance Function as a Learning Objective for Spike Prediction

abstract: A large branch of explainable machine learning is grounded in cooperative game theory. However, research indicates that game-theoretic explanations may mislead or be hard to interpret. We argue that often there is a critical mismatch between what one wishes to explain (e.g. the output of a classifier) and what current methods such as SHAP explain (e.g. the scalar probability of a class). This paper addresses such gap for probabilistic models by generalising cooperative games and value operators. We introduce the distributional values, random variables that track changes in the model output (e.g. flipping of the predicted class) and derive their analytic expressions for games with Gaussian, Bernoulli and Categorical payoffs. We further establish several characterising properties, and show that our framework provides fine-grained and insightful explanations with case studies on vision and language models.

paragraphs: Many explanation methods use cooperative game theory to assign credit for a model’s prediction. This paper identifies a mismatch that can arise when the desired explanation concerns the model’s output, but the method attributes only a scalar quantity such as one class’s probability. A change in that number does not by itself describe all the relevant behavior of the output.

The authors generalize cooperative games and their value operators to introduce distributional values. These are random variables that track changes in model output, including events such as a predicted class switching. The framework therefore represents attribution in a form that can express probabilistic output changes more directly.

The paper derives analytic expressions for Gaussian, Bernoulli, and categorical payoffs and establishes properties that characterize the resulting values. Case studies involving vision and language models demonstrate fine-grained explanations. The contribution is a mathematical framework for bringing the object being explained closer to the behavior a user wants to understand, with demonstrations of how that richer description can be informative.
summary.tldr: Distributional values extend game-theoretic explanations to describe probabilistic changes in model outputs, including changes of predicted class.

title: Explaining Probabilistic Models with Distributional Values

abstract: Instruction Tuning (IT), the process of training large language models (LLMs) using instruction-response pairs, has emerged as the predominant method for transforming base pre-trained LLMs into open-domain conversational agents. While IT has achieved notable success and widespread adoption, its limitations and shortcomings remain underexplored. In this paper, through rigorous experiments and an in-depth analysis of the changes LLMs undergo through IT, we reveal various limitations of IT. In particular, we show that (1) IT fails to enhance knowledge or skills in LLMs. LoRA fine-tuning is limited to learning response initiation and style tokens, and full-parameter fine-tuning leads to knowledge degradation. (2) Copying response patterns from IT datasets derived from knowledgeable sources leads to a decline in response quality. (3) Full-parameter fine-tuning increases hallucination by inaccurately borrowing tokens from conceptually similar instances in the IT dataset for generating responses. (4) Popular methods to improve IT do not lead to performance improvements over a simple LoRA fine-tuned model. Our findings reveal that responses generated solely from pre-trained knowledge consistently outperform responses by models that learn any form of new knowledge from IT on open-source datasets. We hope the insights and challenges revealed in this paper inspire future work in related directions.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning teaches a pretrained language model using examples of instructions and responses. This paper examines what that process actually changes, asking whether better conversational behavior also reflects improved knowledge or skills. Its experiments distinguish between LoRA tuning, which adjusts a restricted set of parameters, and tuning all model parameters.

In the studied settings, LoRA mainly learns how to begin responses and reproduce stylistic features. Full-parameter tuning instead degrades knowledge and increases hallucinations. The authors trace some incorrect responses to tokens borrowed from conceptually similar training examples. They also find that copying response patterns from knowledgeable sources can reduce response quality, despite the apparent quality of those sources.

The tested methods intended to improve instruction tuning do not outperform a simple LoRA model. Responses relying on pretrained knowledge consistently beat those incorporating new knowledge from the studied open-source instruction datasets. These findings separate learning a response format from learning reliable content, and identify ways instruction examples can interfere with knowledge already present in a model.
summary.tldr: Experiments find that instruction tuning can teach response style while degrading factual knowledge and increasing hallucinations.

title: A Closer Look at the Limitations of Instruction Tuning

abstract: State-of-the-art language models can exhibit reasoning refinement capabilities on math, science or coding tasks. However, recent work demonstrates that even the best models struggle to identify when and where to refine without access to external feedback. In this paper, we propose Stepwise ORMs (SORMs) which are trained, only on synthetic data, to approximate the expected future reward of the optimal policy or $V^{\star}$ as a form of Process-based reward modeling. Our experiments show that SORMs can more accurately detect incorrect reasoning steps compared to ORMs, thus enabling them to give precise step-level feedback to refinement models. We then train global refinement models, which take only the question and a draft solution as input and predict a corrected solution, and local refinement models which also take as input a critique indicating the location of the first reasoning error. We generate training data for both models synthetically by reusing data used to train the SORM. We find combining global and local refinements, using the ORM as a reranker, significantly outperforms either one individually, as well as a best of three sample baseline. With this strategy we can improve the accuracy of a LLaMA-2 13B model (already fine-tuned with RL) on GSM8K from 53% to 65% when greedily sampled.

We find combining global and local refinements, using the ORM as a reranker, significantly outperforms either one individually, as well as a best of three sample baseline. With this strategy we can improve the accuracy of a LLaMA-2 13B model (already fine-tuned with RL) on GSM8K from 53% to 65% when greedily sampled.

paragraphs: Language models can revise reasoning, but deciding when revision is needed and where an error begins remains difficult without external feedback. GLoRe addresses this diagnosis problem with Stepwise Outcome Reward Models, or SORMs. These models use synthetic training data to approximate the expected future reward of an optimal policy.

The experiments find that SORMs locate incorrect reasoning steps more accurately than outcome reward models. This feedback supports two kinds of correction: a global refiner receives a question and draft answer, while a local refiner also receives a critique identifying the first reasoning error. Both refiners use synthetic training examples generated by reusing the data employed for SORM training.

Combining global and local corrections with an outcome reward model for reranking significantly outperforms either correction method alone and a best-of-three sampling baseline. On GSM8K, this strategy raises greedy-sampling accuracy for an already reinforcement-learning-finetuned LLaMA-2 13B model from 53% to 65%. The finding supports pairing error localization with complementary revision strategies.
summary.tldr: GLoRe combines step-level error feedback, global revision, and local correction to improve language-model reasoning accuracy.

title: GLoRe: When, Where, and How to Improve LLM Reasoning via Global and Local Refinements

abstract: On-device training is currently the most common approach for training machine learning (ML) models on private, distributed user data. Despite this, on-device training has several drawbacks: (1) most user devices are too small to train large models on-device, (2) on-device training is communication- and computation-intensive, and (3) on-device training can be difficult to debug and deploy. To address these problems, we propose Private Evolution-Text (PrE-Text), a method for generating differentially private (DP) synthetic textual data. First, we show that across multiple datasets, training small models (models that fit on user devices) with PrE-Text synthetic data outperforms small models trained on-device under practical privacy regimes ($\epsilon=1.29$, $\epsilon=7.58$). We achieve these results while using 9$\times$ fewer rounds, 6$\times$ less client computation per round, and 100$\times$ less communication per round. Second, finetuning large models on PrE-Text’s DP synthetic data improves large language model (LLM) performance on private data across the same range of privacy budgets. Altogether, these results suggest that training on DP synthetic data can be a better option than training a model on-device on private distributed data. Code is available at https://github.com/houcharlie/PrE-Text.

paragraphs: Private user data are often distributed across devices that have limited capacity for model training. Training on those devices also requires computation, communication, and deployment effort. PrE-Text addresses these issues by generating differentially private synthetic text that can subsequently be used to train language models.

The reported results use nine times fewer rounds, six times less client computation per round, and one hundred times less communication per round. These comparisons connect predictive performance to the operational costs of using distributed private data.

This extends the approach beyond models small enough to fit on user devices. Taken together, the results suggest that differentially private synthetic text can be a better training option than on-device learning under the evaluated conditions.
summary.tldr: PrE-Text generates differentially private synthetic text that improves evaluated model performance while sharply reducing client training and communication costs.

title: PrE-Text: Training Language Models on Private Federated Data in the Age of LLMs

abstract: Group Equivariant CNNs (G-CNNs) have shown promising efficacy in various tasks, owing to their ability to capture hierarchical features in an equivariant manner. However, their equivariance is fixed to the symmetry of the whole group, limiting adaptability to diverse partial symmetries in real-world datasets, such as limited rotation symmetry of handwritten digit images and limited color-shift symmetry of flower images. Recent efforts address this limitation, one example being Partial G-CNN which restricts the output group space of convolution layers to break full equivariance. However, such an approach still fails to adjust equivariance levels across data. In this paper, we propose a novel approach, Variational Partial G-CNN (VP G-CNN), to capture varying levels of partial equivariance specific to each data instance. VP G-CNN redesigns the distribution of the output group elements to be conditioned on input data, leveraging variational inference to avoid overfitting. This enables the model to adjust its equivariance levels according to the needs of individual data points. Additionally, we address training instability inherent in discrete group equivariance models by redesigning the reparametrizable distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of VP G-CNN on both toy and real-world datasets, including MNIST67-180, CIFAR10, ColorMNIST, and Flowers102. Our results show robust performance, even in uncertainty metrics.

paragraphs: Group-equivariant convolutional networks build in structured responses to transformations such as rotations or color shifts. Real data may support only some of those transformations, and the appropriate degree of symmetry can vary between examples. A fixed symmetry group, or a single fixed restriction of it, cannot fully express that variation.

VP G-CNN makes partial equivariance depend on the input. It conditions the distribution of output group elements on each data instance, allowing different examples to receive different levels of equivariance. Variational inference is used to avoid overfitting. The authors also redesign the reparameterizable distribution to address training instability in models with discrete group equivariance.

Experiments cover toy and real-world datasets, including MNIST67-180, CIFAR10, ColorMNIST, and Flowers102. The authors report robust performance, including on uncertainty metrics. The contribution is an adaptive treatment of symmetry: the model can learn how much rotational or color-shift structure is appropriate for an individual input instead of applying the same equivariance level throughout the dataset.
summary.tldr: VP G-CNN learns input-specific levels of rotation and color-shift equivariance using a variational approach.

title: Variational Partial Group Convolutions for Input-Aware Partial Equivariance of Rotations and Color-Shifts

abstract: Graph Attention Networks (GATs) are designed to provide flexible neighborhood aggregation that assigns weights to neighbors according to their importance. In practice, however, GATs are often unable to switch off task-irrelevant neighborhood aggregation, as we show experimentally and analytically. To address this challenge, we propose GATE, a GAT extension that holds three major advantages: i) It alleviates over-smoothing by addressing its root cause of unnecessary neighborhood aggregation. ii) Similarly to perceptrons, it benefits from higher depth as it can still utilize additional layers for (non-)linear feature transformations in case of (nearly) switched-off neighborhood aggregation. iii) By down-weighting connections to unrelated neighbors, it often outperforms GATs on real-world heterophilic datasets. To further validate our claims, we construct a synthetic test bed to analyze a model’s ability to utilize the appropriate amount of neighborhood aggregation, which could be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Graph Attention Networks assign different importance weights to neighboring nodes when combining information. However, choosing which neighbors matter does not necessarily provide enough control over whether neighborhood information should be used at all. The paper shows analytically and experimentally that these networks often struggle to suppress aggregation that is irrelevant to the task.

GATE extends graph attention to address this unnecessary mixing. By reducing contributions from unrelated neighbors, it alleviates over-smoothing, where repeated aggregation makes node representations less distinct. It also allows additional layers to remain useful when aggregation is almost or entirely switched off: those layers can still transform each node’s features through linear or nonlinear operations.

The reported results show that GATE often outperforms GATs on real-world heterophilic datasets, where connected nodes can be dissimilar. The authors also construct a synthetic test bed for studying how well models select the appropriate amount of aggregation. This directly examines the capability at the center of the proposed architectural change.
summary.tldr: GATE helps graph attention networks suppress irrelevant neighbor aggregation while retaining useful feature transformations at greater depth.

title: GATE: How to Keep Out Intrusive Neighbors

abstract: Although deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success, they often exhibit a significant deficiency in reliable uncertainty calibration. This paper focus on model calibratability, which assesses how amenable a model is to be well recalibrated post-hoc. We find that the widely used weight decay regularizer detrimentally affects model calibratability, subsequently leading to a decline in final calibration performance after post-hoc calibration. To identify the underlying causes leading to poor calibratability, we delve into the calibratability of intermediate features across the hidden layers. We observe a U-shaped trend in the calibratability of intermediate features from the bottom to the top layers, which indicates that over-compression of the top representation layers significantly hinders model calibratability. Based on the observations, this paper introduces a weak classifier hypothesis, i.e., given a weak classification head that has not been over-trained, the representation module can be better learned to produce more calibratable features. Consequently, we propose a progressively layer-peeled training (PLP) method to exploit this hypothesis, thereby enhancing model calibratability. Our comparative experiments show the effectiveness of our method, which improves model calibration and also yields competitive predictive performance.

paragraphs: A model’s confidence can be adjusted after training, but some models are easier to recalibrate than others. This paper studies that property, called calibratability. The authors find that weight decay, a widely used training regularizer, can harm calibratability and consequently worsen confidence calibration even after a separate calibration procedure has been applied.

To investigate why, they examine intermediate representations across hidden layers. They observe a U-shaped pattern in calibratability and connect poor calibratability near the top of the network with excessive representation compression. This motivates their weak classifier hypothesis: a classification head that has not been over-trained can allow the representation module to learn features that are more amenable to calibration.

The proposed progressively layer-peeled training method puts that hypothesis into practice. Comparative experiments show improved calibration alongside competitive predictive performance. The work draws attention to how representations are learned during training, because their suitability for later confidence adjustment can affect the quality of the final calibrated model.
summary.tldr: The paper links excessive representation compression to poor post-hoc calibratability and proposes training that improves calibration while maintaining competitive prediction.

title: Calibration Bottleneck: Over-compressed Representations are Less Calibratable

abstract: Stochastic natural gradient variational inference (NGVI) is a popular posterior inference method with applications in various probabilistic models. Despite its wide usage, little is known about the non-asymptotic convergence rate in the stochastic setting. We aim to lessen this gap and provide a better understanding. For conjugate likelihoods, we prove the first $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{T})$ non-asymptotic convergence rate of stochastic NGVI. The complexity is no worse than stochastic gradient descent (a.k.a. black-box variational inference) and the rate likely has better constant dependency that leads to faster convergence in practice. For non-conjugate likelihoods, we show that stochastic NGVI with the canonical parameterization implicitly optimizes a non-convex objective. Thus, a global convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{T})$ is unlikely without some significant new understanding of optimizing the ELBO using natural gradients.

For non-conjugate likelihoods, we show that stochastic NGVI with the canonical parameterization implicitly optimizes a non-convex objective. paragraphs: Stochastic natural gradient variational inference is widely used to approximate posterior distributions, yet its convergence speed under stochastic updates has been less well understood. This paper examines finite-iteration convergence guarantees, distinguishing likelihood settings in which a clear rate can be proved from those presenting a more difficult optimization problem.

For conjugate likelihoods, the authors prove an O(1/T) non-asymptotic convergence rate, where T is the iteration count. The resulting complexity is no worse than stochastic gradient descent used for black-box variational inference. They also suggest that more favorable constant dependence likely helps explain faster practical convergence; that potential advantage is qualified separately from the proved rate.

For non-conjugate likelihoods, the authors show that the canonical parameterization implicitly leads to a non-convex objective. They consequently regard a global O(1/T) guarantee as unlikely without significant new insight into optimizing the variational objective with natural gradients. The paper thus clarifies both a positive convergence result and a structural obstacle to extending it to the broader setting.
summary.tldr: Stochastic NGVI has a proved O(1/T) rate for conjugate likelihoods, while non-conjugate cases expose a non-convex optimization obstacle.

title: Understanding Stochastic Natural Gradient Variational Inference

abstract: Decisions made by machine learning models can have lasting impacts, making long-term fairness a critical consideration. It has been observed that ignoring the long-term effect and directly applying fairness criterion in static settings can actually worsen bias over time. To address biases in sequential decision-making, we introduce a long-term fairness concept named Equal Long-term Benefit Rate (ELBERT). This concept is seamlessly integrated into a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to consider the future effects of actions on long-term fairness, thus providing a unified framework for fair sequential decision-making problems. ELBERT effectively addresses the temporal discrimination issues found in previous long-term fairness notions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the policy gradient of Long-term Benefit Rate can be analytically simplified to standard policy gradients. This simplification makes conventional policy optimization methods viable for reducing bias, leading to our bias mitigation approach ELBERT-PO. Extensive experiments across various diverse sequential decision-making environments consistently reveal that ELBERT-PO significantly diminishes bias while maintaining high utility. Code is available at https://github.com/umd-huang-lab/ELBERT.

paragraphs: A decision can affect both a person's immediate outcome and the opportunities they encounter later. This paper addresses the resulting fairness problem: a rule that appears fair when decisions are evaluated separately can worsen bias over time. The authors therefore evaluate fairness through the longer-term effects of a sequence of actions.

They introduce Equal Long-term Benefit Rate, or ELBERT, and incorporate it into a Markov decision process. This places the fairness objective inside a model that accounts for future consequences. The proposed concept addresses temporal discrimination issues identified in earlier long-term fairness notions, making the timing and accumulation of benefits part of the decision-making framework.

The authors also show that the policy gradient of the long-term benefit rate can be simplified into standard policy gradients. This makes conventional policy optimization usable for their mitigation method, ELBERT-PO. Across the sequential decision environments studied, the method substantially reduces bias while retaining high utility. The findings support both the usefulness of the fairness concept and the practicality of optimizing it.
summary.tldr: ELBERT turns long-term fairness into an optimizable sequential decision objective and reduces bias while preserving high utility in the reported experiments.

title: Adapting Static Fairness to Sequential Decision-Making: Bias Mitigation Strategies towards Equal Long-term Benefit Rate

abstract: Training autonomous agents with sparse rewards is a long-standing problem in online reinforcement learning (RL), due to low data efficiency. Prior work overcomes this challenge by extracting useful knowledge from offline data, often accomplished through the learning of action distribution from offline data and utilizing the learned distribution to facilitate online RL. However, since the offline data are given and fixed, the extracted knowledge is inherently limited, making it difficult to generalize to new tasks. We propose a novel approach that leverages offline data to learn a generative diffusion model, coined as Adaptive Trajectory Diffuser (ATraDiff). This model generates synthetic trajectories, serving as a form of data augmentation and consequently enhancing the performance of online RL methods. The key strength of our diffuser lies in its adaptability, allowing it to effectively handle varying trajectory lengths and mitigate distribution shifts between online and offline data. Because of its simplicity, ATraDiff seamlessly integrates with a wide spectrum of RL methods. Empirical evaluation shows that ATraDiff consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across a variety of environments, with particularly pronounced improvements in complicated settings. Our code and demo video are available at https://atradiff.github.io.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, an agent may need many interactions before receiving useful feedback. Offline data can help online reinforcement learning, but approaches that extract an action distribution from a fixed dataset have limited knowledge to draw on. This can make transferring that knowledge to new tasks difficult.

Adaptive Trajectory Diffuser, or ATraDiff, learns a diffusion model from offline data and uses it to generate synthetic trajectories. These generated sequences augment the data available to online learning methods. The approach therefore uses offline experience as material for a trajectory generator, giving the learning process additional sequences to train with.

Adaptability is central to the design: ATraDiff handles different trajectory lengths and mitigates shifts between offline and online data distributions. The authors describe it as easy to integrate with a broad range of reinforcement learning methods. Across the evaluated environments, it consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with especially pronounced improvements in complicated settings. These findings support synthetic trajectory generation as a practical way to improve data efficiency in the studied online learning problems.
summary.tldr: ATraDiff generates adaptable synthetic trajectories from offline data to improve online reinforcement learning, particularly in complicated sparse-reward settings.

title: ATraDiff: Accelerating Online Reinforcement Learning with Imaginary Trajectories

abstract: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and its variants have shown remarkable performance in scenarios characterized by a scarcity of labeled data during the training phase of machine learning models. Despite these successes, MAMLbased approaches encounter significant challenges when there is a substantial discrepancy in the distribution of training and testing tasks, resulting in inefficient learning and limited generalization across domains. Inspired by classical proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control theory, this study introduces a Layer-Adaptive PID (LA-PID) Optimizer, a MAML-based optimizer that employs efficient parameter optimization methods to dynamically adjust task-specific PID control gains at each layer of the network, conducting a first-principles analysis of optimal convergence conditions. A series of experiments conducted on four standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the LA-PID optimizer, indicating that LA-PID achieves state-oftheart performance in few-shot classification and cross-domain tasks, accomplishing these objectives with fewer training steps. Code is available on https://github.com/yuguopin/LA-PID.
