paragraphs: Generating a molecule for a protein pocket involves two linked choices: where to place it and how to arrange its internal three-dimensional structure. Existing diffusion approaches perturb both together in a large joint space. DeCoDe separates their diffusion processes to make exploration of placement and molecular shape more effective.

During the forward noising process, DeCoDe emphasizes disruption of the molecule’s internal conformation early, then increases disruption of its global binding position later. Reversing this schedule gives generation a useful order: the model first establishes a rough location inside the pocket and then refines the molecule’s detailed structure. The scheduling change organizes the two tasks into a staged generation process.

On CrossDocked2020, the authors report an average 18% improvement in structural fidelity relative to state-of-the-art baselines, while binding affinity and overall molecular properties remain competitive. The reported advantage is therefore strongest for structural quality, rather than a claimed improvement on every molecular criterion. The findings support separating placement from conformation as a useful design choice for diffusion-based ligand generation.
summary.tldr: DeCoDe separates ligand placement from shape refinement, improving structural fidelity while maintaining competitive binding affinity and molecular properties.

title: DeCoDe: Decoupling Binding Position and Molecular Conformation in 3D Ligand Diffusion for Structure-Based Drug Design

abstract: Digital watermarking is essential for securing generated images from diffusion models. Accurate watermark evaluation is critical for algorithm development, yet existing methods have significant limitations: they lack a unified framework for both residual and semantic watermarks, provide results without interpretability, neglect comprehensive security considerations, and often use inappropriate metrics for semantic watermarks. To address these gaps, we propose WMVLM, the first unified and interpretable evaluation framework for diffusion model image watermarking via vision-language models (VLMs). We redefine quality and security metrics for each watermark type: residual watermarks are evaluated by artifact strength and erasure resistance, while semantic watermarks are assessed through latent distribution shifts. Moreover, we introduce a three-stage training strategy to progressively enable the model to achieve classification, scoring, and interpretable text generation. Experiments show WMVLM outperforms state-of-the-art VLMs with strong generalization across datasets, diffusion models, and watermarking methods.

paragraphs: Image-watermark evaluation needs to assess both quality and security, while accounting for different watermark types. WMVLM provides a unified framework based on vision-language models that also generates interpretable explanations. It addresses evaluation practices that use unsuitable measures for semantic watermarks or return scores without explaining their meaning.

The framework assigns different criteria to the two watermark categories. Residual watermarks are assessed through artifact strength and resistance to erasure, while semantic watermarks are assessed through shifts in latent distributions. This distinction lets the evaluation reflect how each type is represented instead of forcing both into the same measurement scheme.

A three-stage training strategy progressively develops classification, scoring, and explanatory text generation. Experiments show that WMVLM outperforms state-of-the-art vision-language models and generalizes strongly across datasets, diffusion models, and watermarking methods. The reported contribution is an evaluator that combines type-appropriate assessment with readable explanations, making its judgments more informative for watermark development while incorporating security alongside image quality.
summary.tldr: WMVLM evaluates residual and semantic image watermarks with type-specific quality and security measures while generating interpretable explanations.

title: WMVLM: Evaluating Diffusion Model Image Watermarking via Vision-Language Models

abstract: In this position paper, we argue that human-centric vision requires skeletal-topology generalization beyond fixed skeletons. Mainstream pose and body pipelines enforce a fixed skeleton graph with an indexed joint list and fixed adjacency, so the fixed joint inventory does not cover structural absence and anatomical absence becomes an ill-posed target for individuals with limb deficiencies. Anatomical absence is not a visibility state, so masking and forced completion can hide structural mismatch and produce hallucinated structure that contaminates downstream reasoning in prosthesis-facing settings. We argue that scaling data and model size alone does not resolve this mismatch while the skeleton schema remains fixed, and this is not a niche concern because these failures affect a large population and reach accessibility-facing systems. We advocate instance-adaptive skeletal topology, where a model estimates anatomical existence and exposes valid connectivity, either by predicting edges directly or deriving them from explicit structural rules, to produce an instance-specific skeleton graph that supports consistent inference and evaluation. We outline measurement upgrades, including existence-aware annotations with explicit absence semantics, skeletal-topology-aware scoring, and hallucination-under-absence penalties, and we close with a call to action for dataset curators, benchmark organizers, and model builders to treat morphological variation as a first-class generalization axis.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that human pose systems need to accommodate differences in anatomical structure. Many pipelines assume a fixed list of joints and fixed connections between them. For people with limb deficiencies, that representation can demand predictions for anatomy that does not exist, making the prediction target itself inappropriate.

The authors distinguish anatomical absence from a body part merely being out of view. Masking or completing a fixed skeleton can conceal this difference and introduce invented structure into later reasoning, including prosthesis-related applications. They argue that larger models and more data alone cannot repair the mismatch while the underlying skeletal representation remains fixed.

Their proposed direction is a skeleton that adapts to each individual: estimate which anatomical elements exist, then expose valid connections through predicted edges or explicit structural rules. They also call for annotations that represent absence explicitly, scoring that accounts for skeletal structure, and penalties for hallucinating absent anatomy. These changes would make morphological variation part of both model design and evaluation.
summary.tldr: Human pose systems should adapt skeletal structure to each person and explicitly distinguish absent anatomy from hidden anatomy.

abstract: Conditional Random Fields (CRFs; Lafferty, McCallum, & Pereira, 2001) provide a flexible and powerful model for learning to assign labels to elements of sequences in such applications as part-of-speech tagging, text-to-speech mapping, protein and DNA sequence analysis, and information extraction from web pages. However, existing learning algorithms are slow, particularly in problems with large numbers of potential input features. This paper describes a new method for training CRFs by applying Friedman's (1999) gradient tree boosting method. In tree boosting, the CRF potential functions are represented as weighted sums of regression trees. Regression trees are learned by stage-wise optimizations similar to Adaboost, but with the objective of maximizing the conditional likelihood P(Y|X) of the CRF model. By growing regression trees, interactions among features are introduced only as needed, so although the parameter space is potentially immense, the search algorithm does not explicitly consider the large space. As a result, gradient tree boosting scales linearly in the order of the Markov model and in the order of the feature interactions, rather than exponentially like previous algorithms based on iterative scaling and gradient descent.

This paper describes a new method for training CRFs by applying Friedman's (1999) gradient tree boosting method. In tree boosting, the CRF potential functions are represented as weighted sums of regression trees. Regression trees are learned by stage-wise optimizations similar to Adaboost, but with the objective of maximizing the conditional likelihood P(Y|X) of the CRF model. By growing regression trees, interactions among features are introduced only as needed, so although the parameter space is potentially immense, the search algorithm does not explicitly consider the large space. As a result, gradient tree boosting scales linearly in the order of the Markov model and in the order of the feature interactions, rather than exponentially like previous algorithms based on iterative scaling and gradient descent.

paragraphs: Conditional random fields assign labels to sequence elements, but training can become slow when many input features are available. This paper proposes training CRFs with gradient tree boosting. The aim is to handle a potentially enormous feature space without explicitly searching through all possible feature interactions.

The method represents CRF potential functions as weighted sums of regression trees. It builds the trees through successive optimization stages that maximize the model's conditional likelihood of labels given inputs. As trees grow, they introduce feature interactions only where needed, allowing the representation to become more expressive through the training process.

The stated scaling result concerns the order of the Markov model and the order of feature interactions. Gradient tree boosting scales linearly in those quantities, compared with exponential scaling for the earlier iterative-scaling and gradient-descent approaches described in the abstract. This matters because richer sequence dependencies and interactions can otherwise make training expensive. The contribution is a training representation and search strategy that avoids explicitly considering the full potential parameter space.
summary.tldr: Gradient tree boosting trains CRFs by adding feature interactions as needed, with linear scaling in Markov order and interaction order.

title: Training conditional random fields via gradient tree boosting

abstract: Reinforcement learning deals with learning optimal or near optimal policies while interacting with the environment. Application domains with many continuous variables are difficult to solve with existing reinforcement learning methods due to the large search space. In this paper, we use a relational representation to define powerful abstractions that allow us to incorporate domain knowledge and re-use previously learned policies in other similar problems. We also describe how to learn useful actions from human traces using a behavioural cloning approach combined with an exploration phase. Since several conflicting actions may be induced for the same abstract state, reinforcement learning is used to learn an optimal policy over this reduced space. It is shown experimentally how a combination of behavioural cloning and reinforcement learning using a relational representation is powerful enough to learn how to fly an aircraft through different points in space and different turbulence conditions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses reinforcement learning in environments with many continuous variables, where searching for a good policy can be difficult. It uses a relational representation to create abstractions that incorporate domain knowledge. These abstractions also allow previously learned policies to be reused in similar problems, connecting the representation to both search reduction and reuse.

Useful actions are learned from human demonstrations through behavioral cloning combined with an exploration phase. Demonstrations can suggest conflicting actions for the same abstract state, so copying them alone does not settle every decision. Reinforcement learning then learns an optimal policy over the reduced space, selecting among the actions made available through this process.

Experiments demonstrate learning to fly an aircraft through different points in space and under different turbulence conditions. The result supports the combined method in those flight tasks. Its central contribution is the interaction of the components: relational abstraction reduces the decision space, human traces supply useful actions, and reinforcement learning resolves choices that the demonstrations leave ambiguous.
summary.tldr: Relational abstractions, human demonstrations, and reinforcement learning combine to learn aircraft control across different spatial targets and turbulence conditions.

title: Learning to fly by combining reinforcement learning with behavioural cloning

abstract: We consider a dynamic market-place of self-interested agents with differingcapabilities. A task to be completed is proposed to the agent population. Anagent attempts to form a coalition of agents to perform the task. Beforeproposing a coalition, the agent must determine the optimal set of agents withwhom to enter into a coalition for this task; we refer to this activity ascoalition calculation. To determine the optimal coalition, the agent must havea means of calculating the value of any given coalition. Multiple metrics(cost, time, quality etc.) determine the true value of a coalition. However,because of conflicting metrics, differing metric importance and the tendencyof metric importance to vary over time, it is difficult to obtain a truevaluation of a given coalition. Previous work has not addressed these issues.We present a solution based on the adaptation of a multi-objectiveoptimization evolutionary algorithm. In order to obtain a true valuation ofany coalition, we use the concept of Pareto dominance coupled with a distanceweighting algorithm. We determine the Pareto optimal set of coalitions andthen use an instance-based learning algorithm to select the optimal coalition.We show through empirical evaluation that the proposed technique is capable ofeliciting metric importance and adapting to metric variation over time.

paragraphs: The paper studies how an agent should choose collaborators for a task in a changing marketplace of self-interested agents. Candidate coalitions differ in capabilities and must be assessed using several criteria, such as cost, completion time, and quality. Choosing a coalition is difficult because these criteria can conflict and their relative importance can change over time.

The proposed method adapts an evolutionary algorithm for multi-objective optimization. It combines Pareto dominance with a distance weighting method to evaluate coalitions. Pareto comparison identifies tradeoffs among the criteria: a candidate cannot simply be preferred because it improves one measure while sacrificing another. The method determines a Pareto-optimal set before making its final selection.

An instance-based learning algorithm then selects the optimal coalition from that set. This separates the search for competitive tradeoffs from learning which tradeoff is preferred. Empirical evaluation shows that the technique can elicit the importance of different metrics and adapt when that importance changes. The reported result addresses evolving preferences in coalition selection, alongside the problem of finding capable collaborators.
summary.tldr: A multi-objective evolutionary method and instance-based learning select coalitions while adapting to changes in the importance of competing criteria.
